World.title: Why are fewer Mexicans having children? Financial strain, security concerns and fears for the future
World.content:
Mexico’s national statistics agency, INEGI, recently released the results of the 2025 Intercensal Survey, showing that the country’s population has surpassed 130 million. The findings also reveal a striking trend: fertility rates have fallen considerably nationwide, with Mexico City recording the lowest rate, at just 0.8 children per woman.

Mexican families have changed over the decades. In earlier generations, larger families were more common, partly because of limited access to contraception and family planning services, lower levels of education among women and a more rigid division of labor. Men were generally seen as breadwinners, while women handled most household and caregiving responsibilities.

In an exploratory survey conducted by Mexico News Daily, 13 of 35 respondents said they did not want children. Participants were men and women ages 25 to 35 who were single, in relationships or married, and lived in nine cities: Mexico City, Toluca, Monterrey, Querétaro, León, Ensenada, Cancún, Guanajuato and San Miguel de Allende. They were contacted through social media and asked one open question: “Do you want to have children? Please explain your answer.” The sample is not nationally representative, but it highlights recurring concerns: insufficient income, housing, public safety, health, the climate crisis and the lack of a stable partner.

Financial strain and absent support systems

Luis, 34, lives in Querétaro with his girlfriend. He explained why he has not considered having children:

“I had a privileged upbringing. I went to private school, had enough to eat and never lacked anything. But today, I can’t provide those things for someone else, so bringing a child into the world feels unfair. There’s no guarantee of a stable future, either. My job doesn’t guarantee a steady income or the pay raises I would need to live without financial hardship. And the outlook is bleak: water shortages, housing problems, rising costs and so on.

“Another issue is that we both work, and our families live in Toluca, so we don’t have a support network to help us care for our children. We would have to rely on daycare and extracurricular activities, which would mean additional expenses. Finally, I don’t want to repeat the way I was raised. I had everything I needed materially, but not emotionally, and I’m not ready to break those patterns yet.”

Of the 22 respondents who said they wanted children or were considering having them in the future, some said they had not yet found a stable partner or wanted to become more financially secure first. Three people in this group reported health or fertility problems that had prevented them from conceiving.

Vanesa, 29, lives in San Miguel de Allende and has been married for two years.

“Yes, I want to have children, but first I would like to own a home so I can feel more secure,” she said. “I’m also afraid of global warming. I worry that by the time my child is 15, there could be a water crisis.”

Reasons behind decisions to remain child-free

The 13 respondents who did not want children cited financial pressures, insecurity in Mexico and global problems as their main reasons. Many said they did not earn enough to support a family. Others felt that conditions in the country would make it difficult to raise children in a healthy, safe environment. Wars, global warming and water shortages also influenced their decisions. A smaller number said they did not feel ready to become parents or lacked the patience or skills to care for a baby.

Milé, 34, is single and originally from Querétaro.

“I don’t think I have the skills or resources to be a mother,” she said. “Finding a man my age who wants to share that responsibility would also require me to be honest with myself and able to contribute equally. My jobs haven’t provided social security coverage, either, and I wouldn’t have the financial means to support children. I think bringing children into the world under these conditions would be selfish and irresponsible.”

Respondents who already had one or two children said that number was enough to provide a decent standard of living and, above all, give their children the attention they deserved. Some mothers said they did not want to experience pregnancy and its hormonal changes again because of the physical toll. Fathers said their incomes barely covered the cost of raising one or two children.

One respondent pointed to limited living space, describing a three-bedroom home with one room for the parents and one for each of two children. Housing constraints were another reason not to have more children. Some respondents also said that both parents needed to earn an income to support the family, making a return to paid work an economic priority for mothers.

Why parents are stopping at two children

Paul, 31, is married, has two children and lives in León. He explained why he and his wife decided not to have more:

“My wife and I decided to stop at two children, and it wasn’t a decision we took lightly. When you imagine starting a family, you often don’t think about numbers, square footage, school fees or how many chicken nuggets fit on a baking tray. You just think, ‘I want a lovely family.’ Then adulthood comes along and says, ‘Yes, that’s lovely. Now do the math.’

“That’s when we began to realize that having children involves much more than loving them with all your heart. There’s food, clothing, school, doctors, activities, vacations, birthdays, toys, transportation and all those little things that stop being little once you have children.

“We want to give our children a good life, but we also want some financial peace of mind rather than constantly calculating how to make it to the end of the month. We also believe that having two children allows us to give them time, attention and energy in a way that works for our family. We don’t want more children simply because there’s ‘room’ for them. We want to enjoy the children we have, support them, watch them grow, be present and give them the best we can within our means.”

Raising a family of four

How much money does a family of four need to live in Mexico?

The answer depends on where the family lives and its lifestyle. For this report, we focused on five of the cities where respondents lived: Mexico City, Querétaro, León, Monterrey and San Miguel de Allende.

Drawing on the National Household Income and Expenditure Survey (ENIGH), labor-market information from Data México and reference prices, Mexico News Daily estimated that a family of four living in an owner-occupied home in these cities needs between 29,500 and 48,000 Mexican pesos per month. This budget covers everyday needs such as food, clothing, public school expenses, transportation, personal hygiene products, utilities, communications and health care, while setting aside money for emergencies.

The following table breaks down expenses by category and compares costs across the five cities included in this article. Monterrey has the highest basic utility costs, while León has the lowest overall costs among the cities examined.

How do average wages compare?

Data México reports average monthly earnings in these cities, including both formal and informal employment.

The comparison reveals a gap between average earnings and the estimated budget for a family of four. Even two average incomes combined fall short of the amount needed to cover the projected expenses and save for emergencies. To make up the difference, some families seek additional income by selling products through catalogs or preparing food for sale. Others cut spending on health care, food and recreation.

Insecurity in Mexico

Safety concerns weighing on parents

Eduardo and Ana are married but have not yet decided whether to have children. They live in Metepec and regularly travel to Toluca for work.

“I don’t want children for one simple reason: insecurity,” Eduardo said. “The country gets worse every year, and more people go missing every day. If I’m already worried about the situation, I can’t imagine being responsible for a little person. I would rather avoid that worry.”

Perceptions of insecurity also emerged among respondents’ reasons for not having children. The 2026 National Survey of Victimization and Perceptions of Public Security (ENVIPE) does not measure an individual’s risk of becoming a crime victim, nor does it replace crime-rate data. It does, however, show that 74% of adults considered their state unsafe during the survey period.

The highest proportions were recorded in Estado de Mexico, at 90%; Morelos, at 88.7%; Tabasco, at 87.6%; Guanajuato, at 85.9%; and Puebla, at 83.3%. The lowest were in Coahuila, at 27.8%; Yucatán, at 35.5%; and Aguascalientes, at 41%.

Rising crime and missing persons statistics

The 2026 ENVIPE, which covers crimes committed in 2025, reported the highest estimated crime incidence rates in Mexico City, at 68,154 crimes per 100,000 inhabitants; Puebla, at 41,876; and Mexico State, at 40,915. The survey’s crime categories included theft and robbery, fraud, extortion, threats, assault, kidnapping and sexual offenses.

According to a report by the Mexican Institute for Human Rights and Democracy (IMDHD), Mexico’s national missing persons registry listed 134,257 people as missing as of May 16, 2026. That number rose to 135,048 by June 16. The report recorded 12,632 disappearances in 2024 and 12,373 in 2025, and indicated that the trend in 2026 pointed toward similarly high numbers.

As of May 16, 2026, the five states with the largest cumulative numbers of registered missing persons were Mexico State, with 14,648; Tamaulipas, with 13,787; Jalisco, with 12,765; Michoacán, with 7,782; and Nuevo León, with 7,476. Together, they accounted for 42% of the national total, according to Red Lupa’s analysis of the National Registry of Missing and Unlocated Persons (RNPDNO).

Mexico recorded 11,586 victims of intentional homicide from January through August 2026, according to figures reported by the federal Security Cabinet and the Executive Secretariat of the National Public Security System. Although President Claudia Sheinbaum highlighted a decline in homicides earlier in the year, safety concerns remain part of many Mexicans’ daily lives.

Motherhood as a choice

The evolution of women’s roles

Women have always worked and played an important role in society. The Industrial Revolution, which began in the mid-18th century, expanded their participation in factory work and paid employment. During World War I and World War II, their roles in industry became even more prominent as many filled jobs left by men who had gone to fight.

Over time, advances in labor rights, greater access to higher education and the availability of contraception expanded women’s opportunities and their ability to make decisions about their lives, including whether to become mothers, when to have children and how many to have.

Motherhood is now a choice, not an obligation. Women may pursue a career, raise a family or do both. For some of the mothers interviewed, returning to work was both a financial necessity and a professional choice.

Personal perspectives on motherhood and career breaks

Zayra, 32, lives in Monterrey with her husband and their two children.

“At first, I only wanted one child so I could give them the attention and care they needed for their development. But six months later, I became pregnant again,” she said. “It was a shock because I didn’t know how I would manage twice the expenses. I had my second child, but I decided to undergo sterilization so I wouldn’t have any more.

“I made that decision because I struggled badly with hormonal changes during both pregnancies, and there were concerns about preeclampsia. Having children is the most beautiful thing that can happen to you, but it’s also a lot of work and very tiring. Finances also play a role in deciding not to have another child.”

Kiev, 32, is from Querétaro, married, and has two daughters.

“Yes, I’ve thought about having one more, but I’ve practically ruled it out, mainly for financial reasons. Babies are very expensive,” she said. “On top of that, my house only has two bedrooms, and we would need to expand it sooner to live more comfortably.

“Then there’s the career break I’m taking. I wanted to look after the house and the babies myself, with the intention of returning to work once they’re a little older. Having another baby would add more years to that break.”

Rejecting social scripts and facing future challenges

Marcela, 34, lives in Querétaro with her partner and has decided not to have children.

“I don’t like children. I’ve never known how to interact with them or spend time with them, so having one seems strange to me, and I find it difficult to play with them. I don’t have a maternal instinct,” she said.

“I also don’t want to feel obligated to follow a social script of getting married and having children. I firmly believe children should be fully wanted and planned for, not something you have ‘just because’ or because it’s the next step.

“The third reason is the situation in Mexico and the world in general. The thought that having a child would mean never feeling at ease again because of the country we live in and its insecurity — especially if the child were a girl — is a major factor.

Wages, security and the environment

“There’s also the economic situation. Wages make things difficult, and building financial security keeps getting harder. Add the environmental situation, the wars happening now and tensions with the United States, and I can’t picture a bright future for a child.”

Declining fertility poses long-term challenges for Mexico. An aging population will require more health care, caregiving services and sustainable social protection systems. But the answer is not to pressure people into having more children. For those who want to start a family, the challenge is to create conditions that make raising children compatible with stable earnings, affordable housing, childcare, safety, reproductive health care and a more equitable division of caregiving responsibilities.

The interviews in this report do not represent Mexico’s entire population, but they reveal a shared tension. For many people, the question is no longer simply whether they want children, but whether they can have them without sacrificing their stability, health, careers or peace of mind.

María Ruiz is the Director of Digital Marketing at Mexico News Daily. She enjoys photographing her hometown of San Miguel de Allende in her spare time.

World.title: Spider-Man 2099 has a Día de Muertos secret in his origin story
World.content:
There may not be another superhero who is more globally renowned or imitated than Spider-Man (sorry, Superman and Batman, but you can sit this one out).

In my neighborhood’s main square, there is a man who regularly dresses up as Spider-Man and web-thwips his way into photos for a few pesos. Driving around Mexico, I’ve seen motorcyclists wearing Spider-Man-themed helmets. There’s even an official spinoff Spider-Man character, nicknamed Arácnido Jr., who hails from Mexico City and has a luchador father.

Just learned that Marvel has a Mexican Spider-Man named Arácnido Jr. who is the son of a luchador & protects Mexico City. He appeared in one of the “Spider-Verse” comics & was created by Enrique Puig & Francisco Herrera. He’s been around since 2015. Can’t believe I didn’t know 🇲🇽 https://t.co/h38pTyT9m8 — Carlos Aguilar (@Carlos_Film) August 2, 2020

It’s not just Mexicans who love El Hombre Araña, though. Right now, Spider-Man is at an all-time commercial high.

“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” has been the most commercially successful blockbuster of the year so far. As of writing, the movie has generated more than US $923 million globally, beating out “Toy Story 5” and “The Odyssey” as the highest-grossing film of 2026, to date. In July, the movie’s star cast members even visited Mexico City to promote the film.

A futuristic webslinger with Mexican roots

Add to that a newly reinvigorated generation of Spider-Man fanatics with the children’s animated series “Spidey and His Amazing Friends” — a show that currently ranks as the third-most-watched show for kids between ages 2 and 5 (including my son, who is obsessed), with billions of streaming hours on Disney+.

Across every metric, Peter Parker is a tried-and-true hit.

But what about Marvel Comics’ other Spider-Man? The one who lives in a futuristic 2099 version of New York City (creatively renamed Nueva York) and is of Mexican Irish descent? I’m talking about Miguel O’Hara.

Created by Marvel in 1992 as part of a larger effort to refresh the brand and reconfigure its legendary characters with a larger “Marvel 2099” wave of alternate-universe storylines, O’Hara is a geneticist working for a mega-wealthy corporation, Alchemax. Rather than being bitten by a radioactive spider as the original Parker is, O’Hara is researching the by-then-archaic Spider-Man of former New York City (fourth-wall meta stuff, I know) and attempting to replicate that Spider-Man’s powers for the greedy Alchemax corporation, a private entity that happens to govern the United States through its wealth and militant force.

The unusual origin of the Day of the Dead suit

Like any true superhero origin story, O’Hara is unexpectedly turned into Spider-Man 2099 when a villainous Alchemax colleague throws O’Hara into the mutation machine that is conveniently set to the original Spider-Man’s specifications. O’Hara gets zapped. He transforms. He learns how to wield his powers and manage his personal relationships across hundreds of issues. The usual.

Here’s the unusual part, though: O’Hara — or rather, his alter ego Spider-Man 2099 — is equipped with a Day of the Dead costume rather than a traditional Spider-Man onesie.

Early on, the comics (created by Peter David and Rick Leonardi) establish that not only is O’Hara of Mexican descent, but that he took a trip down to Mexico City for a “The Jetsons”-style Day of the Dead.

There are multiple allusions to it in the opening issues of the series, with a backstory that goes something like this: A pre-superpowers O’Hara returns to his mother’s homeland south of the border (her name is Conchata, and she also appears as a character early on). There, he attends a festive Day of the Dead celebration. In this dystopian future, there is a special fabric referred to as “UMF” — or Unstable Molecule Fabric, as explained in the series — that is both indestructible and highly versatile, something O’Hara deems necessary for the rowdy Día de Muertos crowds and festivities in 2099.

Dystopian fashion and geometric design

I know all of this because I ordered a 1,384-page omnibus of “Spider-Man 2099” and have been reading it for weeks.

“Only thing I own made from UMF is this death’s head costume I brought when I went to Mexico last year for the Day of the Dead festival,” O’Hara says in issue No. 2. In the background, silhouettes of festivalgoers dressed as skeletons and demons wander as he recalls: “Festival can get pretty wild. I wanted something extra sturdy.”

The suit itself is futuristically cool, for lack of a better description, though not overly Day of the Dead-themed. It features a bright red skull-like design at the center of the chest, which extends into stripes that flare down and outward in the opposite direction, wrapping around the shoulder in a shape that loosely resembles a spider’s many legs with a geometrically balanced aesthetic. The base of the suit retains a much deeper shade of blue than the original webslinger.

In all, it retains the essence of Spider-Man’s original garb, with subtle nods to Day of the Dead aesthetics.

Reincarnation and honoring the fallen heroes

O’Hara’s suit and abilities are rounded out with razor-edged retractable talons for climbing surfaces and annihilating his foes, and spikes protruding from his forearms, which seem to be a menacing suit accessory. Though not overtly Mexican or Day of the Dead in its presentation, if you squint, you can sense minor inspirations from Mexico’s Indigenous past and geometric design work.

Simple, but striking. Creative, but balanced.

The Day of the Dead theme does, however, emerge in the storyline — with additional references to Mexico, and even an entire issue titled “Day of the Dead.” In it, O’Hara takes a trip to Mexico City, where he battles zombies who have been mass-reincarnated by Fernando Morgez, a Mexican character who had hoped to revive his late sister, Anita, but brought back more than he anticipated.

Mexico’s Day of the Dead is a series undercurrent

The idea of life and death, reincarnation and honoring the deceased is an undercurrent throughout the entire series. In the 2099 timeline, the Avengers are more myth than reality, with previously indestructible characters like Thor and Peter Parker’s Spider-Man being remembered as deceased gods who are revered and worshiped by cultish hordes of followers.

That is, the world’s heroes of yesterday have fallen, and the living must find ways to cope with that remaining void.

In that sense, the series certainly has touches of Mexico’s Day of the Dead — a remembrance of those who are no longer physically present, but perhaps offer spiritual hope and a connection to, if not preservation of, the past.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

BRAZIL · ELECTIONS

Published Sunday, 18 October, 2:16 p.m. ET · Source: Folha de S.Paulo, Brazil’s electoral court (TSE)

Key Facts The country Brazil, Latin America’s largest country, elects its president in a runoff on Sunday 25 October between President Lula and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro.

What changed On Sunday 18 October the electoral court (TSE) updated its data to show 2,033 voting sections with a new address for the runoff.

The numbers About 592,000 voters are affected, and 21.08% of the electorate stayed away in the first round on 4 October.

The request Lula’s coalition asked the court on Sunday to publicise the moves widely and to help voters travel.

Brazil’s electoral court (TSE) changed the voting address of 2,033 sections for the 25 October runoff, affecting about 592,000 voters, according to data it updated on Sunday 18 October. Folha de S.Paulo reported the figures at 11:27 a.m. ET.

The coalition of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Brazil’s president, asked the court the same day to publicise the moves widely before the Brazil election 2026 runoff against Flávio Bolsonaro, senator for Rio de Janeiro. A section is a polling station with its own voter list, and the Brazil runoff date is Sunday 25 October.

What the Electoral Court Changed

The TSE moved 2,033 sections to new buildings between the first round and the runoff, Folha reported. The court said voters can check their address in its Electoral Self-Service portal or in the e-Título app, its voter-ID app.

Why the Addresses Moved

The court said the changes followed storms in some regions, damage to buildings and last-minute repairs, Folha reported. It added that each local electoral zone decides, according to the buildings available, so the TSE does not order the moves centrally.

The TSE had reported a separate count of 4,352 sections as of Friday 16 October, Agência Brasil reported, and we covered it in Brazil Moves 4,352 Polling Sites for Runoff. The sources do not say how that figure relates to today’s 2,033.

What Lula’s Coalition Is Asking

Lula’s coalition, led by his Workers’ Party (PT), filed a request with the court on Sunday, Folha reported. It asked for wide publicity of the changes and for measures to help voters reach their new polling places.

The lawyers pointed to the 21.08% abstention in the first round and said many people could not vote because their polling place had moved. They argued that if the state makes voting compulsory, it must make sure voters know where to go, Folha reported. O Antagonista also reported the request.

What It Means for US Readers

A runoff this close can turn on turnout, so a dispute over how well voters were told where to vote may become part of the post-election argument. Investors in Brazilian stocks, bonds and US-listed shares should expect turnout and process questions to feed the news on the night of 25 October.

For readers following the race from the United States, the practical point is that each Brazilian voter must go to the address now on file with the electoral court.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many Brazilian voters have a new polling place for the runoff?

The TSE data updated on Sunday 18 October show 2,033 sections with a new address, affecting about 592,000 voters. The court announced a separate count of 4,352 sections on Friday 16 October.

How can voters check their polling place?

They can use the TSE Electoral Self-Service portal or the e-Título app, the electoral court’s voter-ID app. Both show the current address for the runoff.

Why did some polling places change?

The court cited storms, building damage and last-minute repairs in some regions. Each local electoral zone decides, so the TSE does not order the moves centrally.

What did Lula’s coalition ask the electoral court to do?

It asked the TSE to publicise the changes widely and to take measures that help voters travel to their new polling places. It cited the 21.08% abstention in the first round.

Brazilians vote on Sunday 25 October, between President Lula and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro. The first round took place on 4 October.

Key Facts What happened A driver struck a 67-year-old man at a pro-Lula rally in Belo Horizonte on Saturday 17 October, at about 5:31 p.m. ET (6:31 p.m. Brasília time).

The arrest Police arrested the driver in flagrante on suspicion of attempted homicide, and he was taken to a Civil Police station.

A driver ran into a 67-year-old man during a pro-Lula demonstration in Belo Horizonte on Saturday 17 October, and police arrested him on suspicion of attempted homicide. The incident, which Folha de S.Paulo reported on Sunday, came a week before the Brazil election 2026 runoff.

Belo Horizonte is the capital of Minas Gerais, one of Brazil’s most populous states. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Brazil’s president, faces Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, senator for Rio de Janeiro, in the 25 October vote.

What Police and Witnesses Report

The man was hit at about 6:31 p.m. Brasília time at the corner of Rua da Bahia and Rua Tupinambás in the city centre, Metrópoles reported. The driver of a yellow Volkswagen Up ran a red light, and a municipal guard saw it happen, according to CNN Brasil.

The driver fled without helping the victim and was caught soon afterwards by the Military Police, Metrópoles said. He was arrested in flagrante, meaning caught in the act, on suspicion of attempted homicide, the Minas Gerais Civil Police told UOL, as Folha reported.

The victim was taken to the João XXIII emergency hospital. Metrópoles reported an ankle fracture, while O Tempo spoke of foot injuries, and Folha said his overall condition had not been disclosed.

The driver told police that protesters threw water bottles and beer cans at his car and hit his wife, who was in the passenger seat. He said his children, aged 8 and 10, panicked, so he accelerated, and that he did not notice hitting anyone, CNN Brasil reported.

O Tempo said video of the moment is inconclusive about where the objects came from. The driver’s wife told police she was hit in the head and stomach, according to CNN Brasil.

Lawmaker Bella Gonçalves of Lula’s Workers’ Party (PT), who was at the rally and chairs a human rights committee, said she will ask for an investigation. She called the driver a supporter of former president Jair Bolsonaro in a video, according to Folha, but police have not said what his politics are.

Folha said pro-Lula rallies have been held across the country since the first round on 4 October. The demonstration in Belo Horizonte was a women’s rally called Mulheres com Lula, or Women with Lula.

Street incidents in the final week can shape how voters and markets read a close race. If you hold Brazilian stocks, bonds or US-listed shares of Brazilian companies, headlines about campaign security can move prices before the result is known.

What happened at the pro-Lula rally in Belo Horizonte?

A driver in a yellow Volkswagen Up struck a 67-year-old man during a pro-Lula demonstration on Saturday 17 October at about 5:31 p.m. ET. Police arrested the driver on suspicion of attempted homicide.

World.title: Sonora Cattle Exports Resume After Calf Test
World.content:
Cattle move through pens at the cattlemen’s union quarantine station in Agua Prieta, Sonora, on 24 August 2026. (Photo: USDA, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

MEXICO · CATTLE TRADE

Key Facts — The country Mexico sends feeder calves to US feedlots, and since 24 August 2026 the Douglas, Arizona crossing has taken cattle from Sonora again.

— Why it matters Douglas is the Arizona port where Sonora calves enter the United States, so a disease scare there can delay supply to American feedlots.

— Why now Mexico’s agriculture ministry said on Saturday 17 October that sores on a calf at Agua Prieta were not foot-and-mouth disease, and Sonora set exports to restart on Tuesday 20 October.

— What happened Laboratory samples tested positive for bovine papular stomatitis, a cattle disease that the ministry says is found worldwide and carries no major risk for animal health.

— The numbers One calf was affected, the result came in under 24 hours, and Sonora expects about 1,300 head a day to cross again.

— What it means for you US feedlots and beef buyers can expect the pause to end on Tuesday, if US inspectors accept the cattle at Douglas.

— Still open Whether the US Department of Agriculture comments on the restart, and whether crossings return to about 1,300 head a day.

— Power Index Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 71.4 points (October 2026 edition).

Sonora cattle exports to the United States will restart on Tuesday 20 October after Mexico’s agriculture ministry ruled out foot-and-mouth disease in a calf found with mouth sores at Agua Prieta. Laboratory tests showed bovine papular stomatitis instead, the ministry said on Saturday 17 October, describing it as a cattle disease found worldwide that carries no major risk for animal health.

For US readers, the finding clears the way for Mexican calves to reach feedlots through the Arizona port of Douglas, which the US Department of Agriculture reopened to Mexican cattle on 24 August 2026. The pause began on Friday 16 October, as our earlier report Sonora Cattle Exports Halt Over Calf Sores explained.

The restart date comes from the Sonora state government and the regional cattlemen’s union, not from a federal order. We found no statement from the US Department of Agriculture on the calf, or on the conditions for resuming crossings, by Sunday 18 October.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 with 71.4 points. Strongest pillar: economic relationships (90); weakest: state capacity & security (46). Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What Happened on Friday and Saturday

On Friday 16 October inspectors at the Agua Prieta quarantine station found a calf with sores in its mouth that was about to be exported to Douglas, Arizona. Staff of the joint Mexico-US foot-and-mouth commission took samples, and the commission ordered the animals at the station sent back to their place of origin and the premises disinfected, N+ reported.

The regional cattlemen’s union, known as UGRS, said that day it had found an animal with a lesion whose symptoms could match foot-and-mouth disease, and exports were halted as a precaution. N+ reported that the commission opened its investigation on 16 October and analyzed the samples on 17 October.

On Saturday the ministry announced the result in a statement dated 17 October. It said the laboratory confirmed the case in under 24 hours, which it said shows Senasica’s capacity for immediate diagnosis.

What the Laboratory Found

The ministry said the samples were positive for the virus of bovine papular stomatitis, a disease of worldwide distribution that it says poses no major risk for animal health. It added that Mexico has been free of foot-and-mouth disease since 1954.

On Friday the ministry’s animal health service, Senasica, had named two look-alike diseases, vesicular stomatitis and bovine papular stomatitis, as possible causes of the sores. The Saturday result points to the second, which El Universal describes as a disease that mainly affects the skin and mucous membranes of cattle.

N+, a Mexican news outlet, reported that a results report from the joint commission shows negative foot-and-mouth tests on swab and whole-blood samples and a positive test for papular stomatitis. Tribuna, a Mexican newspaper, reported that a separate commission report dated 17 October shows a negative foot-and-mouth result on a bovine serum sample using a test called ELISA 3ABC.

The commission is attached to Senasica, and its staff took the samples. The tests ran at the high-security Palo Alto laboratory in Mexico City, according to the ministry.

When Sonora Cattle Exports Resume

Sonora’s agriculture department, known as Sagarhpa, said the Agua Prieta crossing will reopen on Tuesday 20 October, on the schedule it announced on Friday. It said Senasica’s analysis found the case limited to one animal and that nothing justified keeping exports suspended.

The ministry’s Saturday statement does not give a restart date, N+ noted, although its Friday notice had said operations would resume next week once an exotic disease was ruled out. Exports through the San Jerónimo station in Chihuahua kept flowing normally during the pause, according to the same notice.

The union said the Agua Prieta station will resume after cleaning and disinfecting its facilities, which the US Department of Agriculture will verify, Excélsior reported. Excélsior put the combined flow at the two open border ports, in Chihuahua and Sonora, at about 2,500 head a day.

Diario del Yaqui, a Sonora newspaper, reported that the reopening foresees about 1,300 head a day, a volume the state says was already reached the week before the stop. The paper said the pause cost producers, buyers and truckers extra money for corrals, rescheduled shipments and delays.

What the Restart Depends On

Cattle can cross only when US inspectors accept them at Douglas. USDA’s animal health page says the port reopened on 24 August under an import protocol agreed between the two countries, and we found no US statement on whether anything changes after this case.

Our report One Infected Cow in Sonora Lands Days Before the US Reopens Its Cattle Border covers how that reopening came about. It also shows why a single animal can draw so much attention at this border.

Why the Scare Mattered

Infobae, citing the World Organisation for Animal Health, describes foot-and-mouth disease as a highly contagious viral disease of cattle, pigs, sheep and goats that does not pass to humans. A suspected case at a border crossing stops shipments even when the cause turns out to be milder.

The ministry stressed that the signs in the calf resemble those of exotic diseases that are absent from Mexico. Infobae added that a visual check was not enough, so laboratory tests were needed to settle the question.

What It Means for You

US feedlots and cattle buyers can expect the flow of Mexican calves through Douglas to return from Tuesday, if US inspectors accept the animals. At the 1,300 head a day that Sonora’s government plans, each working day lost means that many fewer Mexican calves reaching American pens.

Investors in beef and cattle should watch for a USDA statement and for the first crossings on Tuesday rather than for further disease news. Our Mexico economy outlook and Mexico in North America guides set out how farm trade fits into the wider US-Mexico relationship.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether USDA will accept cattle at Douglas on Tuesday, because no US statement on the case turned up in our checks of its animal health pages on Sunday. The restart date rests on the Sonora government and the cattlemen’s union, and no newer development was found by Sunday afternoon.

We did not see the commission’s reports ourselves, so the swab, blood and serum details come from N+ and Tribuna, which describe different sample types. The ministry’s statement does not say whether other animals from the same consignment were examined.

The sources do not say what became of the calf itself or how many animals the pause delayed. They also do not show whether crossings will reach 1,300 head a day straight away.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there foot-and-mouth disease in Mexico?

No case was found in the Agua Prieta calf, and the ministry says the animal had bovine papular stomatitis. It says Mexico has been free of foot-and-mouth disease since 1954.

When do Sonora cattle exports resume?

Sonora’s government says crossings at Agua Prieta restart on Tuesday 20 October. The date depends on US inspectors accepting cattle at Douglas, and no US statement had been found by Sunday.

What is bovine papular stomatitis?

The ministry calls it a disease of worldwide distribution that carries no major risk for animal health. El Universal says it mainly affects the skin and mucous membranes of cattle.

How many cattle cross at Agua Prieta?

Sonora expects about 1,300 head a day when crossings resume, a level it says was reached the week before the halt. Excélsior put the combined flow at the Sonora and Chihuahua ports at about 2,500 head a day.

What does it mean for US cattle buyers?

Mexican calves should again reach feedlots through Douglas if inspections go ahead on Tuesday. The pause covered the Agua Prieta station only, and Chihuahua exports kept moving.

World.title: Ecuador Priest Killed by Falling Cross
World.content:
The Malecón 2000 riverfront in Guayaquil, capital of Guayas, one of the coastal provinces under the September curfew. (Photo: Sebastian Reategui, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons)

A Catholic priest has died in Guayaquil, Ecuador, after a large wooden cross fell on him during a Mass broadcast live on social media. The Archdiocese of Guayaquil confirmed the death of Father Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari, pastor of the Perpetuo Socorro church, after the accident on Saturday 17 October 2026.

Ecuador is a popular destination for American travellers and expats, and many Ecuadorians live in the United States. The video of the Mass has been widely shared online, so many US readers may already have seen it.

We describe the facts with care and without graphic detail, out of respect for the priest and for those who knew him. Everything below comes from the archdiocese statement and the video as reported by regional media, and we say clearly what is still unknown.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Ecuador ranks 8th of 14 with 38.2 points. Strongest pillar: military means (55); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (14). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (B); 51 homicides per 100,000. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Who: Father Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari, a Redemptorist priest and pastor of the Perpetuo Socorro church

Father Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari, a Redemptorist priest and pastor of the Perpetuo Socorro church What: A large wooden cross fell on him during a Mass streamed live; the Archdiocese of Guayaquil confirmed his death

A large wooden cross fell on him during a Mass streamed live; the Archdiocese of Guayaquil confirmed his death Where: Guayaquil, Ecuador (Vicaría Centro of the archdiocese)

Guayaquil, Ecuador (Vicaría Centro of the archdiocese) When: Saturday 17 October 2026, around minute 27 of the live stream

Saturday 17 October 2026, around minute 27 of the live stream As of 18 October 2026, 15:30 GMT

What We Know

Father Sánchez Molinari belonged to the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer, whose members are known as Redemptorists. He was pastor of the Perpetuo Socorro church, which means Our Lady of Perpetual Help, in the Vicaría Centro of the Archdiocese of Guayaquil.

On Saturday 17 October 2026 he was celebrating a Mass that was broadcast live on social media. A large wooden cross mounted on the wall behind him came loose and fell on him.

File photo: interior of the Metropolitan Cathedral of Guayaquil, Ecuador. This is not the Perpetuo Socorro church. Photo: Paula Kindsvater, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

The fall occurs around minute 27 of the stream. The recording also captures the shocked reactions of worshippers in the church.

The Archdiocese of Guayaquil confirmed his death in a statement signed by Cardinal Luis Gerardo Cabrera Herrera. The statement says he “has departed to the Father’s House”.

The archdiocese also expressed its solidarity with the Redemptorist community, with his family and with his friends. That statement is the main official account available so far.

Because the Mass was streamed live, the moment reached viewers far beyond the congregation in the building. The recording has since circulated widely on social media.

Our account draws on the archdiocese statement and the footage as reported by El Tiempo, Semana, ABC Color and Vanguardia. We have not independently obtained the full text of the statement.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Guayaquil (Ecuador) Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What Is Not Known

The reports we reviewed do not give the priest’s age or the exact time of the Mass. Reports differ on where he died: one outlet says at the scene, while others say the archdiocese did not clarify.

The reason the cross came loose from the wall has not been explained. No report we reviewed says whether an investigation or a safety inspection has begun.

Funeral arrangements have not been reported. We will add them once the archdiocese or the Redemptorist community publishes them.

Until more is confirmed, any explanation for the fall would be speculation. We will not offer one, and we will update this article if official details emerge.

What It Means for Travelers and US Readers

The reports describe a single incident and do not mention a wider safety concern for visitors or other churches. We have seen no official travel guidance linked to the event.

Travellers and expats in the Guayaquil area can follow notices from the Archdiocese of Guayaquil and from local parishes. US citizens in Ecuador can also check the website of the US embassy in Quito for general updates.

Ecuadorians living in the United States may look to their own parishes and to family at home for news of memorial services. No such services have been announced in the reports we reviewed.

Our Ecuador page collects the latest reports from the country for visitors and residents. Readers can return there for further confirmed details on this story.

The story is above all a loss for a religious community, a family and a parish. For readers abroad, the clearest point is that the confirmed facts are still few.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was Father Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari?

He was a Redemptorist priest and pastor of the Perpetuo Socorro church in the Vicaría Centro of the Archdiocese of Guayaquil. The archdiocese confirmed his death in a statement signed by Cardinal Luis Gerardo Cabrera Herrera.

What happened during the Mass?

On Saturday 17 October 2026, during a Mass broadcast live on social media, a large wooden cross mounted on the wall behind him came loose and fell on him. The fall occurs around minute 27 of the stream.

Has the cause been explained?

No. The reports reviewed do not say why the cross came loose or whether an investigation or safety inspection has begun.

Is there any guidance for travellers in Ecuador?

The reports describe a single incident and mention no wider concern. Visitors can follow notices from the Archdiocese of Guayaquil, local parishes and the US embassy in Quito.

Sources: Archdiocese of Guayaquil statement, as reported by El Tiempo, Semana, ABC Color and Vanguardia. Published 18 October 2026, 15:30 GMT.

World.title: Brazil Court Rejects Novo Bid on Artist Acts
World.content:
A results screen at the Electoral Court (TSE) in Brasília shows the first-round count by state on 4 October 2026. (Photo: Agência Senado, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

BRAZIL · ELECTIONS

Published Sunday, 18 October, 9:13 a.m. ET · Source: Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court (TSE) ruling, as reported by Jovem Pan and Revista Fórum

Key Facts The country Brazil, Latin America’s largest country, elects its president in a runoff on Sunday 25 October between President Lula and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro.

What happened On Saturday 17 October, Electoral Court (TSE) minister Ricardo Villas Bôas Cueva rejected a request by the Novo party to suspend pro-democracy concerts with artists planned for Sunday 18 October.

The dispute Novo, a conservative party, argued the events were disguised campaign rallies for Lula, which Brazilian law bans, and targeted Copacabana (Rio de Janeiro), Salvador and Porto Alegre.

The ruling Cueva found no proof at this stage that the events were campaign rallies, and said artists’ political preferences alone are not an electoral offence.

Power Index Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 75.0 points (October 2026 edition).

Prediction markets Polymarket gives Flávio Bolsonaro an 80.8% chance and Lula 19.5% of winning the 25 October runoff (18 October, 9:10 a.m. ET). Polymarket puts Flávio Bolsonaro’s chance of winning at 80% and Kalshi at 80% (Lula: 20% and 21% ), as of 18 October, 1:40 pm ET ; prices are bets, not polls.

Still open The court kept the power to punish concrete violations, so the events themselves can still be reviewed.

Brazil’s electoral court has rejected a request by the Novo party to stop pro-democracy concerts with artists on Sunday 18 October, a week before the Brazil election 2026. The ruling by minister Ricardo Villas Bôas Cueva came on Saturday 17 October, according to Jovem Pan.

Novo had claimed the shows in Copacabana, Salvador and Porto Alegre were disguised campaign rallies for President Lula, which matters because court fights over campaign rules can shape the final days of the race and, with it, Brazilian markets. The Brazil election odds on Polymarket still favour Flávio Bolsonaro, the conservative senator for Rio de Janeiro.

What the Electoral Court Decided

Cueva, a minister of the Superior Electoral Court (TSE), denied Novo’s injunction request, the party’s plea for an immediate order, Jovem Pan reported.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Brazil ranks 1st of 14 with 75.0 points. Strongest pillar: military means (100); weakest: state capacity & security (56). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The minister said the public political preference of artists is not, by itself, an electoral offence, Jovem Pan reported. He added that ideological closeness between organisers and a candidate does not prove a legal, financial or organisational link.

What Novo Argued About the Concerts

Novo said the concerts amounted to “showmícios,” a Brazilian term for music shows used as campaign rallies, which the electoral law (Law 9,504 of 1997) prohibits. Revista Fórum reported the party called them “disguised” rallies.

Brazilian outlets named Caetano Veloso, Djavan and Daniela Mercury among the artists, Jovem Pan reported. The events belong to a movement called “Brasil nas Ruas” (Brazil in the Streets), organised with the 342 Artes collective.

What the Organisers Told the Court

The organiser, UNS Produções Artísticas, told the court the events would defend democracy and avoid vote requests and campaign jingles, according to Plantão Brasil. The 342 Artes collective says electoral law does not stop artists from stating political opinions, Imirante reported.

Cueva stressed that the ruling is not advance approval of the events. The court can still act if actual violations occur on the day, according to Plantão Brasil.

A Second Challenge Failed This Week

A separate challenge to the Copacabana event had already failed. TSE minister André Mendonça closed a case brought by Rio state deputy candidate Leonardo Aragão and an institute, ruling they had no standing to challenge a presidential matter, Metrópoles reported.

Mendonça did not decide whether the event was irregular campaigning, and sent the content of the complaint to the Electoral Prosecutor-General’s Office, according to Perfil Brasil. The Copacabana act was due to start at 4 p.m. in Brasília time, which is 3 p.m. ET.

What It Means for US Readers

For anyone tracking the Brazil election, the rulings show Brazil’s courts reluctant to restrict artists before an event takes place. Expect more complaints about campaign conduct as the 25 October vote nears, and watch the Brazil election polls for new surveys.

For investors in Brazilian stocks, the real or US-listed Brazilian shares, legal disputes like this rarely move prices alone. They add to headline noise in the final week, when the vote result is the main driver.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, an online prediction market, bettors give Flávio Bolsonaro an 80.8% chance of winning the 25 October runoff and Lula 19.5% (18 October, 9:10 a.m. ET). The “Brazil Presidential Election” market has about US$187 million in total bets.

Kalshi, a US exchange regulated by the CFTC (the federal derivatives regulator), also lists runoff markets. These prices are bets, not polls, and they can move fast on news.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Prices are bets, not polls, and can move fast. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What Is Not Known

The court has not ruled on whether any event broke electoral law, and the Prosecutor-General’s Office has not said whether it will act on the earlier complaint. Whether Novo will appeal Cueva’s decision is also not known.

It is not known whether anything said on stage on Sunday will draw new complaints. Any such case would be decided after the events, with the runoff days away.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Brazil’s electoral court decide about the Novo party request?

Minister Ricardo Villas Bôas Cueva rejected Novo’s request to suspend pro-democracy concerts planned for Sunday 18 October. He found no proof at this stage that they were campaign rallies.

What is a showmício?

It is a concert or show used as a campaign rally, which Brazilian electoral law prohibits. Novo claimed the artist events were showmícios for Lula.

Which cities did Novo target?

Novo named Copacabana in Rio de Janeiro, Salvador and Porto Alegre. Artists such as Caetano Veloso, Djavan and Daniela Mercury were named in Brazilian reports.

Can the court still punish violations?

Yes, the ruling is not advance approval of the events. The court can act if concrete violations occur.

When is Brazil’s runoff?

Brazilians vote on Sunday 25 October, one week after these events. The runoff is between President Lula and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro.

World.title: What to Do in São Paulo in October 2026: BTS, Iron Maiden and the Berliner Philharmoniker
World.content:
Culture

Key Facts —K-pop takeover. BTS close the month with three stadium nights at MorumBIS on 28, 30 and 31 October. —Metal and pop. Iron Maiden play Nubank Parque twice, and the Pussycat Dolls follow at the same arena on 30 October. —Classical coup. The Berliner Philharmoniker under Kirill Petrenko play Sala São Paulo on 18 and 19 October. —Film and fashion. The Mostra film festival turns fifty across the city’s cinemas, and São Paulo Fashion Week returns to Ibirapuera. —Fashion week. São Paulo Fashion Week N61 runs at Parque Ibirapuera until Sunday 18 October.

If you are wondering what to do in São Paulo this October, pace yourself: São Paulo in October 2026 is shaping up as the city’s biggest live-music month in years, crowned by three BTS stadium nights and a rare visit from the Berliner Philharmoniker.

The concert calendar alone would fill the month: international acts through 31 October, from club stages in Barra Funda to the city’s two biggest open-air venues. Several shows are already close to sold out, so book early.

Around them, October stacks a national holiday, Latin America’s answer to fashion week, the fiftieth edition of the Mostra film festival and one of the strongest classical line-ups Sala São Paulo has ever hosted. Here is the month in order.

São Paulo in October: The Concert Month

Sunday 18 October Dionne Warwick — Over and Out farewell tour Vibra São Paulo, Av. das Nações Unidas 17955, Santo Amaro · 8 p.m. (doors 6 p.m.), from R$190 (about US$38), via Ticket360 A last chance to see a six-Grammy legend who has loved Brazil back for decades.

Friday 23 October Kneecap Cine Joia, Barra Funda · Tickets via Ingresse The Belfast trio behind the BAFTA-winning film, rapping in Irish in a 700-capacity room. Details.

Sunday 25 and Tuesday 27 October Iron Maiden — Run For Your Lives Nubank Parque · Tickets via Livepass Fifty years of Eddie across two São Paulo nights — the metal event of the year in the band’s most loyal market. Details.

Wednesday 28, Friday 30 and Saturday 31 October BTS — Arirang World Tour MorumBIS stadium · Tickets via Ticketmaster Brasil Three stadium nights, seven years in the waiting. Details.

Friday 30 October Pussycat Dolls — PCD Forever Tour Nubank Parque · Tickets via Eventim The reunited group’s only announced Brazilian show — 2000s pop nostalgia at open-air scale. Details.

Friday 30 October Jorja Smith Espaço Unimed, Barra Funda · Tickets via Tickets For Fun One of Britain’s finest modern soul voices in a mid-size room. Details.

Saturday 31 October The Rasmus Carioca Club, Pinheiros · Tickets via Uhuu “In the Shadows” on Halloween night, in one of the city’s classic rock clubs. Details.

São Paulo in October: Classical, Film and Fashion

Until Sunday 18 October “Os Últimos 5 Anos”, a two-hander musical Teatro Nair Bello, São Paulo · Price from the venue The two-person musical about a couple whose love story is told in opposite directions, billed as a 25th-anniversary run. In Portuguese.

Tuesday 13 – Sunday 18 October São Paulo Fashion Week, N61 Pavilhão das Culturas Brasileiras, Parque Ibirapuera (Tuesday 13 shows are held at other venues) · Tickets via Eventim — details at spfw.com.br Latin America’s leading fashion week returns to its Ibirapuera pavilion with 26 shows over six days — the industry’s twice-yearly takeover of the park.

Thursday 15 – Thursday 29 October 50th Mostra Internacional de Cinema Cinemas across São Paulo · 2026 prices pending; single tickets were R$26–32 (US$5–6) last year The city’s main annual window on world cinema turns fifty — opening with James Gray’s “Paper Tiger”, passes traditionally sell out fast. Details.

Sunday 18 and Monday 19 October Berliner Philharmoniker, conducted by Kirill Petrenko Sala São Paulo · R$1,600–5,000 (about US$300–940); benefit concerts for the TUCCA children’s cancer charity, via salasaopaulo.art.br The classical event of the decade for São Paulo: the world’s most famous orchestra and its chief conductor in two benefit nights — expensive, historic and unlikely to return soon.

Thursday 22 October Theatro Municipal String Quartet: Mayer, Mendelssohn, Schumann Theatro Municipal, Praça Ramos de Azevedo, Centro · Price from the theatre A chamber evening inside the city’s 1911 opera house — the room alone is worth the ticket.

Thursday 22 and Saturday 24 October OSESP: Mendelssohn’s “Scottish” Symphony Sala São Paulo · R$50–330 (about US$9–62), via salasaopaulo.art.br Swiss conductor Thierry Fischer leads Mendelssohn’s Third — a mid-season highlight at standard OSESP prices.

Wednesday 28 October, then Wednesdays and Thursdays to 17 December “Epifania – Uma Fábula Moderna” premieres Teatro Estúdio, São Paulo · Tickets via Sympla, price from the venue A new musical by Vitor Rocha opens its run on 28 October. In Portuguese.

Friday 30 and Saturday 31 October (further dates to 7 November) Theatro Municipal double bill: new Jocy de Oliveira opera and Stravinsky’s “Oedipus Rex” Theatro Municipal, Centro · Price from the theatre The opera season’s boldest pairing: a world premiere by Brazilian pioneer Jocy de Oliveira alongside Stravinsky’s stark opera-oratorio. Opera needs no Portuguese.

Still Running: The Big Exhibitions and Family Picks

Mondays and Tuesdays in October, 8 p.m. “A Igreja do Diabo” — musical with Edyelle Brandão Teatro Estúdio · Price from the venue Companhia A Casa que Fala’s new musical runs through the month on Mondays and Tuesdays — in Portuguese, staged for the music.

3 October – 1 November “Miraculous Ladybug: O Show Musical” Teatro VillaLobos, Shopping VillaLobos · Tickets via Sympla The animated hit’s official stage musical stays for the whole month — the family option of the season, built on spectacle rather than dialogue.

Through 31 January 2027 MASP: “Histórias latino-americanas” MASP, Avenida Paulista 1578 · Paid entry; free days midweek — check masp.org.br The museum’s most ambitious show of the decade fills five floors with Latin American art from Mexico to Argentina. Our full story.

Through 24 January 2027 MAM: 39th Panorama of Brazilian Art Museu de Arte Moderna, Parque Ibirapuera · Regular museum ticket Brazil’s most traditional survey of contemporary art asks what art can still do “after everything has been said”. Pairs naturally with a park walk. Our full story.

Through 7 February 2027 IMS Paulista: Fernando Lemos retrospective Instituto Moreira Salles, Avenida Paulista 2424 · Free Some 400 works mark the centenary of the Portuguese-Brazilian surrealist photographer — and the building adds a library, café and rooftop view over Paulista.

Now showing Pinacoteca: Beatriz Milhazes Pinacoteca, Luz district · Price from the venue — check pinacoteca.org.br for the current building and tickets A solo show for one of Brazil’s central contemporary painters, all colour, rhythm and ornament — combine it with the Museu da Língua Portuguesa next door.

Further Ahead: November and December

November opens with the Formula 1 São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos on 6–8 November, then the city’s biggest goodbye: Sepultura play the final concert of their 42-year career on 7 November at the Suhai Music Hall, after the show moved from the Pacaembu stadium; existing tickets remain valid. Ty Segall finally makes his Brazil debut at Audio Club on 15 November, Best of Blues and Rock takes Ibirapuera on 20–22 November, and the month closes with Of Monsters and Men and Babymetal. December then stacks CCXP (3–6 December) and Primavera Sound with Gorillaz and The Strokes (5–6 December) into one week.

What are the biggest concerts in São Paulo in October 2026?

Three BTS stadium nights at MorumBIS (28–31 October) and two Iron Maiden shows at Nubank Parque (25 and 27 October) top the bill, followed by the Pussycat Dolls at Nubank Parque, and club shows by Kneecap, Jorja Smith and The Rasmus.

Is 2 November 2026 a public holiday in São Paulo?

Yes. Monday 2 November is Finados (All Souls’ Day), a national holiday under Law 10,607 of 2002, which gives a long weekend from 31 October to 2 November. Expect cemeteries to be busy.

What can I do in São Paulo in October for free?

Free options include the Fernando Lemos retrospective at IMS Paulista, MASP’s free midweek days for “Histórias latino-americanas”, and a car-free Avenida Paulista every Sunday, with the Feirinha da Liberdade street market a short metro ride away.

Rio de Janeiro · Culture

A Leblon theatre keeps up its bossa nova weekends until 8 November, The Color Purple plays as a musical in Barra until the 25th, and the CCBB’s October programme is free. The rest of the month, day by day.

RIO DE JANEIRO — There is a great deal to do in Rio in October, and very little of it is written down anywhere in English. This guide is the monthly selection for people who live here rather than visit: what is on, where, when, what it costs, and why it might be worth crossing the city for.

Until 8 November the Teatro Café Pequeno in Leblon keeps up its eighteen-concert bossa nova season, and until 25 October the musical A Cor Púrpura plays a short run in Barra. Here is the rest of the month.

Until 8 November: Bossa Nova Weekends in Leblon

Fridays and Saturdays 8pm, Sundays 7pm Bossa Nova Sessions at the Teatro Café Pequeno Teatro Café Pequeno, Av. Ataulfo de Paiva 269, Leblon · From R$50 (about US$10) Eighteen concerts over five weekends in the neighbourhood where the genre was born. The line-up runs from harmonica player Maurício Einhorn and singer Ithamara Koorax to guitarist Victor Biglione, who marks fifty years on stage this year — his 1995 Montreux live album, co-produced by Quincy Jones, has just been reissued. Small room, reserved tables, the most accessible October programme in the city for a listener without Portuguese.

Mid-October

Wednesdays and Thursdays, until 22 October, 7pm “Pra Quem Não Me Conhece” returns to the Laura Alvim Casa de Cultura Laura Alvim, Ipanema · Price from the venue Nicole Musafir’s comedy about her own life, extended after sold-out shows at its premiere. In the first run her grandmother, the pianist Lydia Musafir, played in public for the first time at 91. In Portuguese.

Until Sunday 25 October A Cor Púrpura — The Color Purple, the musical, fifth Rio season Teatro Multiplan, Shopping VillageMall, Av. das Américas 3900, Barra da Tijuca · From R$60 (about US$11) · Wednesday to Friday 8pm, Saturday 4pm and 8pm, Sunday 3.30pm and 7.30pm Fourteen performances only of the Brazilian production of the Alice Walker musical, with Suzana Santana again as Celie and Tadeu Aguiar directing. English-speaking audiences know the story from the novel and the films, which makes this the easiest musical in town to follow in Portuguese. Tickets through Sympla and the box office; every section also has a solidarity ticket at a special price against one kilo of food.

Thursdays through November, 8pm “Jazz dos Muertos” on Thursdays at La Esquina in Lapa La Esquina, Lapa · Price from the venue A new weekly jazz night in the heart of Rio’s bohemian district, built around jazz, Latin jazz, bossa nova, samba jazz and soul. It opened on 15 October with “Aura Jazz” by the Giovana Adoracion Quinteto, and the name is a playful nod to the idea that the old masters are gone but their music is still on stage. Simple to enjoy without Portuguese.

Sunday 18 October Vanessa da Mata at Vivo Rio Vivo Rio, Av. Infante Dom Henrique 85, Parque do Flamengo · Price from the venue One of the defining voices of Brazilian pop of the last two decades, in the big auditorium inside the Flamengo park. Her catalogue crosses MPB, pop and reggae, and most of the room will know every word.
