World.title: Macron to address France after Trump describes country as ‘burning’
World.content:
“More than 2,000 people have been taken into custody,” Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez wrote on X Sunday afternoon. “More than 600 police officers, gendarmes, and firefighters have been injured amid these scenes of violence.”

Before addressing the nation at 8 p.m., Macron will meet Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu and the ministers responsible for handling the crisis.

U.S. President Donald Trump seized on the violence to blame migration. “France is burning! The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform Sunday afternoon.

“Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!” he added.

Earlier in the day, U.S. Vice President JD Vance had called out European leaders: “Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion” but “ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility.”

He called on Americans to pay attention, as “this is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country.” The U.S. faces crucial midterm elections to both houses of Congress on Nov. 3.

The French government has struggled to deal with the crisis in recent weeks — Lecornu described it as “urban violence” — and is now hoping the student movement will fade due to a two-week school holiday that started Friday.

Guillaume Guérin, the mayor of Limoges, criticized the government’s handling of the demonstrations, saying the national police “simply had no more ammunition left.”

World.title: France says Israel must ‘stop these acts of terror’ following attack on EU diplomats
World.content:
The incident took place in Taybeh, a mainly Christian town north of Jerusalem, where diplomats and other officials from France, Poland and Belgium were watching local people harvest olives. Video footage of the attack showed settlers confronting a convoy of diplomats and a man wearing a French tricolor sash slumped beside a car.

“The mayor of the commune of Aulnoye-Aymeries was violently assaulted by extremist settlers in the West Bank,” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on X, adding that that Israel “must urgently put an end to these criminal acts.”

Belgian Foreign Minister Maxim Prévot said that in addition to the assault on the French mayor, a Belgian vehicle was damaged in the incident. He added that “Israeli authorities must protect Palestinians, ensure the safety of diplomats and journalists, and bring those responsible to justice,” and said Belgium “will continue to press for EU sanctions against those responsible for this violence and those who support them.”

On Sunday morning, an EU spokesperson said that the bloc “strongly condemns” the attacks by violent settlers in the West Bank, “including on European diplomats.”

The spokesperson added: “We take positive note of statements by several Israeli representatives who condemned the attacks but we expect full accountability as well as effective measures to prevent continued acts of violence and violent harassment against Palestinians, including during the ongoing olive harvest season, as well as against journalists.”

Writing on X, the Israel Defense Forces strongly condemned “the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters.”

The IDF added that “according to a preliminary inquiry, no IDF soldiers were present at the scene at the time of the attack”.

However, the office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu urged caution “before drawing conclusions” from reports of the attack, while noting that “any violence against diplomats is unacceptable.”

World.title: Ukraine strikes oil facility in St. Petersburg as part of ‘massive’ drone attack
World.content:
Smoke rises after an attack on the oil terminal in St. Petersburg, Russia on Oct. 18, 2026. | AFP via Getty Images

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said last week he had ordered the resumption of strikes on Russian oil refineries following a three-day pause.

Ukraine struck an oil terminal in St. Petersburg Sunday morning in what Russian state media called “one of the biggest drone attacks of the year.”

Alexander Beglov, governor of St. Petersburg, said on Telegram Sunday that the city underwent a “massive” overnight attack from Ukrainian drones. “The Ministry of Emergency Situations continues to extinguish fires at the Petersburg Oil Terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot, and industrial warehouses in the Kolpino district,” he said, adding that one person died and several others were injured in the incident.

The drone strikes come as Kyiv and Moscow ramp up attacks on each other’s infrastructure. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said last week he had ordered the resumption of strikes on Russian oil refineries following a three-day pause after U.S. President Donald Trump declared he had brokered an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia.

World.title: Starlink restrictions in Ukraine a ‘planned operation’, Zelenskyy says
World.content:
The restrictions have revived questions on Ukraine’s reliance on the satellite system operated by a U.S. company amid escalating tensions between Kyiv and the White House. “This will cost many of us our lives,” an experienced Ukrainian officer told POLITICO and the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network earlier this week.

“We’re reaching out to everyone at the military level, at the Ministry of Defense level, and at the diplomatic level, including to SpaceX. Right now, no one is responding to our military or the Ministry of Defense,” Zelenskyy told reporters.

The European Union is under increasing pressure to provide Ukraine with an alternative to Starlink. But negotiations between Brussels and Kyiv over access to the bloc’s Govsatcom program — which gives participating governments secure communications capabilities— have been stalling. And IRIS², the EU’s in-house planned network to match Starlink, is only expected to come online in 2030.

“The Europeans are now raising the question of alternatives themselves. And they’re already working on them. They’re already making progress, and they’ll succeed in this area. I can already see that,” Zelenskyy said.

SpaceX did not immediately responded to a request for comment.

Earlier on Saturday, Zelenskyy accused Russia of looking to create a blackout across Ukraine, amid attacks on energy infrastructure and the waiver of U.S. sanctions on Moscow.

World.title: Police, demonstrators clash on sidelines of mass French protests
World.content:
“A very large majority of people are protesting without violence,” Paris’s police prefecture said on Saturday afternoon.

Around 4,500 secondary school pupils and university students involved in the Yellow Vests movement demonstrated side by side against the cost of living in Pau, south-west of France on 17 October 2026. | Jean-Christophe Chartre/AFP via Getty Images

Saturday’s demonstrations grew out of the student protests that began last month with school blockades and calls for better study conditions, more teachers and more funding. The movement has since spread nationwide — and become a political issue as the campaign for next year’s presidential election heats up.

In recent weeks, the government has struggled to deal with the crisis — which Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu described as “urban violence” — and is hoping the student movement will now fade because of a two-week school holiday that started Friday evening.

“The mobilization is marked by a very strong involvement of the ultra-left movement, which is only looking to cause disorder,” Nuñez’s office said Saturday, adding that the minister reiterated his “instructions of utmost firmness” to local prefects and police forces.

Footage showed Lyon’s tourist board office engulfed in flames on the city’s Place Bellecour. A police station was vandalized in Marseille, where a group of “rioters” also entered city hall, Mayor Benoît Payan said. He told BFMTV that “damage was objectively fairly limited,” although the act of vandalism was “unacceptable.” The headquarters of right-wing TV channel CNews in Paris was also targeted , authorities said.

World.title: Spain’s far left fails to unite ahead of November vote
World.content:
The Broad Front is made up of Sumar, the current junior partner in the Socialist-led government, the Catalan Comuns, the Communist-led United Left and Más Madrid. Some smaller local parties have also joined the ticket. The lead candidate for prime minister will be Ada Colau, the former mayor of Barcelona.

Sumar, the dominant force in the alliance, has seen its vote share more than halve since 2023, to 5%, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls.

Although Podemos has only been polling at 3%, its full involvement in the Broad Front would have meant a greater overall share of seats for the far left, according to analysts.

The PSOE has been trailing the conservative People’s Party and would need a strong performance by parties to its left in order to keep Sánchez in office. The more likely scenario, polls show, is that the PP will be able to form a majority with the far-right Vox, whose support has been rising.

“The Spanish left is caught up in a game of thrones that demobilizes [voters],” said Irene de Miguel, coordinator of Podemos in the western region of Extremadura, as the deadline loomed.

World.title: Macron vows to hold those who sought to “bring down the Republic” accountable after riots
World.content:
French President Emmanuel Macron vowed to hold accountable those who “sought to bring down the Republic” after protests descended into looting and rioting across major cities on Saturday, deepening the country’s political crisis.

 

In a televised address on Sunday, Macron said “nothing justified” the scenes of unrest across France, where a historic town hall in Limoges was engulfed in flames.

"Those who looted will have to pay for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable," the French President said.

Macron acknowledged the public’s frustration and anger over the unrest, while condemning what he described as “insurrectionist elements from the radical far left, joined by numerous criminals”. He urged all politicians to condemn the violence.

Macron also urged the public to distinguish between those peacefully protesting over what he called “legitimate demands” and those using the demonstrations as a pretext to destroy, smash and loot.

Macron’s address was highly anticipated, as the president, interior minister and prime minister faced scrutiny over the handling of the police operation.

Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who is leading in polls ahead of next April’s presidential election, accused Macron of laxisme, or being too soft, while progressive and Green groups criticised what they saw as excessive police force against protesters.

Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the far-left (LFI), has been accused by critics of fuelling chaos and further violence.

Macron, who is due to travel to Kuwait on Monday, announced no new security measures but said local authorities would work directly with police to protect “our cities, our public buildings and our stores”.

On Saturday, large crowds gathered in major French cities to protest over the cost of living and deteriorating student conditions. What began as peaceful demonstrations descended into chaos, with rioting, looting, fires and widespread damage to shops.

More than 2,000 people were arrested and over 600 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters injured, according to official figures.

The unrest comes as France prepares for next year’s contentious presidential election. Macron said the country deserved a “beautiful election” driven by debate, not violence.

World.title: Tensions remain high in Paris after violent protests across France
World.content:
People gathered and fires were lit in Paris as tensions remained high amid nationwide protests over the cost of living. The gathering comes after several days of unrest in France, with concerns over possible further confrontations.

 

On Sunday evening, a fire broke out near Place de la République, where police secured the area and firefighters worked to extinguish the flames.

Footage showed the looting of a clothing store in the neighbourhood. Bikes were also set alight nearby.

Euronews crews were on the ground as the situation developed.

World.title: Spain changes Ceuta patrol rules over ships' "innocent passage"
World.content:
The maritime law concept of "innocent passage" allows foreign vessels to transit through a coastal state's territorial waters. This is the legal basis Morocco invokes in incidents such as that of 30 July and for the presence of Moroccan ships while the mass influx of migrants at the Ceuta border was under way.

 

This concept is governed by the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. In fact, until 30 July Spain monitored these movements without intervening, but the situation has changed since the last two days of July.

A military source cited by the Spanish daily "El Mundo (source in Spanish)" confirms that previously innocent passage was monitored by the Maritime Action Operations and Surveillance Centre (COVAM). Now that monitoring is reinforced with ships that sail out to meet Moroccan vessels: "We are more alert; we no longer wait for them to enter before we act."

Activity by ships flying the Moroccan flag has decreased and, according to the Interior Ministry, the Civil Guard and the Navy, there was no innocent passage during the royal visit nor in the days afterwards.

Patrol vessels are deployed

The patrol vessel Atalaya (source in Spanish), part of the Navy's Maritime Action Force, has been deployed to Ceuta. Its mission is to protect Spain's maritime interests, detect unusual activity and enforce compliance with international law.

Patrol vessel Atalaya Armada Española

The Atalaya is based in Ferrol, carries four machine guns and one cannon, and has a crew of 48.

In Melilla the patrol vessel Isla de León (source in Spanish) has been deployed, with a crew of 10 and a Browning machine gun. It also operates in the waters off Ceuta and Perejil Island. At present it is focused on Melilla because of the Moroccan offensive.

Patrol vessel Isla de León Armada española

The newspaper "El País (source in Spanish)" reported on 12 October that, during the land breach of the Ceuta border at the end of July, the warship Mohammed VI had entered Spanish waters. The Defence Ministry was forced to send two more patrol vessels from Rota. The Chief of the Defence Staff contacted Morocco to demand that the incursion stop.

Monitoring without giving up relations with Rabat

According to "El Mundo", the difference compared with the period before the mass arrival of migrants and the presence of a Moroccan ship in Ceuta's waters does not lie in detection capability, which was already functioning, but in the addition of an active response, namely the direct deployment of patrol vessels.

In this way Spanish ships shadow the movements of Moroccan vessels. The key to this shift is distinguishing between innocent passage, as defined under international law, and conduct that could threaten Ceuta's sovereignty or security.

The dispatch of patrol vessels to intercept ships will therefore be used as a tool for surveillance and deterrence.

World.title: Shopkeepers defend their livelihood from masked looters during the French riots
World.content:
Desperate shopkeepers in several French cities confronted gangs of black-masked looters during Saturday’s ordeal, trying to protect their businesses as violence and chaos spread through city centers.

 

Footage shows owners pleading with thugs to leave their stores and attempting to defend their premises as confrontations escalated into pushing and fighting.Despite their efforts, shops were attacked, looted and damaged.

Other shopkeepers were seen sitting in front of their businesses in tears, surrounded by the wreckage, as they struggled to come to terms with the destruction. The scenes captured the distress of local business owners caught up in the unrest and fighting to protect their livelihoods.

World.title: Marine Le Pen warns of 'threat to democracy' and blasts 'exhausted Macronist power'
World.content:
"We are experiencing a crisis of confidence," declares presidential candidate Marine Le Pen. She describes it as "a threat to democracy". The National Rally leader lays responsibility at the door of the far left and of Emmanuel Macron, a president who she says is "without credibility or authority."

 

Marine Le Pen spoke less than two hours before Emmanuel Macron’s address, expected at 20:00.

For his part, the president of the National Rally believes that "order no longer exists in France today". According to Jordan Bardella, "France was humiliated" on Saturday night. The RN leader made the statement during a visit to a police station in Paris.

Violence flares up again in Paris

Marine Le Pen and her number two are speaking out just as looting has resumed in Paris, less than 24 hours after a day of chaos that has left France reeling.

Fresh scenes of violence erupted in the French capital on Sunday afternoon.

CRS-8, the specialist riot police unit that provides rapid response to urban unrest, has been deployed for the second day in a row.

Tensions are once again centred in the heart of Paris, particularly around Place de la République.

Clashes are pitting several hundred rioters against the forces of law and order.

According to the Paris police prefecture, "An undeclared call to assemble at Place de la République today at 14:00 was circulated on social media".

Groups of hooded youths have attacked shops and looted them.

30,000 looters in Marseille on Saturday

The latest figures for Saturday’s violence are staggering.

For Saturday alone, the Bouches-du-Rhône prefecture counted more than 30,000 looters. A dizzying figure that has left observers specialising in policing and justice dumbfounded.

World.title: Magyar links French riots to migration, says ‘shocking scenes’ justify hard line
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar linked the riots in France to immigration, saying the “shocking scenes” vindicated his government’s tough migration policies.

 

Anti-austerity protests turned violent in several French cities on Saturday, with looting reported in Paris, Lyon and Marseille. Several buildings were set on fire, including the historic town hall in Limoges.

“Seeing this senseless destruction and unjustified violence, perhaps it is now clear to everyone why Hungary takes the toughest possible stance on migration,” Magyar wrote on social media on Sunday, alongside a video showing buildings on fire.

“We will not relax our efforts to protect our external borders or change our immigration policy,” he added.

In his post, Magyar also said that the "overwhelming majority of European countries" want a tougher approach to migration and have "finally woken up".

“The Europe we all love is in serious trouble today. We also have a responsibility to help preserve our continent as the most wonderful place for our grandchildren," he said.

At a European summit held this week, a group of countries, including Denmark, Italy and Hungary, pushed for stronger language on migration in the conclusions.

French President Emmanuel Macron warned against “the stigmatisation” of immigrants and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez praised their positive contribution.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also commented on Sunday, without explicitly referring to France. He said Poland would “neither repeat nor pay for” other countries’ mistakes, stressing that Warsaw would maintain its strict asylum policy.

“We are firmly defending the border against illegal migration; we have our own asylum policy (we do not accept applications); we deport those who break Polish law,” Tusk wrote on X on Sunday.

“On security issues, we will be relentless. That is what I told the leaders of Europe in Brussels,” he added.

Magyar’s remarks drew criticism in Hungary. András Jámbor, a left-wing activist and Budapest councillor, accused the prime minister of exploiting footage of the French riots for political gain.

“It is deeply disturbing that the Hungarian Prime Minister chose not to address the people’s legitimate demands and the unjustified violence, but instead to label them migrants,” Jámbor said.

“Although some protesters have an immigrant background, as do some members of the wider population, this demonstration is about more than that,” he added.

Macron will deliver an address to the nation at 8pm Sunday.

World.title: Southern Valencia coast on alert as storm Adam may dump 300 mm of rain in 12 hours
World.content:
Spain's State Meteorological Agency has issued a special warning for "very heavy and persistent" showers and thunderstorms in Spain's Levante region and parts of the Balearic Islands, from this Sunday and over the next 48 hours.

 

The combination of the DANA Adam, cut off and isolated from the general atmospheric circulation, together with a very humid easterly flow, will bring widespread rainfall to four provinces (southern Valencia, Alicante, the Region of Murcia and the Almería coastline) and up to three of the Balearic Islands, with a particular impact on the Pityusic Islands (Ibiza and Formentera) but also leaving significant totals in Mallorca.

Aemet's information note refers to the possibility that the showers could become "torrential", but specifies that it is difficult to calculate exactly where in these regions the highest totals will be recorded. At the time of writing, the agency is maintaining red alerts only along the southern Valencian coast and in the north of Alicante and, in addition to the Mediterranean areas mentioned, orange alerts in the Seville lowlands, Ronda and the Sierra de Grazalema in the province of Cádiz.

"The most likely scenario indicates that the highest accumulations may occur along the southern coast of Valencia and around Cape La Nao, where amounts in excess of 60-90 millimetres in one hour and up to 200-300 mm in 12 hours are expected, with the possibility that they may extend to adjacent areas; as well as in the Pityusic Islands, where more than 160 mm could accumulate in 12 hours," the agency's statement says.

"From late in the day, rainfall could also be significant in coastal and pre-coastal areas of Alicante, Murcia and Almería, and across the Balearics spreading to the island of Mallorca, with totals above 50 mm in one hour and 100-140 mm in 12 hours," it adds. The impact on this latter island will be much more pronounced along its southern coast, where the Balearic capital, Palma, is located.

Aemet warns that late on Monday the episode could shift towards the north of the Valencia region and even reach Tarragona, before finally losing strength as Tuesday approaches.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | October 18th, 2026 – Evening
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: Shipping attacks threaten Turkey's resolve to keep warships out of Black Sea
World.content:
A wave of deadly attacks on cargo ships in the waters of NATO members Bulgaria and Romania has jolted the alliance into calling an emergency meeting on Black Sea security. Yet any move to send NATO ships hinges on Turkey reversing its steadfast refusal to allow warships into the Black Sea.

Advertising

Thursday saw two chemical tankers struck by drones close to a Romanian port.

It follows two similar attacks in Bulgarian waters in the past week. More than 20 sailors have been killed or remain missing.

“The war has come in full force to the Black Sea now,” said Yoruk Isik, a maritime analyst who runs the Istanbul-based Bosphorus Observer consultancy. “With the change in technology compared to the beginning of the war, drones really disrupted maritime traffic.”

According to Isik, the latest attacks underscore the growing spread of the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. “Russian ports and Ukrainian ports are heavily targeted, but now even in NATO waters ships are getting hit, in Bulgarian waters, Romanian waters.

“We are at a point where there is no safe place.”

The latest strikes targeted vessels along a key Ukrainian shipping route, casting Russia as NATO’s prime suspect as Moscow intensifies its assault on Ukrainian trade.

After meeting on Thursday with the leaders of Bulgaria and Romania, both NATO members, Secretary-General Mark Rutte said the military alliance would “continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed”.

Romanian President Nicușor Dan said NATO would hold a crisis meeting next week to discuss the situation.

Gatekeeper to the Black Sea

NATO could deploy air defence systems against drones to protect Bulgarian and Romanian waters.

But any deployment of naval ships will depend on NATO member Turkey, which controls access to the Black Sea through the Turkish Straits under a long-standing international treaty, the 1936 Montreux Convention.

Since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, Ankara has blocked entry of Russian and Ukrainian warships or military vessels belonging to NATO members without a Black Sea coast, arguing for a diplomatic solution.

In recent weeks the Turkish government has sought to broker a ceasefire on commercial shipping, without success. Isik claims that failure, coupled with the latest escalation in attacks, is increasingly calling into question Ankara’s reliance on diplomacy alone.

“Either they’re going to have a breakthrough and the Kremlin is going to de-escalate, or Ankara is going to accept the reality that there needs to be a more credible force here – bigger vessels have to come,” the analyst said.

He pointed out that the navies of Romania and Bulgaria are not equipped to handle such an operation alone, with Cold War-era ships nearing the end of their lifespan.

“So Turkey's engagement is key to any successful NATO planning in the Black Sea.”

Russian leverage

Despite Turkish-owned cargo ships coming under attack in recent weeks, and Turkey’s deep reliance on Black Sea trade, Ankara has so far kept its powerful navy on the sidelines.

International relations expert Huseyin Bagci, of Ankara’s Middle East Technical University, says Turkey fears an escalation in the conflict and will be wary of allowing NATO ships into the Black Sea.

“I do not think the government would dare,” said Bagci. “Probably the government considers this a provocation to drag Turkey into the war... Turkey is afraid of getting involved in the Black Sea against Russia, this is somehow a trauma in the Turkish mind.”

Moscow also retains powerful leverage over Ankara, he suggested.

Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom is about to complete a multi-billion-dollar nuclear power station in Akkuyu, southern Turkey. Ankara sees it as vital to the drive to reduce its heavy dependence on imported energy. “It is illogical to oppose Russia now while you let the Russians complete the nuclear plant,” said Bagci.

Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies

Ankara also knows that letting NATO vessels in while barring Russian warships could provoke Moscow into contesting Turkey’s prized status as the gatekeeper to the Black Sea.

However, retired Turkish diplomat Selim Kuneralp, an expert on the Montreux Convention, warns Turkey’s control over Black Sea access is likely already in Russian President Vladimir Putin’s sights.

“This has probably had an impact on Russia’s ability to conduct the war, and I doubt that Putin is very happy with the situation,” said Kuneralp. “So if he were to win the war, there is a very strong risk that he will take the initiative of saying: ‘this is unacceptable and we want to have free passage of warships from now on, regardless of whether there is a war’.”

As a signatory, Moscow has the right to call for a revision of the Montreux Convention every five years.

For centuries, Russia fought repeated wars with the then Ottoman Empire for control of the Turkish Straits. In the early years of the Cold War, even Joseph Stalin tried his hand, but the United States intervened and thwarted him.

Now Ankara walks a tightrope between Moscow and its NATO partners to avoid a resurrection of those historical rivalries.

World.title: Israel: Trump endorses Netanyahu ahead of elections
World.content:
The US president said he supports Israel's current prime minister in the country's elections on October 27. But polls say Netanyahu and his far-right partners currently lack the majority to secure a new term.

US President Donald Trump has announced his "complete and total" endorsement of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Israel will hold parliamentary elections on October 27, with opinion polls suggesting neither Netanyahu nor the opposition will manage to secure the 61 seats needed to form a coalition.

"Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu," Trump posted on his Truth Social account.

Iran war at center of Trump announcement

According to Trump, Netanyahu is a "Great Warrior Prime Minister," also commending him for his role in the war against Iran.

"BIBI NETANYAHU WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!" Trump added.

Netanyahu thanked the US leader for his "tremendous support."

"Together we will complete the mission," Netanyahu posted on his X account, alluding to the joint campaign by the two countries against Iran.

Netanyahu has been vocal in his objection to Iran's nuclear program Image: Richard Drew/AP Photo/picture alliance

Trump said the US would be alone in the war against Iran if Netanyahu were not re-elected, also mentioning the chant often sung at events by Iran's Revolutionary Guards that calls for both the US' and Israel's death, also labeling the two countries "the big and small Satans."

"If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Trump said.

Netanyahu opponent reacts

The war between Israel, the US and Iran began in February and resulted in Tehran blocking some global oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz.

Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's main challenger, reacted to Trump's endorsement by saying the Israeli public are the only ones who decide who is the country's next leader.

Speaking at an event in Tel Aviv, Eisenkot voiced his appreciation of Trump's "large contribution" to Israel's security.

"But Israel is a democratic state," he said, adding that the US administration will learn to work with whichever government the public decides on.

Netanyahu boasts Trump friendship once again

This is not the first time Netanyahu's election campaign has invoked Trump's support to augment the Israeli leader's international status.

In 2019, Netanyahu's Likud party posted billboards showing the Israeli leader shaking hands with Trump during the latter's first term as US president, as well as with Russian President Vladimir Putin, describing Netanyahu as a leader of a "different league."

Netanyahu is the longest serving prime minister in Israel's history. Much of Israeli society is divided on his far-right coalition's role in the failure to foresee and prevent the October 7 terrorist attack by Islamist Palestinian group Hamasand its affiliates in Gaza, in which some 1,200 Israelis were killed.

Netanyahu has refused to establish a state inquiry with the authority to look into government documents and summon ministers and officials to testify. Instead, the prime minister wants a commission with less authority to see confidential documents and with no authority to force testimonies by the country's leading politicians and officials.

Israeli opposition have been protesting against Benjamin Netanyahu's "failure" to prevent the October 7 attacks Image: Aviv Atlas/REUTERS

Another point of contention is Israel's war in Gaza that followed the attack, in which some 74,000 Palestinians have been killed.

Despite repeatedly promising a "total victory" after the war began, opposition supporters believe Netanyahu failed to deliver, with Hamas still in charge of many parts of the Gaza Strip. Netanyahu and his coalition partners have also promised to support what they called the "wilful migration" of Gaza residents, while also deepening Israel's hold on its territories in the West Bank, which is largely considered illegal under international law.

Other issues at the center of Israel's elections are the conscription of young ultraorthodox men into the military, the cost of living, and Israel's international status.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

World.title: Saudi Arabia sends skyscraper employees home amid Houthi threats
World.content:
Riyadh's Kingdom Center tower's management told the people employed there to work from home "until further notice," without giving a reason. This comes as Houthi attacks escalate.

The Kingdom Center skyscraper in Riyadh told people employed there to work from home due to possible attacks by Yemen's Houthirebels.

The 99-storey tower is one of Saudi Arabia's tallest buildings.

Kingdom Center made working from home "mandatory" with no reason given. The new order is effective immediately and will be in power until further notice, the building's management told tenants, AFP reported.

Among the building's tenants are important financial institutions such as the International Monetary Fund, as well as wealth management company Merril Lynch.

At the building's foot is a shopping center, which will remain open for now.

Attacks increase

Studies in schools across Saudi capital Riyadh and the surrounding areas will take place online for a second week, with the city's King Khalid International Airport still being closed after a Houthi attack resulted in 13 casualties.

The conflict between the Saudi-led coalition and Iran-backed Islamist group Houthis has continued to escalate, with the coalition reporting its first military deaths since the escalation's beginning.

Two helicopter pilots were killed near the Yemen border due to a "technical malfunction," the coalition said, with the Houthis earlier announcing the downing of an Apache helicopter "belonging to the Saudi enemy," the group said.

The Houthis have carried out attacks on international airports in Saudi Arabia Image: Social Media/REUTERS

Conflict flares up again

On the Saudi side, two drones were intercepted over Riyadh overnight, with a third being shot down over the country's Eastern Province, a known oil-rich area, according to the authorities in the country.

Two ballistic missiles were also intercepted in Saudi Arabia's south.

The two sides have been confronting each other on various intensities over the past decade. After a four-year ceasefire, the conflict between the two sides saw an escalation after the Yemen-based Islamist militia took over strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month.

The Houthis have targeted oil facilities, tankers and Riyadh's international airport, with the coalition carrying out strikes on Houthi areas.

World.title: Meloni backs police after cost-of-living protests turn violent in Italian cities
World.content:
Anger over living costs and low wages has brought Italians onto the streets. A major union has called a general strike for November 20.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni on Sunday condemned rioting during cost-of-living protests, expressing solidarity with police after clashes in several cities.

The violence broke out during cost-of-living demonstrations on Saturday, leaving at least four police officers and 20 demonstrators injured in Milan.

The unrest comes amid anger over high prices, stagnant real wages and a shortage of affordable housing in major cities.

What happened during the protests?

In Milan, black-clad, masked youths threw fireworks and bottles at police and erected barricades in the central Piazza Duomo, the Italian news agency ANSA reported.

Police initially withdrew to await reinforcements and later used tear gas to clear the square. Some 50 young people were arrested, about half of them minors, according to ANSA.

Clashes also broke out in Turin, Bologna and Bergamo. Police in Bologna used water cannon and made four arrests, all minors, with seven people reported to prosecutors.

How did Italy's PM Meloni respond?

Meloni expressed solidarity with police on Sunday, condemning criminals who she said exploited demonstrations to provoke confrontations and "sow chaos."

Italy tightens restrictions on the right to protest To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Demonstrating is a right, but setting our cities on fire is not," she said.

Milan Mayor Giuseppe Sala also condemned the violence while acknowledging the grievances behind the demonstrations.

"The reasons for the protest were understandable. The violence against police and the serious damage to the city, however, cannot be justified," he said.

Why were people demonstrating?

Protesters rallied against high living costs and low wages, with households facing expensive fuel and difficulty finding affordable housing.

In Rome, thousands joined a demonstration organized by the Italian General Confederation of Labour (CGIL). Its leader, Maurizio Landini, announced a general strike for November 20.

The violence came as similar demonstrations in France descended into rioting, arson and looting, with more than 1,800 people arrested nationwide.

World.title: Ukraine apologizes after a suspected drone crashes in Lithuania, damaging a moving car.
World.content:
Debris has damaged a moving car in Lithuania, where NATO jets were scrambled. Kyiv says Russian jamming may have diverted drones targeting Russia.

Ukraine apologized Sunday after a suspected drone crashed in northern Lithuania, prompting shelter warnings and the deployment of NATO fighter jets.

The incident raised fresh concerns about the spillover of Russia's war against Ukraine into NATO territory, although the drone's origin and whether it carried explosives remained under investigation.

What happened in Lithuania?

Lithuanian authorities told residents in central and northern regions to seek shelter Sunday morning after detecting an unidentified flying object.

Debris damaged a moving civilian vehicle, but no one was injured, national crisis management centre chief Vilmantas Vitkauskas told Lithuanian radio.

Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said the drone probably entered from neighboring Poland. He proposed a joint investigation with Warsaw.

Lithuanian PM warns of Russian nuclear threat To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Two Italian Eurofighter jets operating under NATO command were deployed, a NATO spokesperson said. Kaunas said weather conditions prevented visual identification.

Have similar incidents happened before?

Lithuania and its Baltic neighbors have experienced several drone incursions during the war.

Ukrainian drones intended to strike targets in northwestern Russia have previously strayed into Baltic airspace and crashed. Russian-made drones have also entered Lithuania from Belarus.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda described Sunday's incident as another example of the war spilling onto NATO's eastern flank.

Meanwhile, Lithuania said it was treating an attempted arson attack on a Starlink base station near Vilnius as Russia-linked sabotage aimed at undermining Ukraine's military capacity.

National crisis management chief Vilmantas Vitkauskas said Sunday that authorities were searching for suspects who tried to set fire to the facility at about 2 a.m. (2300 GMT Saturday).

World.title: Pope appears in public for first time since surgery
World.content:
After undergoing a lung operation, the pope said he will resume his duties gradually. There is no "clinical reason" for his South America trip not to go ahead, his surgeon said.

Pope Leo XIV said he would resume his duties "gradually" as he addressed the crowd for the first time since his lung cancer surgery.

Part of the pope's right lung was removed as part of the operation, which took place at the Gemelli Hospital in Rome. He was discharged on Saturday.

The Catholic leader thanked those who prayed for him while he was hospitalized, saying he would "gradually assume" his activities as the crowd cheered upon seeing him appearing. The 71-year-old spoke normally and looked physically well.

The people said the "delicate phase" is behind him, thanking "God and your prayers" for it and also expressing his gratitude to the medical staff at the Rome hospital.

During his time at hospital, the pope still communicated his worries about the Ukrainian civilian population. He held a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, urging for a ceasefire in the Ukrainian town of Oleshky, located on the front line.

Putin reacted by saying Ukraine is responsible for the situation.

Recovery in ten days

According to his surgeon, the pontiff is in an "absolutely satisfactory clinical condition," with his full recovery probably taking some ten days.

The crowds cheered as the pope made his first appearance Image: Gregorio Borgia/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

"His determination to achieve a very quick and very effective recovery from every point of view was really commendable," Dr. Stefano Margaritora told Vatican News.

Margaritora said the tumor had been found during a routine X-ray checkup, while also saying the operation to remove it was "routine."

The pope's next major assignment would be his trip to South America, in which visits to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru are planned. The trip should take place between November 6 and 17.

Speaking about the pope's recovery, Dr. Margaritora said he sees "no clinical reason" why the trip should be called off.

Testing of the tumor and related lymph nodes was underway, with the results determining whether Pope Leo needs additional medical treatment.

The 71-year-old Pope Leo was born in Chicago. He's been in his role since May 2025.

World.title: France: Young voters blase about Glucksmann's Socialists
World.content:
Raphael Glucksmann wants to lead France's Socialists to power without working with the left-populist Jean-Luc Melenchon, who is particularly popular with young voters. How can the center-left candidate win them over?

The historically working-class Parisian neighborhood of Belleville has gentrified in recent years. It was here that Raphael Glucksmann, a member of the European Parliament for France's center-left Socialists, celebrated his victory in the party's presidential primary on October 11.

Two rounds of voting had been anticipated, but the 46-year-old son of philosopher and essayist Andre Glucksmann triumphed in the first round with a convincing 66% of the vote and will be the Socialist candidate in France's 2027 presidential election.

As he left the Cantine de Belleville restaurant, Glucksmann was flour-bombed by an unidentified assailant. The following morning, he called on his rival, the left-wing French populist Jean-Luc Melenchon, to condemn attacks carried out by his supporters, though it is not clear that the attacker was indeed a supporter of Melenchon's La France Insoumise (LFI).

The incident has highlighted the issue set to dog Glucksmann's presidential candidacy over the coming weeks: How can he win over Melenchon's supporters if he refuses to work with their candidate?

Glucksmann was flour-bombed while leaving his victory celebration Image: Raphael Lafargue/abaca/picture alliance

Gluckmann's rapid rise

"Where do you stand on Melenchon?" That was the question that dominated much of the Socialists' primary campaign. Party leader Olivier Faure spoke in favor of leaving the door open for cooperation with the LFI, but Glucksmann called for a clear break with the far left. His decisive victory is therefore also seen as a vote in favor of a clear demarcation.

The other primary candidates questioned Glucksmann's political experience. Segolene Royal, a previous presidential candidate, compared his bid for the Elysee with that of an "intern" wanting to take charge of a company. She said Glucksmann had no experience in government or even running a local authority.

Despite Glucksmann's victory in the primary, his starting position is a difficult one. A poll by Toluna Harris Interactive, published the day after his win, projects that he would win 10–11% of the vote. The same poll put Melenchon on 18%, meaning the far-left man would be much more likely to reach the runoff. But the survey was conducted before Glucksmann won the primary, and so does not take into account any potential boost the nomination may give him. Still, 10% would be an improvement on the Socialists' performance in the last presidential election in 2022, when their candidate Anne Hidalgo won just 1.75% of the national vote.

There is also the complication that the Socialists are banking on a man who is not even a party member to lead them from irrelevance. Raphael Glucksmann actually belongs to a small center-left party called Place Publique.

France students demand better schools To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Melenchon's youth appeal

Glucksmann has his work cut out for him — especially with young people. In an Ipsos survey in September, which posited Glucksmann as the social-democratic candidate and Edouard Philippe as the only candidate from the political center, Melenchon scored 41% among the under-25s. Meanwhile, 20% of this age group supported the far-right nationalist Marine Le Pen. France's young electorate is politically divided, but Melenchon still dominates on the left.

The 75-year-old is currently rallying alongside the students whose protests have drawn international attention. At a rally near Clermont-Ferrand in central France , he expressed solidarity with their movement and reiterated his calls for lowering the voting age to 16 and abolishing Parcoursup, France's national admissions procedure for higher education.

In an analysis for the Fondation Jean-Jaures, a Socialist-aligned think tank, the political scientist Antoine Bristielle distinguishes between a core group of committed LFI voters and the broader left. Melenchon's most loyal supporters, he says, are often young, educated city-dwellers, and many are under a lot of financial pressure. Four in ten households in this group live on a net monthly income of less than €2,000 ($2,200).

Bristielle estimates that just under a third of the left-wing electorate in his study care more about a left-wing victory than their allegiance to any particular party. Almost half of the people in this group are younger than 35, and would consider voting for the Socialists, the Greens, or LFI. Redistribution and an active government are important to them, but most would prefer politicians who are willing to compromise.

Melenchon in Paris during a public sector strike on September 29 Image: Tom Nicholson/REUTERS

Glucksmann's youth efforts

The pattern recently observed in Germany, where young women are more likely to vote for the left and young men for the right, does not apply in France. Political scientists Anja Durovic, Nonna Mayer and Noemie Piolat found that in the 2024 European and parliamentary elections, young French women were not significantly more likely to vote for the left, or less likely to vote for the far right, than men of the same age. It remains to be seen whether this pattern will be replicated in the 2027 presidential election.

Glucksmann says he would ease the burden on earned income by reducing France's CSG social security tax while increasing taxes on inheritances worth more than €2 million. He also presents himself as a committed supporter of European integration, while Melenchon has called the EU a neoliberal institution. Glucksmann's political profile combines social policy demands with foreign policy positions that could also appeal to voters from the camp of the current president, Emmanuel Macron.

France's Ukraine policy is one such issue. Glucksmann favors decisive support for Kyiv. Manon Aubry, a member of the European Parliament for Melenchon's LFI, says her party supports military assistance only under certain conditions, namely: The provision of aid to Ukraine must first be subject to democratic debate; it must not enable attacks deep inside Russian territory; and it must not weaken France's own defense capabilities. In 2024, LFI MPs voted against the French–Ukrainian security agreement.

The tension between the parties of the left was once again apparent in the aftermath of the flour attack in Belleville. The LFI MP Sebastien Delogu posted a declaration of support on X for the taxi driver who was going to have to clean his car.

Glucksmann must win over a lot of voters from Melenchon's camp if he is to have a chance of winning the presidency. This is likely to prove a much more difficult task than simply distancing himself from Melenchon.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Is Germany's eight-hour workday under threat?
World.content:
Would you work 12 hours straight? The CDU/CSU and SPD are locked in a dispute over reforms to the Working Hours Act. Workplace flexibility, collective bargaining agreements and worker protection rules are at stake.

The town of Leuna, in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, is one of the country's largest chemical industry hub, where more than 100 companies have established operations. Among them is the Finnish biotechnology group UPM, which has recently built a biorefinery for wood-based chemicals in Leuna. It's now hiring.

One of the job listings is for a chemical technician to oversee the rollout of new facilities. But to qualify, candidates must be willing to work 12-hour shifts. Is that legal? According to German law, standard working hours are limited to eight hours per day. It is permissible to extend this to ten hours, provided that workers receive compensatory time off for the overtime, and there must be at least 11 hours of rest between two shifts.

Twelve-hour shifts? What German law permits

Business associations and the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties have long called for these rules to be made more flexible.

Rainer Dulger, president of the Confederation of German Employers' Associations (BDA), points to the European Working Time Directive, which allows for a maximum weekly working time of 48 hours. "The allowance is being taken advantage of almost everywhere else — except here," Dulger told the dpa news agency in August.

Companies say they often find the existing rules too rigid, particularly in industries with seasonal fluctuations — such as tourism — or in project-based work, or during irregular peaks in workload, such as in the restaurant industry. They could deploy their staff more efficiently, says Dulger: "The Working Hours Act dates back to the era of fax machines and rotary-dial phones. It knows nothing of laptops or daycare hours."

4-day workweek: A model for the future? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

CDU and SPD divided on working hours

In their 2025 coalition agreement, the CDU/CSU and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) agreed to reform the Working Hours Act. "In keeping with the European Working Time Directive, we want to allow for a maximum weekly rather than daily working time — also and especially to promote a better work-life balance," the agreement said.

The SPD would have preferred to leave the law unchanged, but had to accept the conservative parties' plans. The Social Democrats pointed out that longer working hours are already permitted in exceptional cases, such as in emergency services, the health care sector and security services. Workers in power plants, refineries and the chemical industry are also allowed to work up to 12 hours at a time.

A surprise for Chancellor Friedrich Merz

Even Chancellor Friedrich Merz himself seemed unaware of this exception until quite recently. After visiting the UPM refinery in Leuna in September, he recounted to business leaders at the German Employers' Day in Berlin that he was "completely surprised" to learn that the facilities operate on a continuous 12-hour shift schedule, thanks to the approval of the works council.

Merz recounted the shift supervisor describing the work schedule as "really great" — with three-day work weeks. "He said we have plenty of time for our families — it's a great way to organize things." Merz went on to conclude that this demonstrates the benefits of relaxing the Working Hours Act.

"Working more than eight hours is not exploitation. Rather, it can be a good opportunity to organize working hours more flexibly — both for businesses and for the people working there," the chancellor said. "We should do it."

SPD agrees to longer working hours, but with conditions

But there is resistance from within the SPD and from trade unions opposed to amending the Working Hours Act. The trade union Verdi argues that significantly longer workdays would have negative consequences for employees' health and would disadvantage people with family and caregiving responsibilities. In certain industries, employees could also be put under pressure to accept longer shifts.

An initial reform draft was drawn up in June 2026 by the Labor and Social Affairs Ministry, headed at the time by Bärbel Bas, an SPD politician who has since resigned for personal reasons.

The draft includes some conditions, including a collective bargaining agreement between employers and unions if any schedule changes were made, as well as health and safety regulations, and working hours to be tracked electronically.

Bärbel Bas' reform plan had the CDU up in arms Image: Christophe Gateau/dpa/picture alliance

Dispute over collective bargaining rights and worker protection

Annika Klose, spokesperson for labor and social policy for the SPD parliamentary group, explained the thinking behind the idea. Flexibility, she said, is "not a one-way street." The coalition agreement explicitly aims to promote a better balance between family and work. "So that it's sometimes possible to take your child to football practice in the afternoon and then continue working afterward — but not that my boss tells me against my will: 'You're working the shift from 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. tomorrow.'"

The CDU/CSU immediately rejected the draft. Businesses were also up in arms. "This draft must be withdrawn and completely revised," demanded Dulger in a statement, saying it was "steeped in mistrust." The German Confederation of Skilled Crafts (ZDH) spoke of a "breach of the commitments agreed to in the coalition agreement." The reform has been on hold ever since.

Why the reform stalled

At the Employers' Day event, Merz held out the prospect of progress. "This is indeed long overdue. I believe we can accomplish this relatively quickly and create flexibility in the labor market."

It remains to be seen, however, whether the new SPD Labor Minister, Alexander Schweitzer, shares this view. In early October, his party released a paper on reforming working hours that read like a declaration of war against the CDU. "Self-determination, Not Deregulation" is the title of the seven-page document that was signed by the SPD working group on labor, the youth organization Jusos, the "60plus" working group and the women's wing of the SPD.

In the paper, the Social Democrats not only reiterate the points that already appeared in Bas' draft back in June. They also demand that, in the future, employers and employees should decide on working hours "jointly and by mutual agreement." They argued that it is not "in the spirit of a modern reform of working time law" if only employers can determine when employees finish work.

From a political perspective, the dispute over reforming work hours has long become more than just a debate over legal provisions. It is a fundamental dispute over how much flexibility workers should be expected to tolerate in the future and to what extent the state should protect them. And it is yet another stumbling block for the already beleaguered government in Berlin.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: France reports almost 2,400 arrests after riots, looting and arson during cost-of-living protests
World.content:
Rioters torched public buildings and looted shops across France, destroying Limoges' historic town hall. The violence erupted during nationwide cost-of-living protests.

Almost 2,400 people were arrested across France following riots, looting and arson during cost-of-living protests, France's authorities said.

The unrest on Saturday has sharpened tensions ahead of France's 2027 presidential election, as anger over living costs collides with tight limits on government spending.

What happened during the protests?

Clashes, fires and looting broke out in several cities during Saturday's demonstrations. The country's Interior Ministry said about 1,000 officers were injured.

Paris police reported 855 arrests, describing the figure as a record. Prosecutors said 517 people remained in custody, including 171 minors. Those figures were provisional, with arrests continuing until early Sunday.

Most arrests in the capital were linked to suspected handling of stolen goods, participation in a group intending to commit violence, and vandalism.

In central France, rioters set fire to Limoges' historic town hall, leaving much of it gutted. Mayor Guillaume Guerin condemned the destruction.

Rioters set fire to Limoges' historic town hall during nationwide demonstrations over living costs Image: Pascal Lachenaud/AFP

"There are no words to condemn what happened, so appalling is it," he told broadcaster LCI. "The country is in chaos."

Authorities reported attacks on public buildings and shops in Marseille, Lyon, Avignon and Grenoble. Police used tear gas, batons and water cannon in several cities.

Demonstrators were also reported injured. The newspaper Le Figaro reported that a 17-year-old lost a hand to a grenade fired by police in Saint-Etienne.

What have leading French politicians said?

President Emmanuel Macron addressed the nation due to the protests, saying "nothing justifies" the violence.

"Tonight, we feel anger and shame," Macron said in a speech, adding that there needs to be a separation between protesters with what he called "legitimate demands" and people who "destroyed, smashed and looted."

The France leader also promised "full transparency" on police's response to the protests.

France protests escalate as unrest spreads across cities To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Opposition politicians seeking to succeed Macron in presidential elections in April and May also responded to the unrest.

Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen accused the party of her far-left rival Jean-Luc Melenchon of having "legitimized the violence." She pledged to protect the French "from the violence of the extreme left."

Melenchon, who had backed the demonstrations and preceding student protests, urged demonstrators to stay away from looting, calling it "contrary to our methods."

US President Donald Trump blamed the protests in France on immigration.

"The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country," Trump posted on his Truth Social account.

The demonstrations brought together grievances over fuel prices, low wages and problems facing farmers and firefighters. School and university students demanding better learning conditions also participated.

The interior ministry put nationwide turnout at 550,000, including 110,000 in Paris. The CGT trade union gave a higher national estimate of 800,000.

France's high debt and budget deficit limit the government's ability to meet demands for additional spending.

Online calls to revive the yellow vest movement have added to government concerns that student demonstrations could grow into broader unrest.

The yellow vest movement began in 2018 over planned fuel tax increases and grew into wider protests over living costs and inequality. Named after the high-visibility vests worn by demonstrators, it brought months of nationwide demonstrations, some marked by violent clashes with police.

World.title: Información genética para una medicación más segura y eficiente
World.content:
Con una simple muestra de saliva, la farmacogenética permite el análisis de decenas de genes y cientos de fármacos de uso habitual y revela por qué un simple analgésico quita el dolor a una persona y a otra le produce una reacción adversa

Según estima la Agencia Española de Medicamentos y Productos Sanitarios, entre el 3% y el 6,5% de la población tiene una variante genética que provoca que su hígado transforme la codeína (un compuesto presente en medicamentos o soluciones tan frecuentes como las pastillas para la tos) en morfina. Este proceso, que se produce a gran velocidad incluso si la dosis administrada es normal, puede desembocar en una sobredosis accidental, que en algunos casos termina en el fallecimiento del paciente.

El ejemplo lo pone Javier Suela, director técnico del laboratorio de genética de Sanitas (Madrid). Él mismo pertenece a este pequeño grupo poblacional de riesgo: “Hay mucha evidencia acumulada de la toxicidad de ciertos medicamentos en ciertos pacientes. Estas reacciones adversas van desde un brote cutáneo hasta la muerte en casos extremos, como este mismo de la codeína”, explica.

Suela trabaja para reducir esa peligrosidad al mínimo. En el laboratorio que dirige, desde el pasado mayo, se extrae el perfil genético de quien lo solicite para “determinar si tiene un componente genético, una proteína, que produce que determinados fármacos se procesen de una forma que no es habitual”, sintetiza.

El perfil genético, en tres pasos 1 Recepción de las muestras e identificación de cada paciente El paciente lleva una muestra genética (basta la saliva, por ejemplo) en un tubo. Este tubo va a una primera máquina que realiza una preanalítica y transforma las muestras en placas que identifican a cada persona: en la posición A1 está la muestra de un paciente concreto y en la B1, otro, y así sucesivamente. 2 Procesado del material genético El material genético de la placa, que contiene muestras de hasta 96 pacientes, se prepara y depura (se corta, se colorea...) en otra máquina para el análisis final. Lo que se obtiene, tras cuatro horas de refinado, es la placa definitiva (en la imagen) que se usará para extraer el perfil genético. 3 Obtención del perfil genético La placa, con el material genético ya refinado, se introduce en un escáner que analiza cada celda, que contiene más de un millón de variables (cada una asociada a un genotipo) que procesar. Cuando este escáner finaliza se obtiene el perfil genético del paciente, el resultado final del proceso.

Esta disciplina se conoce como farmacogenética y en Sanitas está disponible para todos sus asegurados bajo el nombre de Mi Farmagen. “Un ser humano puede metabolizar todos los fármacos, pero en función de ciertas variables genéticas los metaboliza a distintas velocidades; entonces el medicamento puede funcionar demasiado bien o demasiado mal. Esto es lo que da lugar a reacciones adversas o reacciones inexistentes, es decir, cuando el fármaco no funciona”, detalla.

29 genes y 125 fármacos analizados

Mi Farmagen analiza hasta 29 genes y más de 125 fármacos de uso habitual, y ofrece un informe con las reacciones a cada uno de estos medicamentos. Y siempre es útil, tanto si se obtiene antes o después de la prescripción, ya que “permite ajustar la medicación sin perder efectividad, pero evitando posibles efectos adversos y aumentando la seguridad”, incide Suela.

Hay casos en los que un cambio anticipado de medicación puede salvar la vida del paciente, pero también situaciones más cotidianas en las que esta información es de mucha utilidad. Así lo explica Andrea Azcárate, jefe de servicio de Endocrinología del hospital Sanitas de La Moraleja (Madrid): “Es el ejemplo de un paciente con colesterol alto al que le sienta mal un tipo de estatina, que es el tratamiento habitual para esta patología. Para corroborarlo, se le hace la prueba farmacogenética. A partir de ahí, probablemente escojamos otro tipo de estatina que vaya a tolerar mejor”. Sin embargo, cada caso, en opinión de Azcárate, no es blanco o negro: “Lo que el análisis nos da es una predisposición de respuesta, una información probabilística que nos permite individualizar el tratamiento”, puntualiza.

0:00 ANDREA AZCÁRATE, jefe de servicio de Endocrinología del hospital Sanitas de La Moraleja (Madrid)

Azcárate y Suela inciden, precisamente, en la importancia de la interpretación facultativa de esta información, que por sí sola vale poco. “Es fundamental la interpretación y el ajuste, algo que siempre se ha hecho: la medicación, en función de las características clínicas del paciente, las casuísticas y las edades, se individualiza”. Y eso mismo se hará a partir de ahora, subraya: “Ajustaremos caso a caso, pero con más información. Es una herramienta más, muy buena y útil, pero hay que tener prudencia a la hora de incorporarla”.

En esa misma línea se expresa Suela: “El informe son páginas de metabolización, nada más. No vale de nada sin facultativo detrás que las interprete. Y, sobre todo, hay que combinar toda la información: igual tienes un paciente del que el análisis dice que el fármaco le va a sentar muy bien, pero esa misma persona tiene unas condiciones físicas complicadas o es un paciente polimedicado, en el que es fundamental medir las interacciones entre fármacos”. Es una cuestión de personalización, como dicta la tendencia actual en la medicina, pero con un conocimiento más preciso.

Así funciona Mi Farmagen Mi Farmagen analiza cómo las variantes genéticas influyen en la respuesta a determinados medicamentos.

influyen en la respuesta a determinados medicamentos. Permite conocer cómo metabolizamos determinados fármacos para aumentar su eficacia y reducir posibles efectos adversos.
