World.title: They fled violence in their own country, but are still at risk, advocates say
World.content:
WARNING: This story contains descriptions of domestic violence which may cause distress

Grace* only needs to look at the dark lines traversing her wrists to remember the life she fled.

"There are some marks on my hand here; he cut my hand and also my lips," she said.

"He used to punch me, he used to kick me, like throw … beer bottle at my face."

Grace bears scars on her arms from violence inflicted by a partner in Papua New Guinea. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

The Papua New Guinean said her ex-partner would break into her rental drunk and raging while her young son slept, breaking her possessions, and one time even stealing her educational certificates.

"I used to hang around with [my son] in the street, hide in the flower gardens or trees, let my partner go away," she said.

Grace tried to report the violence to the PNG police but said it did not go anywhere.

Desperate, with support from her mother and grandmother, she relocated to Australia as a seasonal worker through the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme, leaving her son in her relatives' care.

Grace has met a new partner in Australia, with whom she has had a daughter. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

It was a temporary plan, but as the magnitude of what she had escaped dawned on her, Grace knew she could not go back.

"Every day of my life in Papua New Guinea was not safe," she said.

PNG's national crisis of domestic violence Women are twice as likely to suffer domestic violence in Papua New Guinea compared with the rest of the world, a new report finds. Here's what the country is doing to fix it.

That realisation sent her down the road to protection in Australia, laying bare the violence and trauma, as over about two years she went through a rejection, an appeal, and at last, asylum.

In its decision, the then-Administrative Appeals Tribunal noted violence in PNG was "among the most common in the world", and that "almost all" women and girls would be subject to it at some point in their lives.

It found that if Grace returned, her ex would likely attempt to find her and pressure her back into a relationship, and accepted there was "a real chance" she would be harmed.

"I was so excited that I cried; like it's been a long time," Grace said.

The Administrative Appeals Tribunal found there was a "real chance" Grace would be harmed if she returned to Papua New Guinea. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

A caseload only growing

The Tasmanian Refugee Legal Service (TRLS) has seen more than 400 victim-survivors since it began taking on family violence cases in 2021, and the caseload is only increasing.

"They often are required to provide dates; they're required to provide documentary evidence like photographs, police reports, medical reports," lawyer Jarin White said.

" That process is extremely distressing for many people, especially for people from communities and cultures where family violence is not talked about or is a taboo topic. "

Ms White said for women who came to Australia with a partner, the violence often intensified once they arrived, and could manifest in immigration-related abuse and control.

Jarin White says women on temporary visas are particularly vulnerable. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Australia has family violence provisions that allow these women to apply for consideration for permanent residency, which a spokesperson for the Department of Home Affairs said aimed to ensure they did not feel compelled to stay in a violent relationship to secure a permanent visa.

But Ms White said because the provisions applied only to certain visa categories, like a partner visa or some skilled visas, women who were not eligible, like those listed as a dependant on a student visa, could often only seek asylum.

It has prompted calls to introduce an additional substantive family violence visa for temporary visa holders.

Ms White said women who came alone, like Grace, tended to claim refugee status on the basis that it was unsafe to return to their home country, where they were likely to experience serious harm.

Barriers to support

It is difficult, and often dangerous, for any woman to leave an abusive relationship, but can be even more so in a foreign country, up against language and cultural barriers.

That they were often ineligible for services like Centrelink and sometimes Medicare while they waited for their claim to resolve only magnified their disadvantage, Ms White said.

Grace could work and had support from friends and a partner, but other temporary visa holders are more vulnerable. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Grace worked casual agricultural jobs, bounced between temporary living arrangements, and had support from friends and a new partner, but others can fall through the cracks.

"For people that might have no work rights and be on a bridging visa, that can leave them on the street, and the protection visa process can take up to five years, so that's a long time for someone to try and survive," Ms White said.

It is a challenge for Australia's shelters, which often rely on a small financial contribution from the women they support.

"So, when we take women in this situation, we know that we will not get that contribution," said Janet Saunders, Hobart Women's Shelter chief executive.

"But more importantly, we also are taking on … the challenges of making sure that they have enough food, medication, they can see a doctor, transport costs … all the things that we all use day to day."

Janet Saunders says when shelters support women on temporary visas it is often a long-term commitment. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

The National Advocacy Group on Women on Temporary Visas Experiencing Violence, made up of more than 30 state and national peak bodies and frontline organisations, is calling on governments to ramp up support.

Among other measures, they want more support for shelters and crisis accommodation providers to guarantee access, and for state and territory governments to expand eligibility to social and public housing, to prevent women from overstaying at refuges.

They also want the Commonwealth to ensure access to Centrelink and health care.

"In Australia, we talk about how we will not tolerate violence against women, but what we're actually doing is excluding a group of women because of their visa status, and that's not OK," Ms Saunders said.

A spokesperson for the Department of Social Services said the Commonwealth offered a range of support for victim-survivors regardless of visa status, including the Leaving Violence Program, which provides packages of up to $5,155 and connects them to other forms of support.

Grace was able to work and had support from friends and a partner, but other women can fall through the cracks. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

The federal Health Department said individuals might be eligible for Medicare by a ministerial order, and there was a range of orders in place for temporary visa holders in government programs, including the Forced Marriage Specialist Support Program.

A spokesperson for the federal housing minister said the government was investing $1.2 billion in new crisis and transitional housing for women and children escaping violence.

Tasmania's Minister for Women and the Prevention of Family and Sexual Violence Jo Palmer said eliminating violence was a priority, and that the government would continue working with frontline services.

Hopes for reunion

It has pained Grace to miss her son growing up, and she is working to bring him to Australia.

She has since had another child, and says her son is excited to meet his sister.

"I can't wait for my son to come here and live with me," she said.

Grace cannot wait for her son to meet his sister for the first time. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

*Name has been changed

World.title: Helping snap brilliant photos of orchids all part of conservation work
World.content:
Native orchids are a sought-after subject for photographers.

"They're very variable but they're also really cryptic and so you have to really know your landscape and your place, so it's like a special discovery," Landscape Recovery Foundation chief executive Josie Kelman said.

But with the joy of photographing orchids comes dangers to the more than 200 species recorded in Tasmania. Of those, 77 are listed as threatened under state legislation.

The majority of threatened orchid populations occur in dry forests and woodlands, grasslands, and coastal areas — all of which have been subject to "significant loss and modification" since colonisation, according to the state and federal governments' flora recovery plan for Tasmania's threatened orchids.

Black-tipped spider orchids and sagg spider orchids are among the species being grown by the Landscape Recovery Foundation. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

The Landscape Recovery Foundation works with other conservation organisations and private landowners to help understand and improve orchid distribution.

The foundation's Magali Wright said one of the biggest issues orchids faced was the cumulative effect of visitation.

The Landscape Recovery Foundation recently held a workshop for people interested in photographing orchids. (ABC News)

"It's not the visit of one person, it's the visit of multiple people to the same place and I think social media plays a big role in this, particularly when we post photos," Dr Wright said.

The foundation recently held a workshop for people interested in photographing the different species to help them understand the impact photographers can have on the environment.

It has also provided some tips.

The Landscape Recovery Foundation recommends photographers: Stay on formed tracks. Orchids are easy to miss, especially once they have finished flowering or when they are seedlings.

Orchids are easy to miss, especially once they have finished flowering or when they are seedlings. Think about cumulative impacts. Repeated trampling can damage orchid plants and seedlings, compact soil and reduce fungal activity needed for seedling germination.

Repeated trampling can damage orchid plants and seedlings, compact soil and reduce fungal activity needed for seedling germination. Avoid cumulative impacts. Avoid repeated visits to the same site, and avoid visits to places where threatened species are growing unless you are taking part in conservation activities. Do not post the location of threatened orchid sites on social media.

Avoid repeated visits to the same site, and avoid visits to places where threatened species are growing unless you are taking part in conservation activities. Do not post the location of threatened orchid sites on social media. Choose your equipment wisely. Use a long lens and a tripod so you can photograph from a distance and keep off the ground.

Use a long lens and a tripod so you can photograph from a distance and keep off the ground. Respect the habitat. Refrain from "gardening" the area around your subject and moving other foliage or plants out of the way.

Refrain from "gardening" the area around your subject and moving other foliage or plants out of the way. Respect property boundaries. Make sure you have permission to enter private land.

Make sure you have permission to enter private land. Keep it clean. Make sure your equipment and footwear are clean and dry to avoid spreading weeds and diseases.

Despite the risks from social media and photographers trampling through the wilderness, interest in native orchids can also help conservation efforts.

"It's very hard to encourage people to act if they don't understand what's there or how they can be part of things," Dr Kelman said.

" You have to fall in love with something before you want to make an effort to do something to conserve it. "

Josie Kelman says finding orchids can be "a special discovery". (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

One of the species conservationists have had success propagating is the golfers leek orchid, paraprasophyllum incorrectum, known from two sites in the Tasmanian midlands.

"We've been working out how to grow it for the last eight years and I think we've finally got it right," Dr Wright said.

The critically endangered golfers leek orchid, which is known from two sites in the Tasmanian midlands. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

For orchid seeds to germinate and grow, they need to be colonised by a fungus.

"For some species it's really tough to find the right fungus," Dr Wright said.

Magali Wright says the cumulative impact of people visiting orchids can have a significant effect on the plants. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

"For years we grew it [golfers leek orchid] on an oatmeal jelly and this last couple of years we've been trying things like quinoa and polenta and brown rice. The fungus and the orchid combination seems to quite like that."

Golfers leek orchid seedlings are being grown to be planted out in native grasslands over the next couple of years.

The Landscape Recovery Foundation has been growing golfers leek orchids to plant out in native grasslands. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

Scent detection dog helps map orchids

To better understand orchid distribution and population numbers, the Landscape Recovery Foundation is working with Canines for Wildlife.

Miki, a cocker spaniel, has been trained to find two species of threatened leek orchids. (Supplied: Fiona Walsh)

"Last year Miki, a cocker spaniel came down to Tasmania and found 73 orchids that we had walked past … including tiny seedlings that were growing in poa tussocks," Dr Wright said.

Orchids propagated by Dr Wright's team were used to train Miki and the dog can find both the golfers leek orchid and another threatened orchid the Tunbridge leek orchid, paraprasophyllum tunbridgense.

Miki and another scent detection dog will be involved in further field survey work in the Tasmanian midlands next month.

Detection dog Miki found 73 orchids that scientists had missed. (Supplied: Fiona Walsh)

Dr Kelman said orchid conservation was the project that drove the most interest in the Landscape Recovery Foundation's work.

"[Orchids] are beautiful flowers in the environment, they're unusual," she said.

World.title: ‘Long reads’ and ‘frothy fun’ in store as Sydney Festival 2027 unveiled
World.content:
CultureTheatreSydney Festival ‘Long reads’ and ‘frothy fun’ in store as Sydney Festival 2027 unveiled Michaela Boland October 19, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The 2027 Sydney Festival will include a nod to wellness culture with an outdoor installation of old cars transformed into saunas, cold plunges and spas, free for public use. If that is a sentence you never expected to read, that makes two of us. Sydney Festival Director Kris Nelson in one of the old cars that will be turned into a spa experience during the festival in Barangaroo. Janie Barrett Upon reflection the waynapuni pools public bathhouse, to be created by industrial designer Benjamin Paul, working with First Nations teenagers, and installed in Barangaroo Reserve from January 7 to 25, is quintessentially Sydney Festival. Since it began, Sydney’s annual arts jamboree has demonstrated a knack for reflecting our city back to us and public bathing is certainly having a moment.



At the first Sydney Festival in 1977, during the craft era, Haymarket was transformed into a bustling arts and crafts market. Nelson says ‘long reads’ are important, but fun party nights are also a big part of festival programming. Janie Barrett A decade later, 14 bands were on the line-up for an overnight Twelve-Hour Rockathon at Sydney Entertainment Centre, and who can forget Festival First Night from 2008-2012, which drew 250,000 people to the centre of Sydney during the GFC, when we all really needed a party. Artistic director Kris Nelson’s second Sydney Festival boasts a huge contemporary dance program, Dance Reflections, backed by high-end French jewellery house Van Cleef & Arpels and the return of First Nations-led multi-arts strand Blak Out. Among the highlights outside of these programs is a new show from comedian Hannah Gadsby, American clown Spencer Novich and free dance event, The Party, at the Cutaway.



Nelson frames his programming style through the prism of summer beach reading. “It’s equal parts fluff, pulp and big heavy reads, and there’s something about that in a summer program that I want,” he says. “I want a frothy fun party or a great gig night, as much as I want something that is like the long read.” Fulfilling that slot is Irish company Dead Centre, which will transform Ukrainian poet Ilya Kaminsky’s poetry into a contemporary drama wherein a soldier shoots a deaf boy who can’t hear his orders, the next day, the townspeople are deaf. “It’s heavy and it’s beautiful. It’s an allegory, a protest,” Nelson says.



The Ballet du Grand Théâtre de Genève will bring choreographer Rachid Ouramdane’s Outsider to Sydney Festival 2027. Gregory Batardon It is also the closest the 2027 program comes to engaging with the current febrile geopolitical climate. “Lots of people in the program are touched by what’s happening in the world, it’s a program that’s engaged in our times,” Nelson says. Dance Reflections is an ongoing international festival overseen by former New York City Ballet dancer Serge Laurent, who gathers some of the world’s premier dance troupes into curated programs staged in varying combinations since 2022 in nine cities, from London to Shanghai. The 10th iteration in Sydney will present a physical theatre smorgasbord of 13 different shows at venues across Sydney and a dozen dance workshops at Sydney Dance Company.



France’s Rachid Ouramdane has devised an aerial work wherein 20 dancers and four extreme sports athletes will be suspended by tightropes and thrown through space at the Cutaway Barangaroo. Famed choreographer Anne Teresa de Keersmaeker and Morocco’s Radouan Mriziga will collaborate on Together at Carriageworks, a reimagining of Vivaldi’s The Four Seasons. A decade after her death, Trisha Brown’s company will perform Roof Piece at the Art Gallery NSW. The world premiere of Ngurragabu, a major new work exploring an environmental apocalypse from Australia’s pan-national First Nations dance company Marrugeku has been included in the program. Marrugeku’s ensemble of First Nations, Filipino and Melanesian dancers will perform within a monumental mangrove forest being devised by visual artist Abdul-Rahman Abdullah.



Up Late with Bianca Hunt will consist of conversations with artists and cultural leaders. Arts festivals at their best showcase incredible international artists alongside new Australian works, inspiring audiences and artists and seeding potential ongoing collaborations. Laurent is non-committal about Marrugeku being included in future international Dance Reflections programs. “With artists you have to know each other, it’s a story each time,” he says. His curatorial approach is to provide a platform for artists from different backgrounds. Budjerah will be performing Donny Hathaway songs at the Metro Theatre for Black and Blues. Paul Harris



“Dance Reflections is a way to bring together very diverse artists [with] a very strong common point. They are researchers trying to find their own voice, so it’s quite eclectic, but in fact very consistent.” Marrugeku’s artistic co-director Dalisa Pigram has a similar approach to choreography. “We have nine artists spanning regions of maritime knowledge, including the Melanesian and Torres Straits, Singapore and East Indonesia and on the mainland Bardi Jawi and Nyaru knowledges within the region of the Kimberley.” Ancient saltwater knowledge systems have a lot to offer us as we contemplate melting ice caps and increased precipitation, she says. “I’m not a choreographer at the front asking people to move in certain ways, we have an approach that’s inspired by what moves the dancer,” she says.



MO’JU will be channelling the music of Bill Withers for Black and Blues. Justin McManus First Nations programming head Aidan Rowlingson has expanded the festival’s established Blak Out program to include a music series, Black and Blues. “I love the [concept of] First Nations musicians taking on their favourite soul blues artists at the Metro Theatre,” Nelson says. ARIA Award-winner Budjerah will channel Donny Hathaway, Wiradyuri/Filipinx artist MO’JU will conjure the music of Bill Withers and Etta James will be celebrated by Jamaican/Arrernte artist SOLCHLD. “Expect a sense of familiarity and discovery,” Nelson says.



Emily in Sydney will present another opportunity to see one of our most recognisable artists anew. The curated exhibition of paintings by Emily Kame Kngwarreye, drawn largely from private Sydney collections, will be on at S. H. Ervin Gallery. Up Late with Bianca Hunt at Belvoir St Theatre will consist of conversations with artists and cultural leaders. Wiradjuri Yuin actor Angeline Penrith will return for the third year with Redfern Renaissance, a series of performance readings and discussions about the revolutionaries and activism of Redfern’s National Black Theatre in the 1970s. Sydney Festival runs from January 7–25, 2027. Tickets go on sale Thursday, October 22 at sydneyfestival.org.au, with 10,000 prime seats available from $49 or less across all ticketed shows.

World.title: Spender and Chalmers’ reform adviser back GST change to offset tax cuts
World.content:
PoliticsFederalFederal budget Spender and Chalmers’ reform adviser back GST change to offset tax cuts Paul Sakkal October 19, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A leading member of Treasurer Jim Chalmers’ economic advisory panel and MP Allegra Spender have separately raised the alarm on high levels of state and federal spending and called for a GST hike to pay for tax cuts for workers. The Grattan Institute, an influential independent think-tank, has come out in favour of a tax mix switch at a time of near-record tax and spending levels under the Albanese government. Federal ministers and backbenchers have become concerned about inflation and productivity in recent weeks as tension has emerged between Chalmers and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. Anthony Albanese and Jim Chalmers in question time last Wednesday. Alex Ellinghausen In a report to be released on Monday, Grattan chief executive Aruna Sathanapally urges politicians to raise the GST from 10 to 15 per cent and expand it to include all types of food, raising $76 billion per year. The think tank says $33 billion should be used to cut income taxes for lower- and middle-income workers while $25 billion should be put to boosting JobSeeker, pensions and rent assistance. Sathanapally, who Chalmers picked for his economic reform roundtable last year, called for fiscal rules to force profligate state governments to curb spending as the RBA threatens more rate rises to reduce demand that is partly fuelled by government spending.



“There are no easy paths back to budget sustainability. But with smarter spending decisions and a tax system that raises sufficient revenue to care for our ageing population, both current and future generations can be better off,” Sathanapally said, adding that lower-income families would be left about $8000 a year better off under the proposed changes. Related Article Political leadership In a funk: How economic pain is straining the PM and treasurer’s relationship The institute says state government spending has grown even more quickly than the Commonwealth’s. Federal spending has still grown “substantially”, its report states, but Australia’s credit rating has remained steady while Queensland, Victoria, Tasmania and the ACT have all experienced rating downgrades. The think tank’s intervention in the economic debate adds to recent calls for tax reform from former Coalition ministers Josh Frydenberg and Mathias Cormann, both of whom argue for change to the GST, and Labor figures Bill Kelty, Paul Keating and Lachlan Harris. Albanese and Chalmers have been under internal and external pressure to address Australia’s economic problems. Their political headache was exacerbated by an own goal on credit card surcharges, which lead to the tax office refusing to accept credit card payments.



Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino admitted on Sunday that ministers knew the ATO might stop accepting credit cards as far back as July. Before Mulino’s comments in an interview on ABC’s Insiders, the government only emphasised its knowledge about the ATO’s final decision, which it learned in September. “In July, the government became aware that the ATO was looking at options,” Mulino said. Wentworth MP Allegra Spender. Alex Ellinghausen Only about 5 per cent of taxpayers pay bills via credit card, but the move has added to arguments from the business lobby that Labor is not in touch with the concerns of business owners. Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson seized on Mulino failing to rule out 60 or 70 per cent tax rates for small businesses who use trusts and pay into a “bucket company”. These firms will be incentivised to rearrange their structure.



On the proposal for fiscal rules, Wilson said: “They are like a diet and we know Labor can’t kick their spending addiction.” Spender, a tax reform advocate who was also on Chalmers’ reform panel last year, said fiscal rules were needed at the federal level, going beyond the Grattan Institute’s call for restrictions at state level. Rules that would cap expenditure and tax were proposed by former Treasury secretary Ken Henry in last year’s roundtable, but Chalmers has argued against arbitrary caps. “The government should adopt stronger fiscal rules, particularly to manage expenditure. Spending has grown too fast particularly for a high-inflation environment and we’re not bringing it back quick enough,” Spender said. “The GST should be on the table, as must better resource taxation, digital taxes and a shift from stamp duty to land taxes.”



Related Article Letters Difficult times aren’t a sign of schism at the top of the ALP ACCI chief executive Andrew McKellar also supported fiscal rules in that meeting, and said on Sunday they were necessary. Frydenberg, the former Coalition treasurer mulling a return to politics, called for debate on the GST last week but was quickly slapped down by Opposition Leader Angus Taylor. Australia’s income tax rates are relatively high by international standards and the highest rate kicks in at relatively low-income threshold. Many tax experts say that income taxes reduce the incentive to work, whereas people notice less if the GST creates slightly higher prices, creating fewer distortions and a more efficient system. The Grattan report says that the Commonwealth should use the higher GST take to cut back on the ballooning level of grant funding to the states in education and health, which are often subject to political dispute and compromise.



Under Grattan’s proposals, a low-income single-parent family who rents would pay nearly $80 more in GST per week but receive $202 in extra welfare and receive a $27 income tax cut, leaving them $150 a week better off. A higher-income working family would pay about $162 more in tax because they consume more and pay more GST. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Trump urges Israelis to re-elect ‘Great Warrior’ Netanyahu in stunning intervention
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastIsraeli-Palestinian conflict Trump urges Israelis to re-elect ‘Great Warrior’ Netanyahu in stunning intervention Matthew Knott Updated October 19, 2026 — 5:51am ,first published 5:02am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Tel Aviv: US President Donald Trump has made a stunning late intervention in Israel’s elections, endorsing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in a move the veteran leader hopes could help him to remain in office. Netanyahu had eagerly sought the official endorsement of his longtime ally while his rivals had urged Trump to refrain from interfering in the contest, reflecting the belief that the president’s verdict could affect the outcome. Trump’s once warm relationship with Netanyahu has appeared to cool since their war in Iran began to falter, raising doubts about whether he would endorse a candidate. Trump and Netanyahu have formed a close bond. AP But, in an enthusiastic social media post peppered with capital letters and exclamation points, Trump delivered his “Complete and Total Endorsement” of Netanyahu, urging Israelis to support him when they vote on October 27.



“Bibi Netanyahu has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump said in his post, uploaded in the early hours of Monday Australian time. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict ‘I’m afraid of civil war’: The voters travelling from Australia to vote against Netanyahu “If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so. “Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself. Despite all of that, he has endured and, in fact, he has thrived!” The US is Israel’s most important security partner, and Trump remains popular in Israel, despite the war in Iran failing to deliver a decisive blow against the regime in Tehran.



Trump did not meet Netanyahu during the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month, triggering speculation of a snub, but the longstanding and close relationship between the two conservative leaders ultimately overcame any friction and frustration. Related Article World elections Israel is having its most important elections in history. How do they work? Netanyahu has viewed his close relationship with Trump and his ability to influence the American leader – cultivated over two presidential terms – as a key advantage over his rivals for the prime ministership. However, Nadav Pollak, a lecturer on Middle East affairs at Reichman University, questioned whether Trump’s endorsement would shift voter perceptions of a polarising figure who was first elected in 1996 and in power for most of the time since 2009. “Not sure that a Trump endorsement is worth so much for him right now,” he said on social media.



Describing Trump as “my dear friend Donald”, Netanyahu responded in a video, effusively thanking him for his “extraordinary” endorsement and praising Trump as the best friend Israel had ever had in the White House. The world, Israel and the Jewish people have been lucky to have a leader of “such clarity, consistency, conviction and courage” as Trump, Netanyahu said. Trump has made a habit of endorsing world leaders running for election in his second stint in office, including Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Colombian conservative candidate, Abelardo de la Espriella. Netanyahu has faced grim poll numbers for most of his past term in office, and many thought his career was over after he failed to prevent the worst security failure in Israel’s history: the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack, during which about 1200 people were killed or taken hostage. But his coalition government, the most right-wing in Israeli history, saw out a full term.



The latest average of three main television polls by Israeli newspaper Haaretz shows the bloc of parties aligned with Netanyahu on 51 seats, the anti-Netanyahu Zionist bloc also on 51 seats and 18 seats unaligned to either bloc, suggesting an extremely tight result. World.title: ASX set to dip, tech stocks weigh on Wall Street
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to dip, tech stocks weigh on Wall Street Alex Veiga October 19, 2026 — 5:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A broad sell-off in technology companies pulled stocks lower on Wall Street, capping off the market’s worst week since late June. The S&P 500 fell 1.1 per cent. Its roughly 2 per cent drop for the week wiped out its gains from last week, when it set an all-time high. Wall Street wrapped up its worst week since June with more losses. Bloomberg The Nasdaq composite, which is heavily weighted with technology stocks, sank 2.1 per cent and posted its first weekly loss in five weeks and its worst since June. The Dow Jones Industrial Average held up better, closing 0.3 per cent lower. The Australian sharemarket is set to edge lower, with futures pointing to a loss of 11 points or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.57¢.



Slightly more than half of the stocks in the S&P 500 fell, but all but seven of the 75 stocks in the index’s tech sector closed lower. Among the biggest decliners were chip companies, reflecting mounting worries about how long the frenzy over the AI buildout will last. Related Article Analysis

Sharemarket ‘Only the sharks are left’: The $388 billion change shaking up the sharemarket Micron Technology fell 5.6 per cent, Advanced Micro Devices dropped 6 per cent, Broadcom lost 4.5 per cent and Intel gave up 5.8 per cent. Among the other tech companies that finished in the red were Meta, which fell 3.7 per cent, and Google parent Alphabet, which dropped 2.5 per cent. It’s been a choppy week for chipmakers and other big tech stocks central to the artificial intelligence industry. Investors are now worried that the companies, which have relied on debt markets to finance an investment spree into their technology, may not be able to keep borrowing and spending as heavily with yields in bond markets worldwide recently climbing to their highest levels in years.



Netflix’s stock fell 2.9 per cent a day after the company announced that Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria will be replaced by Peter Rice. The news comes just days after Netflix said that it plans to lay off about 6 per cent of its workforce, amounting to nearly 1,000 positions. Energy stocks held up better than most. Exxon rose 2.5 per cent and Chevron added 2.6 per cent. European and Asian markets closed higher. In the bond market, Treasury yields held relatively steady. The yield on the 10-year Treasury slipped to 5.09 per cent from 5.10 per cent late Thursday. It had topped 5.30 per cent earlier this month and touched its highest level since 2002 because of worries about high inflation, signals of a strong U.S. economy and other factors. Yields are down despite reports this week showing that inflation at the consumer and wholesale level rose more in the U.S. than economists expected.



The reports could persuade the inflation-fighters at the Federal Reserve to hike their key interest rate before the end of this year. The central bank increased its key interest rate by a quarter-point to about 3.9 per cent in September, its first increase in three years. Related Article Energy Australia clashes with Asian energy giants over gas export crackdown Wall Street traders expect the Fed will keep its short-term rate unchanged at its policy meeting this month, but the odds of a rate increase at the December meeting have jumped to 74.3 per cent from 50.2 per cent a month ago, according to data from the CME Group. On Friday, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh offered no fresh signals about potential interest rate policy moves by the Fed while attending a meeting of financial leaders in Bangkok. Elsewhere in the market, shares in Tesla fell 2.1 per cent after the electric vehicle company unveiled a new model of its Roadster sports car that can thrust itself up in the air.



Alcoa rose 2.5 per cent and The Travelers Cos. gained 1.5 per cent after the companies reported quarterly results that topped Wall Street forecasts. Expectations are high for growth in profits from all kinds of companies this reporting season, which began in earnest this week. That’s what’s allowed U.S. stocks to set records despite high inflation and the many other worries weighing on Wall Street. All told, the S&P 500 fell 84.62 points to 7,659.44. The Dow dropped 175.28 points to 52,002.41, and the Nasdaq declined 572.99 points to close at 26,140.03. In energy markets, oil prices remained elevated as the global oil supply continues to be under pressure without a deal between the U.S. and Iran to end the Iran war. Brent crude, the international standard, jumped 3.7 per cent to settle at $US109.86 per barrel. That is up from around $US72 a barrel in late February before the start of the war. Brent climbed into triple digits last month, the first time since July.



The national average for gasoline is at $US4.33 a gallon on Friday, according to AAA. While that’s lower than the $US4.37 a gallon that it averaged last month, it’s sharply higher than the $US3.06 a gallon from a year ago. Oil remains well-supported as uncertainties surrounding the situation in the Middle East and concerns over oil flows in the Strait of Hormuz had the market “pricing in a significant risk premium,” ING commodities strategists Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey wrote in a commentary. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Macron addresses nation after riots, looting as Trump says ‘France is burning’
World.content:
Breaking WorldEuropeProtests Macron addresses nation after riots, looting as Trump says ‘France is burning’ David Crowe October 19, 2026 — 5:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Paris: Protesters clashed with police for a second day of chaos in major French cities after massive rallies descended into violence and looting over the weekend, sparking anger at the rioters and an argument among national leaders. French President Emmanuel Macron condemned the violence in an emergency address to the nation on Sunday night (Monday AEDT) amid a political row over whether the national government did enough to prevent the destruction. Limoges protesters set fire to the town hall in Limoges Haute-Vienne in the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region of France. Hans Lucas via AFP The violence began on Saturday after 550,000 people attended rallies to protest about the cost of living and school standards, with masked rioters setting fire to cars and buildings, including the historic town hall in the city of Limoges, which was largely destroyed. On Sunday, police fired tear gas at protesters in central Paris during a series of confrontations as the authorities sought to arrest suspects and disperse large crowds.



Fires were lit on the streets around the Place de la Republique when protesters tried to set up barricades, triggering a response from the police to assert control of the streets. While the tear gas forced protesters to retreat quickly along the streets around the square, it did not prevent them from regrouping in new locations to try to challenge the authorities. “France is burning!” US President Donald Trump declared on social media on Sunday. Macron prepares to address the nation. Bloomberg “The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country. Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!”



Trump’s comment followed a similar warning from US Vice President JD Vance on Saturday night. “Western liberals imported the Third World into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion,” said Vance. Fires burn in the street in central Paris on Sunday. AP Photo/Emma Da Silva “They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility.” Speaking to the nation, the French leader pledged action on education concerns, saying ministers were already working to improve schools, but also outlined tough measures against violence.



Macron said gatherings would be prohibited around major public buildings if necessary to keep the peace, and urged politicians and trade unions to condemn the violence and call for calm, a challenge to left-wing figures who support the protests. A charred car near Place de la Republique the day after protests. AP Photo/Emma Da Silva He also highlighted the danger of political division when the nation is due to choose its next president in March and April. (Macron has served two terms and cannot run.) “To all those who tell you today that the urgent thing to do is to take to the streets, to demonstrate, and to sow disorder – with the ultimate goal of damaging the Republic and hijacking the debate – I say this: the choices for the future that you, and all of us, will have to make in six months are vital”. Protests spiral



The protests began last month as rallies over school quality and have featured a broad variety of young French people, many of them attending peaceful demonstrations to call for more spending on teachers and basic school facilities. But the footage of the looting on Saturday night included young men of migrant backgrounds and intensified a debate over the link between the mob violence and migration. Protesters vandalise a retail store during a demonstration near Place de la République in Paris. Getty Images The protests led to about 2000 arrests across the country, while the government said about 600 police were injured. France is engulfed in an argument over the weekend riots and social cohesion after progressive politician Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of political party France Unbowed, repeatedly endorsed the protest rallies in recent weeks.



Mélenchon, who is running for president in the elections due in March and April next year, joined the rallies last Saturday. Related Article Analysis

Protests Flames, tear gas and stun grenades: How a stoush over classrooms and toilets exploded into violent mass protests On Sunday, he argued the protest movement was driven by genuine grievances over real issues, saying that people could no longer bear the high cost of living. “The situation for high school students and college students is hellish. It is the widespread suffering that lies at the heart of the situation.” Mélenchon called on Macron to freeze prices to address the social emergency, abolish the current system that dictates how school students get into university – a key complaint among protesters – and set aside €10 billion ($16 billion) for education.



He also called for public compensation for shop owners who suffered from damage and looting on the weekend. But the left-wing stance has drawn rebukes from rivals such as Marine Le Pen, who leads the right-wing National Rally and is seeking the presidency next year on a platform of cutting migration, affirming traditional French values and cutting welfare spending. “You saw yesterday our cities, our streets, our country, battered, mistreated, ransacked,” Le Pen said on Sunday night (Monday, AEDT) “We are living through a profound crisis of trust, of authority that poses a threat to democracy. This observation must alert us: our country is caught in a vice, or even taken hostage, between violence and powerlessness.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: The mercy dash to save a tiny, hairy creature from the brink of extinction
World.content:
Exclusive EnvironmentConservationEndangered species The mercy dash to save a tiny, hairy creature from the brink of extinction Caitlin Fitzsimmons October 19, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In a tiny gully on a tiny island in the vast Pacific Ocean lives a tiny creature found nowhere else on the planet. In August, a crack anti-extinction team flew to Norfolk Island in a last-ditch bid to save the rare animal – a critically endangered snail that is smaller than a pinky fingernail and covered with yellow fuzz. The endangered Fanulena imitatrix, the Norfolk Island hairy snail. Audrey Richardson Dr Isabel Hyman, a malacologist from the Australian Museum, has spent her career studying snails. Her eyes light up when she describes the little gastropod and its “beautiful golden hairs”.



“They’ve got a little domed shell, and they’re quite small, only about seven millimetres across in shell width,” Hyman said. “There are ribs on the shell and from every rib, there are little fine hairs that come out from the shell. We’re not sure exactly what the function of the hairs is, but in other species with hairy shells, it’s often to do with moving around in a really moist environment.” Meet the Norfolk Island hairy snail (Fanulena imitatrix). Its only known home is a 10-20 square-metre patch of rainforest in Selwyn Reserve, land owned by the federal government on the western side of Norfolk Island. Here, where pine trees grow in the rainforest, the mysterious mollusc lives under the bark of fallen branches and logs on the forest floor. But the hairy snails are under threat from feral rats and chickens, invasive Argentine ants and the pesticide used to control the ants, and the drying effects of climate change. Norfolk Island Regional Council has found the ants in the reserve, but refrained from spraying for fear of wiping out the snails. Dr Isabel Hyman, research scientist with Australian Museum, in Selwyn Reserve on Norfolk Island. Audrey Richardson



The Norfolk Island hairy snail likes the pine litter on the forest floor. Audrey Richardson The population has plummeted. In August last year, timed surveys found 68 live hairy snails. That dropped to 50 by November, 12 in February this year, and four in May, using the same methodology. The number of empty shells climbed, in a sign of increased mortality. Concerned, Hyman asked for a more thorough search. The comprehensive survey, conducted by national park ranger Sam Burridge from Parks Australia, Western Sydney University researcher James Roberts, and Simon Brown from Taronga Zoo in late July, found just 24 live specimens in about two hours. The snail’s spiralling decline prompted a mercy dash to save the species – within a month, Hyman and Taronga zookeeper Tarryn Williams Clow were on a plane to retrieve specimens for a breeding program, accompanied by this masthead. A PhD project will study whether the feral chickens are preying on Norfolk Island’s endangered snails. Audrey Richardson



Tarryn Williams Clow, zookeeper at Taronga Zoo, stayed on the island for two weeks refining the habitat and diet with the surrogate species. Audrey Richardson Dr Isabel Hyman from the Australian Museum and zookeeper Tarryn Williams Clow from Taronga Zoo in Hundred Acres Reserve, looking for specimens of Fanulena insculpta, a close relative of the hairy snail. Audrey Richardson This followed a successful release of another rare snail endemic to Norfolk Island – the Campbell’s keeled glass-snail (Advena campbellii) – after a captive breeding program at Taronga Zoo from 2021 to 2025. The project took several years of trial and error to ensure the snails would both survive and reproduce. Related Article Wildlife The aphrodisiac that unlocked the secret sex life of snails “When we first brought our previous species into the zoo, we were very aware that it was some of the very last remaining of its species,” Williams Clow said. “There was a nervousness that any changes we made within their habitat may be detrimental to their survival, so we approached it very cautiously, and sometimes maybe too cautiously.”



The mission to save the hairy snail aims to move faster, so the team has also collected specimens of small sculptured glass-snails (Fanulena insculpta), a closely related species that is widespread on Norfolk Island. This species will be used as a surrogate, allowing the Taronga zookeepers to trial changes to habitat, humidity and diet with lower stakes. “They’re kind of the little guinea pigs, but they’re going to play a really important role with how our target species goes,” Williams Clow said. Tarryn Williams Clow from Taronga Zoo, left, and Dr Isabel Hyman from the Australian Museum with the surrogate species in the “snail shack” on Norfolk Island. Audrey Richardson Fanulena insculpta, a closely related species of snail that will be used to test changes to habitat and diet. Audrey Richardson In late August, the team discovered 20 live hairy snails in a timed survey and 73 in the comprehensive search, providing more reason for optimism than the previous month.



Nearly two weeks later, Williams Clow took 30 hairy snails back to Taronga for the breeding program, along with about 20 of the surrogates. All snails have adapted well and started to give birth to live young, she said. Norfolk Island, a rocky outcrop about 1500 kilometres east of the Australian mainland, is known for its marine biodiversity but is also a critically important global hotspot for land snails. Burridge said there were about 60 unique snail species recorded on the island. “We’ve got other snail species that only exist in palm forests, and other snails that only exist arboreally in the trees,” Burridge said. “There is a large range of native tree species here on Norfolk Island, and that is reflected as well in the habitats that the snails like themselves.”



The hairy snails are part of a genus endemic to the island. Of the six original species, three were extinct and Fanulena imitatrix was the rarest of the remaining three, Hyman said. Related Article Sharks The strange story of Norfolk Island’s super-sized sharks Hyman said the snails played a key role in the ecosystem, breaking down the leaf litter and providing food to other native animals. Caitlin Fitzsimmons and Audrey Richardson travelled to Norfolk Island as guests of the Australian Museum. Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Love fast food? The dietitian’s go-to orders for a higher protein, lower-calorie hit
World.content:
Tips & adviceDietitian’s guide Love fast food? The dietitian’s go-to orders for a higher protein, lower-calorie hit Yes, you can still have your takeaway Mexican, charcoal chicken and burgers without the side of guilt. Just keep an eye on the creeping fat and carbs. Susie Burrell October 19, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A



Life is busy, and sometimes lunch or dinner on the run is unavoidable. And that’s okay. A growing range of higher-protein meal options heavily marketed by fast food chains can make it seem like there are plenty of good options, nutritionally. But often there’s a high-fat, processed-carb catch. The key is being able to cut through the fine print to identify the healthier menu items. Typical fast food menu items tend to pack in more fat and processed carbohydrate from white bread, rice, wraps and fries, compared to lean protein and fresh salad ingredients. For example, a fast-food meal deal with a large burger, fries and soft drink or a fried chicken meal may contain up to 1000 calories, for as little as 20g of protein. Ideally, a well-balanced, calorie-controlled meal, even from a fast food outlet, will offer 400 to 600 calories and at least 30 to 40g of lean protein from chicken breast, salmon or tuna, lean mince or vegetarian options such as tofu, with minimal fried ingredients or added sauces, which pile on the calories. With this in mind, here are some of the more nutritious fast food options, with higher protein and calorie control a priority. Charcoal chicken at El Jannah. Marco Del Grande



Charcoal chicken The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up The charcoal chicken craze continues to grow, but tasty as it may be, that crispy skinned, highly seasoned bird is neither overly high in protein, nor especially healthy, being high in fat and calories. Rather, if the goal is to maximise your protein intake, seek out grilled breast meat options, and order extra salad rather than high-fat chips and dip. El Jannah Grilled chicken burger

One of the lightest options. Ask for no mayo to further reduce calories.

408 cal / 30g protein Chargrill Charlie’s



Pulled chicken wrap

Ditching the aioli will significantly lower the calorie load.

708 cal/ 46g protein Nando’s Portuguese chicken. Portuguese chicken Slightly different to charcoal chicken options as these are typically cooked butterflied and with a tasty marinade. While the overall sodium content tends to be on the high side, there are a few good higher protein, calorie-controlled options if you stick to chicken strips and are fussy with the sides. Oporto



Double fillet Oprego burger

You can lighten the calorie load by opting for a single fillet option, but this will also take the protein down to 25g.

590 cal / 41g protein Nando’s PERinaise classic burger or wrap

A satisfying flame-grilled chicken option which helps to keep the fat and calories under control.

496 cal / 41g protein Bowls and burritos from Zambrero’s. Mexican



Mexican can be a great option, simply because it is one of the few cuisines that offer vegetables and salad as a regular part of menu items. Whether you opt for a burrito, naked bowl or tacos, you can get a protein-packed fix of meats and vegetables relatively easily. For the best high protein, lower fat options, go for naked-style bowls, chicken strips and salads − and go easy on the extra cheese, guacamole, sour cream and chips. Guzman y Gomez Mini grilled chicken burrito

A burrito in a bowl, not a wrap, means you get all the salad, vegies and meat, minus a lot of fat and calories from extra sauces, rice and bread.

521 cal / 29g protein



Subway: pick the six-inch sub and choose a chicken filling. Rebecca Hallas Burgers and sandwiches Burgers tend to be made with higher fat meats and lashings of high-fat sauces and mayo, which typically meals they contain upwards of 800 to 1000 calories for as little as 20 to 30g of protein. Grill’d It may appear to be healthier, but be aware that the salads and burgers made using lower-carb buns can still pack a serious calorie punch.

Not only does this grilled option contain a decent serve of chicken breast, but also plenty of fresh salad on a better quality bun than the average burger, meaning you get more than 40g of protein for just over 400 calories, which works out at about half the calories and double the protein of the average fast food burger.

435 cal / 41g protein Subway While there are plenty of options marketed as high in protein, with 40 to 50g of protein per sandwich, these tend to be the long 12-inch subs which can also have up to 1000 calories per serve. Opt for 6-inchers instead. Chicken Protein Wrap

World.title: Friends used to tell me to avoid this suburb at night. Then I moved there
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I was at the KFC across the road from the plaza recently and a woman was waiting for her food with us in this busy store. She had most of the waiting area to herself. Her fidgeting and verbal ticks signalled: keep your distance. It was difficult to know her age. I suspect she was in her mid-20s, yet the face and eyes looked like they had seen way too much for such tender years. The only spare seat was near her, and it was from this vantage point that I saw her spill her drink, spoiling some of her meal. She threw the bottle and wept. I was leaving at this stage and decided to put my unopened can of drink on her table. She saw me for the first time and her eyes were a mystery. There was confusion. Did she not recognise kindness? I think this was the case. What I saw was coldness and probably suspicion. So I left the can and exited without a word. Inala is great; however, occasional sobering encounters such as this do leave a mark. Inala’s KFC on Inala Avenue and Jonquil Street. Morgan Roberts I’m new to Inala, and I love it. Morgan Roberts Growing up in Central Queensland and on a cattle farm, my world was monocultural, and the fare was steak and three veg, every night. Moving to the inner west of Brisbane in the early 1990s, life took on a new, heady mix of sounds and smells.



Settling into the lifestyle of a cab driver, I received a few words of wisdom from the older hands that I mostly ignored. One message that stuck with me though was: avoid Inala at night. The fruit and vegetable markets. Morgan Roberts Inala Fish Market in the Inala Civic Centre, adjacent to the plaza. Morgan Roberts You won’t get fish at prices like this in Taringa. Morgan Roberts This was my first hearing of the word “Inala” and because of the advice, it seemed to be a scary unknown I didn’t need in my life. I did, however, bravely venture to the Inala Plaza during daytime, and it was a sensory assault. Unfamiliar languages, foreign faces, food I did not recognise: enough to send this country boy scurrying back to the relative safety of Taringa. Life has taken many twists and turns since then, and early this year, I was faced with the prospect of living in Inala. Fifteen minutes from work, comparatively well-priced: a lot of boxes were ticked. Unconfirmed opinions from decades earlier still resonated, but were pushed aside to embrace a new chapter.



The diversity in the suburb has to be experienced to be fully appreciated. Some of the best people I have ever met call 4077 home. I have seen generosity and kindness. Often this generosity comes from people who have little or nothing to give, but they look and want to help anyway. There are also the desperately unfortunate who are fighting an often losing the battle with drugs. It is easy to go about your business without interacting with any of this, and most do. It takes some serious tunnel vision not to see, though. Lunchtime at Pho An Dien. Morgan Roberts You can practically smell the lemongrass. Morgan Roberts Quan Nhu restaurant at closing time. Morgan Roberts Much of the melting pot which is Inala comes together in the plaza. It is the hub of the community, parking is at a premium, and no matter the time, the lanes and corridors are heaving with a broad cross-section of humanity. The exteriors are home to fresh seafood, along with fruit and vegetable markets. It is loud, and interesting to watch the vendors and customers frantically going about their business.



In the outdoor square, the dominant scene is a large group of elderly Asian gentlemen playing a board game I don’t recognise. They never leave; the game never finishes. These men are fixtures. I don’t know their stories. What is clear though is that they are very much at home – and they are not to be interrupted. The square at Inala Plaza where people eat, gather and play Chinese chess. Morgan Roberts Huong Trinh at Minh Tan Bakery. Markus Ravik A day in Inala will rarely be boring. Morgan Roberts The suburb has won me over. Morgan Roberts The variety of foods is a delight. Lebanese, Korean, Chinese and Japanese are all here, but Vietnamese is naturally the star, given the state’s largest Vietnamese community lives here. Pho, bun bo hue, and the banh mi look, smell and taste amazing, and it feels a million miles from my childhood days of eating a different version of beef every day. A day in Inala will rarely be boring, and there is a community here with a lot of pride. Yes, some of the negative stereotypes may be true, yet some of the best people in the world are here, and it has quickly taken me by the heart.

World.title: ‘Long reads’ and ‘frothy fun’ in store as Sydney Festival 2027 unveiled
World.content:
CultureTheatreSydney Festival ‘Long reads’ and ‘frothy fun’ in store as Sydney Festival 2027 unveiled Michaela Boland October 19, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The 2027 Sydney Festival will include a nod to wellness culture with an outdoor installation of old cars transformed into saunas, cold plunges and spas, free for public use. If that is a sentence you never expected to read, that makes two of us. Sydney Festival Director Kris Nelson in one of the old cars that will be turned into a spa experience during the festival in Barangaroo. Janie Barrett Upon reflection the waynapuni pools public bathhouse, to be created by industrial designer Benjamin Paul, working with First Nations teenagers, and installed in Barangaroo Reserve from January 7 to 25, is quintessentially Sydney Festival. Since it began, Sydney’s annual arts jamboree has demonstrated a knack for reflecting our city back to us and public bathing is certainly having a moment.



At the first Sydney Festival in 1977, during the craft era, Haymarket was transformed into a bustling arts and crafts market. Nelson says ‘long reads’ are important, but fun party nights are also a big part of festival programming. Janie Barrett A decade later, 14 bands were on the line-up for an overnight Twelve-Hour Rockathon at Sydney Entertainment Centre, and who can forget Festival First Night from 2008-2012, which drew 250,000 people to the centre of Sydney during the GFC, when we all really needed a party. Artistic director Kris Nelson’s second Sydney Festival boasts a huge contemporary dance program, Dance Reflections, backed by high-end French jewellery house Van Cleef & Arpels and the return of First Nations-led multi-arts strand Blak Out. Among the highlights outside of these programs is a new show from comedian Hannah Gadsby, American clown Spencer Novich and free dance event, The Party, at the Cutaway.



Nelson frames his programming style through the prism of summer beach reading. “It’s equal parts fluff, pulp and big heavy reads, and there’s something about that in a summer program that I want,” he says. “I want a frothy fun party or a great gig night, as much as I want something that is like the long read.” Fulfilling that slot is Irish company Dead Centre, which will transform Ukrainian poet Ilya Kaminsky’s poetry into a contemporary drama wherein a soldier shoots a deaf boy who can’t hear his orders, the next day, the townspeople are deaf. “It’s heavy and it’s beautiful. It’s an allegory, a protest,” Nelson says.



The Ballet du Grand Théâtre de Genève will bring choreographer Rachid Ouramdane’s Outsider to Sydney Festival 2027. Gregory Batardon It is also the closest the 2027 program comes to engaging with the current febrile geopolitical climate. “Lots of people in the program are touched by what’s happening in the world, it’s a program that’s engaged in our times,” Nelson says. Dance Reflections is an ongoing international festival overseen by former New York City Ballet dancer Serge Laurent, who gathers some of the world’s premier dance troupes into curated programs staged in varying combinations since 2022 in nine cities, from London to Shanghai. The 10th iteration in Sydney will present a physical theatre smorgasbord of 13 different shows at venues across Sydney and a dozen dance workshops at Sydney Dance Company.



France’s Rachid Ouramdane has devised an aerial work wherein 20 dancers and four extreme sports athletes will be suspended by tightropes and thrown through space at the Cutaway Barangaroo. Famed choreographer Anne Teresa de Keersmaeker and Morocco’s Radouan Mriziga will collaborate on Together at Carriageworks, a reimagining of Vivaldi’s The Four Seasons. A decade after her death, Trisha Brown’s company will perform Roof Piece at the Art Gallery NSW. The world premiere of Ngurragabu, a major new work exploring an environmental apocalypse from Australia’s pan-national First Nations dance company Marrugeku has been included in the program. Marrugeku’s ensemble of First Nations, Filipino and Melanesian dancers will perform within a monumental mangrove forest being devised by visual artist Abdul-Rahman Abdullah.



Up Late with Bianca Hunt will consist of conversations with artists and cultural leaders. Arts festivals at their best showcase incredible international artists alongside new Australian works, inspiring audiences and artists and seeding potential ongoing collaborations. Laurent is non-committal about Marrugeku being included in future international Dance Reflections programs. “With artists you have to know each other, it’s a story each time,” he says. His curatorial approach is to provide a platform for artists from different backgrounds. Budjerah will be performing Donny Hathaway songs at the Metro Theatre for Black and Blues. Paul Harris



“Dance Reflections is a way to bring together very diverse artists [with] a very strong common point. They are researchers trying to find their own voice, so it’s quite eclectic, but in fact very consistent.” Marrugeku’s artistic co-director Dalisa Pigram has a similar approach to choreography. “We have nine artists spanning regions of maritime knowledge, including the Melanesian and Torres Straits, Singapore and East Indonesia and on the mainland Bardi Jawi and Nyaru knowledges within the region of the Kimberley.” Ancient saltwater knowledge systems have a lot to offer us as we contemplate melting ice caps and increased precipitation, she says. “I’m not a choreographer at the front asking people to move in certain ways, we have an approach that’s inspired by what moves the dancer,” she says.



MO’JU will be channelling the music of Bill Withers for Black and Blues. Justin McManus First Nations programming head Aidan Rowlingson has expanded the festival’s established Blak Out program to include a music series, Black and Blues. “I love the [concept of] First Nations musicians taking on their favourite soul blues artists at the Metro Theatre,” Nelson says. ARIA Award-winner Budjerah will channel Donny Hathaway, Wiradyuri/Filipinx artist MO’JU will conjure the music of Bill Withers and Etta James will be celebrated by Jamaican/Arrernte artist SOLCHLD. “Expect a sense of familiarity and discovery,” Nelson says.



Emily in Sydney will present another opportunity to see one of our most recognisable artists anew. The curated exhibition of paintings by Emily Kame Kngwarreye, drawn largely from private Sydney collections, will be on at S. H. Ervin Gallery. Up Late with Bianca Hunt at Belvoir St Theatre will consist of conversations with artists and cultural leaders. Wiradjuri Yuin actor Angeline Penrith will return for the third year with Redfern Renaissance, a series of performance readings and discussions about the revolutionaries and activism of Redfern’s National Black Theatre in the 1970s. Sydney Festival runs from January 7–25, 2027. Tickets go on sale Thursday, October 22 at sydneyfestival.org.au, with 10,000 prime seats available from $49 or less across all ticketed shows.

World.title: Spender and Chalmers’ reform adviser back GST change to offset tax cuts
World.content:
PoliticsFederalFederal budget Spender and Chalmers’ reform adviser back GST change to offset tax cuts Paul Sakkal October 19, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A leading member of Treasurer Jim Chalmers’ economic advisory panel and MP Allegra Spender have separately raised the alarm on high levels of state and federal spending and called for a GST hike to pay for tax cuts for workers. The Grattan Institute, an influential independent think-tank, has come out in favour of a tax mix switch at a time of near-record tax and spending levels under the Albanese government. Federal ministers and backbenchers have become concerned about inflation and productivity in recent weeks as tension has emerged between Chalmers and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. Anthony Albanese and Jim Chalmers in question time last Wednesday. Alex Ellinghausen In a report to be released on Monday, Grattan chief executive Aruna Sathanapally urges politicians to raise the GST from 10 to 15 per cent and expand it to include all types of food, raising $76 billion per year. The think tank says $33 billion should be used to cut income taxes for lower- and middle-income workers while $25 billion should be put to boosting JobSeeker, pensions and rent assistance. Sathanapally, who Chalmers picked for his economic reform roundtable last year, called for fiscal rules to force profligate state governments to curb spending as the RBA threatens more rate rises to reduce demand that is partly fuelled by government spending.



“There are no easy paths back to budget sustainability. But with smarter spending decisions and a tax system that raises sufficient revenue to care for our ageing population, both current and future generations can be better off,” Sathanapally said, adding that lower-income families would be left about $8000 a year better off under the proposed changes. Related Article Political leadership In a funk: How economic pain is straining the PM and treasurer’s relationship The institute says state government spending has grown even more quickly than the Commonwealth’s. Federal spending has still grown “substantially”, its report states, but Australia’s credit rating has remained steady while Queensland, Victoria, Tasmania and the ACT have all experienced rating downgrades. The think tank’s intervention in the economic debate adds to recent calls for tax reform from former Coalition ministers Josh Frydenberg and Mathias Cormann, both of whom argue for change to the GST, and Labor figures Bill Kelty, Paul Keating and Lachlan Harris. Albanese and Chalmers have been under internal and external pressure to address Australia’s economic problems. Their political headache was exacerbated by an own goal on credit card surcharges, which lead to the tax office refusing to accept credit card payments.



Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino admitted on Sunday that ministers knew the ATO might stop accepting credit cards as far back as July. Before Mulino’s comments in an interview on ABC’s Insiders, the government only emphasised its knowledge about the ATO’s final decision, which it learned in September. “In July, the government became aware that the ATO was looking at options,” Mulino said. Wentworth MP Allegra Spender. Alex Ellinghausen Only about 5 per cent of taxpayers pay bills via credit card, but the move has added to arguments from the business lobby that Labor is not in touch with the concerns of business owners. Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson seized on Mulino failing to rule out 60 or 70 per cent tax rates for small businesses who use trusts and pay into a “bucket company”. These firms will be incentivised to rearrange their structure.



On the proposal for fiscal rules, Wilson said: “They are like a diet and we know Labor can’t kick their spending addiction.” Spender, a tax reform advocate who was also on Chalmers’ reform panel last year, said fiscal rules were needed at the federal level, going beyond the Grattan Institute’s call for restrictions at state level. Rules that would cap expenditure and tax were proposed by former Treasury secretary Ken Henry in last year’s roundtable, but Chalmers has argued against arbitrary caps. “The government should adopt stronger fiscal rules, particularly to manage expenditure. Spending has grown too fast particularly for a high-inflation environment and we’re not bringing it back quick enough,” Spender said. “The GST should be on the table, as must better resource taxation, digital taxes and a shift from stamp duty to land taxes.”



Related Article Letters Difficult times aren’t a sign of schism at the top of the ALP ACCI chief executive Andrew McKellar also supported fiscal rules in that meeting, and said on Sunday they were necessary. Frydenberg, the former Coalition treasurer mulling a return to politics, called for debate on the GST last week but was quickly slapped down by Opposition Leader Angus Taylor. Australia’s income tax rates are relatively high by international standards and the highest rate kicks in at relatively low-income threshold. Many tax experts say that income taxes reduce the incentive to work, whereas people notice less if the GST creates slightly higher prices, creating fewer distortions and a more efficient system. The Grattan report says that the Commonwealth should use the higher GST take to cut back on the ballooning level of grant funding to the states in education and health, which are often subject to political dispute and compromise.



Under Grattan’s proposals, a low-income single-parent family who rents would pay nearly $80 more in GST per week but receive $202 in extra welfare and receive a $27 income tax cut, leaving them $150 a week better off. A higher-income working family would pay about $162 more in tax because they consume more and pay more GST. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Trump urges Israelis to re-elect ‘Great Warrior’ Netanyahu in stunning intervention
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastIsraeli-Palestinian conflict Trump urges Israelis to re-elect ‘Great Warrior’ Netanyahu in stunning intervention Matthew Knott Updated October 19, 2026 — 5:51am ,first published 5:02am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Tel Aviv: US President Donald Trump has made a stunning late intervention in Israel’s elections, endorsing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in a move the veteran leader hopes could help him to remain in office. Netanyahu had eagerly sought the official endorsement of his longtime ally while his rivals had urged Trump to refrain from interfering in the contest, reflecting the belief that the president’s verdict could affect the outcome. Trump’s once warm relationship with Netanyahu has appeared to cool since their war in Iran began to falter, raising doubts about whether he would endorse a candidate. Trump and Netanyahu have formed a close bond. AP But, in an enthusiastic social media post peppered with capital letters and exclamation points, Trump delivered his “Complete and Total Endorsement” of Netanyahu, urging Israelis to support him when they vote on October 27.



“Bibi Netanyahu has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump said in his post, uploaded in the early hours of Monday Australian time. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict ‘I’m afraid of civil war’: The voters travelling from Australia to vote against Netanyahu “If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so. “Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself. Despite all of that, he has endured and, in fact, he has thrived!” The US is Israel’s most important security partner, and Trump remains popular in Israel, despite the war in Iran failing to deliver a decisive blow against the regime in Tehran.



Trump did not meet Netanyahu during the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month, triggering speculation of a snub, but the longstanding and close relationship between the two conservative leaders ultimately overcame any friction and frustration. Related Article World elections Israel is having its most important elections in history. How do they work? Netanyahu has viewed his close relationship with Trump and his ability to influence the American leader – cultivated over two presidential terms – as a key advantage over his rivals for the prime ministership. However, Nadav Pollak, a lecturer on Middle East affairs at Reichman University, questioned whether Trump’s endorsement would shift voter perceptions of a polarising figure who was first elected in 1996 and in power for most of the time since 2009. “Not sure that a Trump endorsement is worth so much for him right now,” he said on social media.



Describing Trump as “my dear friend Donald”, Netanyahu responded in a video, effusively thanking him for his “extraordinary” endorsement and praising Trump as the best friend Israel had ever had in the White House. The world, Israel and the Jewish people have been lucky to have a leader of “such clarity, consistency, conviction and courage” as Trump, Netanyahu said. Trump has made a habit of endorsing world leaders running for election in his second stint in office, including Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Colombian conservative candidate, Abelardo de la Espriella. Netanyahu has faced grim poll numbers for most of his past term in office, and many thought his career was over after he failed to prevent the worst security failure in Israel’s history: the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack, during which about 1200 people were killed or taken hostage. But his coalition government, the most right-wing in Israeli history, saw out a full term.



The latest average of three main television polls by Israeli newspaper Haaretz shows the bloc of parties aligned with Netanyahu on 51 seats, the anti-Netanyahu Zionist bloc also on 51 seats and 18 seats unaligned to either bloc, suggesting an extremely tight result. World.title: ASX set to dip, tech stocks weigh on Wall Street
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to dip, tech stocks weigh on Wall Street Alex Veiga October 19, 2026 — 5:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
