A broad sell-off in technology companies pulled stocks lower on Wall Street, capping off the market’s worst week since late June. The S&P 500 fell 1.1 per cent. Its roughly 2 per cent drop for the week wiped out its gains from last week, when it set an all-time high. Wall Street wrapped up its worst week since June with more losses. Bloomberg The Nasdaq composite, which is heavily weighted with technology stocks, sank 2.1 per cent and posted its first weekly loss in five weeks and its worst since June. The Dow Jones Industrial Average held up better, closing 0.3 per cent lower. The Australian sharemarket is set to edge lower, with futures pointing to a loss of 11 points or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.57¢.



Slightly more than half of the stocks in the S&P 500 fell, but all but seven of the 75 stocks in the index’s tech sector closed lower. Among the biggest decliners were chip companies, reflecting mounting worries about how long the frenzy over the AI buildout will last. Related Article Analysis

Sharemarket ‘Only the sharks are left’: The $388 billion change shaking up the sharemarket Micron Technology fell 5.6 per cent, Advanced Micro Devices dropped 6 per cent, Broadcom lost 4.5 per cent and Intel gave up 5.8 per cent. Among the other tech companies that finished in the red were Meta, which fell 3.7 per cent, and Google parent Alphabet, which dropped 2.5 per cent. It’s been a choppy week for chipmakers and other big tech stocks central to the artificial intelligence industry. Investors are now worried that the companies, which have relied on debt markets to finance an investment spree into their technology, may not be able to keep borrowing and spending as heavily with yields in bond markets worldwide recently climbing to their highest levels in years.



Netflix’s stock fell 2.9 per cent a day after the company announced that Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria will be replaced by Peter Rice. The news comes just days after Netflix said that it plans to lay off about 6 per cent of its workforce, amounting to nearly 1,000 positions. Energy stocks held up better than most. Exxon rose 2.5 per cent and Chevron added 2.6 per cent. European and Asian markets closed higher. In the bond market, Treasury yields held relatively steady. The yield on the 10-year Treasury slipped to 5.09 per cent from 5.10 per cent late Thursday. It had topped 5.30 per cent earlier this month and touched its highest level since 2002 because of worries about high inflation, signals of a strong U.S. economy and other factors. Yields are down despite reports this week showing that inflation at the consumer and wholesale level rose more in the U.S. than economists expected.



The reports could persuade the inflation-fighters at the Federal Reserve to hike their key interest rate before the end of this year. The central bank increased its key interest rate by a quarter-point to about 3.9 per cent in September, its first increase in three years. Related Article Energy Australia clashes with Asian energy giants over gas export crackdown Wall Street traders expect the Fed will keep its short-term rate unchanged at its policy meeting this month, but the odds of a rate increase at the December meeting have jumped to 74.3 per cent from 50.2 per cent a month ago, according to data from the CME Group. On Friday, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh offered no fresh signals about potential interest rate policy moves by the Fed while attending a meeting of financial leaders in Bangkok. Elsewhere in the market, shares in Tesla fell 2.1 per cent after the electric vehicle company unveiled a new model of its Roadster sports car that can thrust itself up in the air.



Alcoa rose 2.5 per cent and The Travelers Cos. gained 1.5 per cent after the companies reported quarterly results that topped Wall Street forecasts. Expectations are high for growth in profits from all kinds of companies this reporting season, which began in earnest this week. That’s what’s allowed U.S. stocks to set records despite high inflation and the many other worries weighing on Wall Street. All told, the S&P 500 fell 84.62 points to 7,659.44. The Dow dropped 175.28 points to 52,002.41, and the Nasdaq declined 572.99 points to close at 26,140.03. In energy markets, oil prices remained elevated as the global oil supply continues to be under pressure without a deal between the U.S. and Iran to end the Iran war. Brent crude, the international standard, jumped 3.7 per cent to settle at $US109.86 per barrel. That is up from around $US72 a barrel in late February before the start of the war. Brent climbed into triple digits last month, the first time since July.



The national average for gasoline is at $US4.33 a gallon on Friday, according to AAA. While that’s lower than the $US4.37 a gallon that it averaged last month, it’s sharply higher than the $US3.06 a gallon from a year ago. Oil remains well-supported as uncertainties surrounding the situation in the Middle East and concerns over oil flows in the Strait of Hormuz had the market “pricing in a significant risk premium,” ING commodities strategists Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey wrote in a commentary. World.content:
Breaking WorldEuropeProtests Macron addresses nation after riots, looting as Trump says ‘France is burning’ David Crowe October 19, 2026 — 5:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Paris: Protesters clashed with police for a second day of chaos in major French cities after massive rallies descended into violence and looting over the weekend, sparking anger at the rioters and an argument among national leaders. French President Emmanuel Macron condemned the violence in an emergency address to the nation on Sunday night (Monday AEDT) amid a political row over whether the national government did enough to prevent the destruction. Limoges protesters set fire to the town hall in Limoges Haute-Vienne in the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region of France. Hans Lucas via AFP The violence began on Saturday after 550,000 people attended rallies to protest about the cost of living and school standards, with masked rioters setting fire to cars and buildings, including the historic town hall in the city of Limoges, which was largely destroyed. On Sunday, police fired tear gas at protesters in central Paris during a series of confrontations as the authorities sought to arrest suspects and disperse large crowds.



Fires were lit on the streets around the Place de la Republique when protesters tried to set up barricades, triggering a response from the police to assert control of the streets. While the tear gas forced protesters to retreat quickly along the streets around the square, it did not prevent them from regrouping in new locations to try to challenge the authorities. “France is burning!” US President Donald Trump declared on social media on Sunday. Macron prepares to address the nation. Bloomberg “The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country. Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!”



Trump’s comment followed a similar warning from US Vice President JD Vance on Saturday night. “Western liberals imported the Third World into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion,” said Vance. Fires burn in the street in central Paris on Sunday. AP Photo/Emma Da Silva “They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility.” Speaking to the nation, the French leader pledged action on education concerns, saying ministers were already working to improve schools, but also outlined tough measures against violence.



Macron said gatherings would be prohibited around major public buildings if necessary to keep the peace, and urged politicians and trade unions to condemn the violence and call for calm, a challenge to left-wing figures who support the protests. A charred car near Place de la Republique the day after protests. AP Photo/Emma Da Silva He also highlighted the danger of political division when the nation is due to choose its next president in March and April. (Macron has served two terms and cannot run.) “To all those who tell you today that the urgent thing to do is to take to the streets, to demonstrate, and to sow disorder – with the ultimate goal of damaging the Republic and hijacking the debate – I say this: the choices for the future that you, and all of us, will have to make in six months are vital”. Protests spiral



The protests began last month as rallies over school quality and have featured a broad variety of young French people, many of them attending peaceful demonstrations to call for more spending on teachers and basic school facilities. But the footage of the looting on Saturday night included young men of migrant backgrounds and intensified a debate over the link between the mob violence and migration. Protesters vandalise a retail store during a demonstration near Place de la République in Paris. Getty Images The protests led to about 2000 arrests across the country, while the government said about 600 police were injured. France is engulfed in an argument over the weekend riots and social cohesion after progressive politician Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of political party France Unbowed, repeatedly endorsed the protest rallies in recent weeks.



Mélenchon, who is running for president in the elections due in March and April next year, joined the rallies last Saturday. Related Article Analysis

Protests Flames, tear gas and stun grenades: How a stoush over classrooms and toilets exploded into violent mass protests On Sunday, he argued the protest movement was driven by genuine grievances over real issues, saying that people could no longer bear the high cost of living. “The situation for high school students and college students is hellish. It is the widespread suffering that lies at the heart of the situation.” Mélenchon called on Macron to freeze prices to address the social emergency, abolish the current system that dictates how school students get into university – a key complaint among protesters – and set aside €10 billion ($16 billion) for education.



He also called for public compensation for shop owners who suffered from damage and looting on the weekend. But the left-wing stance has drawn rebukes from rivals such as Marine Le Pen, who leads the right-wing National Rally and is seeking the presidency next year on a platform of cutting migration, affirming traditional French values and cutting welfare spending. “You saw yesterday our cities, our streets, our country, battered, mistreated, ransacked,” Le Pen said on Sunday night (Monday, AEDT) “We are living through a profound crisis of trust, of authority that poses a threat to democracy. This observation must alert us: our country is caught in a vice, or even taken hostage, between violence and powerlessness.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: The mercy dash to save a tiny, hairy creature from the brink of extinction
World.content:
Exclusive EnvironmentConservationEndangered species The mercy dash to save a tiny, hairy creature from the brink of extinction Caitlin Fitzsimmons October 19, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In a tiny gully on a tiny island in the vast Pacific Ocean lives a tiny creature found nowhere else on the planet. In August, a crack anti-extinction team flew to Norfolk Island in a last-ditch bid to save the rare animal – a critically endangered snail that is smaller than a pinky fingernail and covered with yellow fuzz. The endangered Fanulena imitatrix, the Norfolk Island hairy snail. Audrey Richardson Dr Isabel Hyman, a malacologist from the Australian Museum, has spent her career studying snails. Her eyes light up when she describes the little gastropod and its “beautiful golden hairs”.



“They’ve got a little domed shell, and they’re quite small, only about seven millimetres across in shell width,” Hyman said. “There are ribs on the shell and from every rib, there are little fine hairs that come out from the shell. We’re not sure exactly what the function of the hairs is, but in other species with hairy shells, it’s often to do with moving around in a really moist environment.” Meet the Norfolk Island hairy snail (Fanulena imitatrix). Its only known home is a 10-20 square-metre patch of rainforest in Selwyn Reserve, land owned by the federal government on the western side of Norfolk Island. Here, where pine trees grow in the rainforest, the mysterious mollusc lives under the bark of fallen branches and logs on the forest floor. But the hairy snails are under threat from feral rats and chickens, invasive Argentine ants and the pesticide used to control the ants, and the drying effects of climate change. Norfolk Island Regional Council has found the ants in the reserve, but refrained from spraying for fear of wiping out the snails. Dr Isabel Hyman, research scientist with Australian Museum, in Selwyn Reserve on Norfolk Island. Audrey Richardson



The Norfolk Island hairy snail likes the pine litter on the forest floor. Audrey Richardson The population has plummeted. In August last year, timed surveys found 68 live hairy snails. That dropped to 50 by November, 12 in February this year, and four in May, using the same methodology. The number of empty shells climbed, in a sign of increased mortality. Concerned, Hyman asked for a more thorough search. The comprehensive survey, conducted by national park ranger Sam Burridge from Parks Australia, Western Sydney University researcher James Roberts, and Simon Brown from Taronga Zoo in late July, found just 24 live specimens in about two hours. The snail’s spiralling decline prompted a mercy dash to save the species – within a month, Hyman and Taronga zookeeper Tarryn Williams Clow were on a plane to retrieve specimens for a breeding program, accompanied by this masthead. A PhD project will study whether the feral chickens are preying on Norfolk Island’s endangered snails. Audrey Richardson



Tarryn Williams Clow, zookeeper at Taronga Zoo, stayed on the island for two weeks refining the habitat and diet with the surrogate species. Audrey Richardson Dr Isabel Hyman from the Australian Museum and zookeeper Tarryn Williams Clow from Taronga Zoo in Hundred Acres Reserve, looking for specimens of Fanulena insculpta, a close relative of the hairy snail. Audrey Richardson This followed a successful release of another rare snail endemic to Norfolk Island – the Campbell’s keeled glass-snail (Advena campbellii) – after a captive breeding program at Taronga Zoo from 2021 to 2025. The project took several years of trial and error to ensure the snails would both survive and reproduce. Related Article Wildlife The aphrodisiac that unlocked the secret sex life of snails “When we first brought our previous species into the zoo, we were very aware that it was some of the very last remaining of its species,” Williams Clow said. “There was a nervousness that any changes we made within their habitat may be detrimental to their survival, so we approached it very cautiously, and sometimes maybe too cautiously.”



The mission to save the hairy snail aims to move faster, so the team has also collected specimens of small sculptured glass-snails (Fanulena insculpta), a closely related species that is widespread on Norfolk Island. This species will be used as a surrogate, allowing the Taronga zookeepers to trial changes to habitat, humidity and diet with lower stakes. “They’re kind of the little guinea pigs, but they’re going to play a really important role with how our target species goes,” Williams Clow said. Tarryn Williams Clow from Taronga Zoo, left, and Dr Isabel Hyman from the Australian Museum with the surrogate species in the “snail shack” on Norfolk Island. Audrey Richardson Fanulena insculpta, a closely related species of snail that will be used to test changes to habitat and diet. Audrey Richardson In late August, the team discovered 20 live hairy snails in a timed survey and 73 in the comprehensive search, providing more reason for optimism than the previous month.



Nearly two weeks later, Williams Clow took 30 hairy snails back to Taronga for the breeding program, along with about 20 of the surrogates. All snails have adapted well and started to give birth to live young, she said. Norfolk Island, a rocky outcrop about 1500 kilometres east of the Australian mainland, is known for its marine biodiversity but is also a critically important global hotspot for land snails. Burridge said there were about 60 unique snail species recorded on the island. “We’ve got other snail species that only exist in palm forests, and other snails that only exist arboreally in the trees,” Burridge said. “There is a large range of native tree species here on Norfolk Island, and that is reflected as well in the habitats that the snails like themselves.”



The hairy snails are part of a genus endemic to the island. Of the six original species, three were extinct and Fanulena imitatrix was the rarest of the remaining three, Hyman said. Related Article Sharks The strange story of Norfolk Island’s super-sized sharks Hyman said the snails played a key role in the ecosystem, breaking down the leaf litter and providing food to other native animals. Caitlin Fitzsimmons and Audrey Richardson travelled to Norfolk Island as guests of the Australian Museum. Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Love fast food? The dietitian’s go-to orders for a higher protein, lower-calorie hit
World.content:
Tips & adviceDietitian’s guide Love fast food? The dietitian’s go-to orders for a higher protein, lower-calorie hit Yes, you can still have your takeaway Mexican, charcoal chicken and burgers without the side of guilt. Just keep an eye on the creeping fat and carbs. Susie Burrell October 19, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A



Life is busy, and sometimes lunch or dinner on the run is unavoidable. And that’s okay. A growing range of higher-protein meal options heavily marketed by fast food chains can make it seem like there are plenty of good options, nutritionally. But often there’s a high-fat, processed-carb catch. The key is being able to cut through the fine print to identify the healthier menu items. Typical fast food menu items tend to pack in more fat and processed carbohydrate from white bread, rice, wraps and fries, compared to lean protein and fresh salad ingredients. For example, a fast-food meal deal with a large burger, fries and soft drink or a fried chicken meal may contain up to 1000 calories, for as little as 20g of protein. Ideally, a well-balanced, calorie-controlled meal, even from a fast food outlet, will offer 400 to 600 calories and at least 30 to 40g of lean protein from chicken breast, salmon or tuna, lean mince or vegetarian options such as tofu, with minimal fried ingredients or added sauces, which pile on the calories. With this in mind, here are some of the more nutritious fast food options, with higher protein and calorie control a priority. Charcoal chicken at El Jannah. Marco Del Grande



Charcoal chicken The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up The charcoal chicken craze continues to grow, but tasty as it may be, that crispy skinned, highly seasoned bird is neither overly high in protein, nor especially healthy, being high in fat and calories. Rather, if the goal is to maximise your protein intake, seek out grilled breast meat options, and order extra salad rather than high-fat chips and dip. El Jannah Grilled chicken burger

One of the lightest options. Ask for no mayo to further reduce calories.

408 cal / 30g protein Chargrill Charlie’s



Pulled chicken wrap

Ditching the aioli will significantly lower the calorie load.

708 cal/ 46g protein Nando’s Portuguese chicken. Portuguese chicken Slightly different to charcoal chicken options as these are typically cooked butterflied and with a tasty marinade. While the overall sodium content tends to be on the high side, there are a few good higher protein, calorie-controlled options if you stick to chicken strips and are fussy with the sides. Oporto



Double fillet Oprego burger

You can lighten the calorie load by opting for a single fillet option, but this will also take the protein down to 25g.

590 cal / 41g protein Nando’s PERinaise classic burger or wrap

A satisfying flame-grilled chicken option which helps to keep the fat and calories under control.

496 cal / 41g protein Bowls and burritos from Zambrero’s. Mexican



Mexican can be a great option, simply because it is one of the few cuisines that offer vegetables and salad as a regular part of menu items. Whether you opt for a burrito, naked bowl or tacos, you can get a protein-packed fix of meats and vegetables relatively easily. For the best high protein, lower fat options, go for naked-style bowls, chicken strips and salads − and go easy on the extra cheese, guacamole, sour cream and chips. Guzman y Gomez Mini grilled chicken burrito

The best option to keep the calories under control is to order from the “minis” range, and hang back on the extra sour cream, cheese and rice temptations. Choosing chicken brings higher protein and less fat than the shredded meat or mince options.

453cal / 26g protein Zambrero’s Classic bowl (without sauce)

A burrito in a bowl, not a wrap, means you get all the salad, vegies and meat, minus a lot of fat and calories from extra sauces, rice and bread.

521 cal / 29g protein



Subway: pick the six-inch sub and choose a chicken filling. Rebecca Hallas Burgers and sandwiches Burgers tend to be made with higher fat meats and lashings of high-fat sauces and mayo, which typically meals they contain upwards of 800 to 1000 calories for as little as 20 to 30g of protein. Grill’d It may appear to be healthier, but be aware that the salads and burgers made using lower-carb buns can still pack a serious calorie punch.



Hot bird on panini

Not only does this grilled option contain a decent serve of chicken breast, but also plenty of fresh salad on a better quality bun than the average burger, meaning you get more than 40g of protein for just over 400 calories, which works out at about half the calories and double the protein of the average fast food burger.

435 cal / 41g protein Subway While there are plenty of options marketed as high in protein, with 40 to 50g of protein per sandwich, these tend to be the long 12-inch subs which can also have up to 1000 calories per serve. Opt for 6-inchers instead. Chicken Protein Wrap

The wrap range is slightly lower in calories than the more common sub sandwiches and the chicken option is one of the leanest protein choices.

452 cal / 26g protein Korean-Style BBQ Steak 6-inch Sub

One of the best menu items when ordering a traditional Subway sandwich, ask for extra lean steak for an even better option.

390 cal / 26g protein



Betty’s Burgers Grilled Chicken Burger

One of the few grilled at options at Betty’s which means it is significantly lower in fat and calories than other menu items.

396 cal / 32g protein Opt for sashimi over sushi rolls. Michael Woods Sushi and bowls Japanese can be an extremely healthy option, but try to stick to sashimi, miso, edamame and pickled vegetables for more than 30g of protein for just 400 to 500 calories.



Avoid heavy rice-based dishes, including sushi, that add more carbs and calories, and less protein. Choose edamame beans which offer dietary fibre and plant-based protein, and tofu which is naturally high in protein.



Fish Bowl The popular chain’s wide range of menu items makes it easier to find appealing high protein, low-carb options. Chilli chicken bowl with brown rice With a fresh food base and lean poached chicken breast, this is a protein and vegie rich option that can be made even lighter if you swap out the rice for extra veg or edamame.

520cal / 29g protein Yuzu days chicken

World.title: Friends used to tell me to avoid this suburb at night. Then I moved there
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I was at the KFC across the road from the plaza recently and a woman was waiting for her food with us in this busy store. She had most of the waiting area to herself. Her fidgeting and verbal ticks signalled: keep your distance. It was difficult to know her age. I suspect she was in her mid-20s, yet the face and eyes looked like they had seen way too much for such tender years. The only spare seat was near her, and it was from this vantage point that I saw her spill her drink, spoiling some of her meal. She threw the bottle and wept. I was leaving at this stage and decided to put my unopened can of drink on her table. She saw me for the first time and her eyes were a mystery. There was confusion. Did she not recognise kindness? I think this was the case. What I saw was coldness and probably suspicion. So I left the can and exited without a word. Inala is great; however, occasional sobering encounters such as this do leave a mark. Inala’s KFC on Inala Avenue and Jonquil Street. Morgan Roberts I’m new to Inala, and I love it. Morgan Roberts Growing up in Central Queensland and on a cattle farm, my world was monocultural, and the fare was steak and three veg, every night. Moving to the inner west of Brisbane in the early 1990s, life took on a new, heady mix of sounds and smells.



Settling into the lifestyle of a cab driver, I received a few words of wisdom from the older hands that I mostly ignored. One message that stuck with me though was: avoid Inala at night. The fruit and vegetable markets. Morgan Roberts Inala Fish Market in the Inala Civic Centre, adjacent to the plaza. Morgan Roberts You won’t get fish at prices like this in Taringa. Morgan Roberts This was my first hearing of the word “Inala” and because of the advice, it seemed to be a scary unknown I didn’t need in my life. I did, however, bravely venture to the Inala Plaza during daytime, and it was a sensory assault. Unfamiliar languages, foreign faces, food I did not recognise: enough to send this country boy scurrying back to the relative safety of Taringa. Life has taken many twists and turns since then, and early this year, I was faced with the prospect of living in Inala. Fifteen minutes from work, comparatively well-priced: a lot of boxes were ticked. Unconfirmed opinions from decades earlier still resonated, but were pushed aside to embrace a new chapter.



The diversity in the suburb has to be experienced to be fully appreciated. Some of the best people I have ever met call 4077 home. I have seen generosity and kindness. Often this generosity comes from people who have little or nothing to give, but they look and want to help anyway. There are also the desperately unfortunate who are fighting an often losing the battle with drugs. It is easy to go about your business without interacting with any of this, and most do. It takes some serious tunnel vision not to see, though. Lunchtime at Pho An Dien. Morgan Roberts You can practically smell the lemongrass. Morgan Roberts Quan Nhu restaurant at closing time. Morgan Roberts Much of the melting pot which is Inala comes together in the plaza. It is the hub of the community, parking is at a premium, and no matter the time, the lanes and corridors are heaving with a broad cross-section of humanity. The exteriors are home to fresh seafood, along with fruit and vegetable markets. It is loud, and interesting to watch the vendors and customers frantically going about their business.



In the outdoor square, the dominant scene is a large group of elderly Asian gentlemen playing a board game I don’t recognise. They never leave; the game never finishes. These men are fixtures. I don’t know their stories. What is clear though is that they are very much at home – and they are not to be interrupted. The square at Inala Plaza where people eat, gather and play Chinese chess. Morgan Roberts Huong Trinh at Minh Tan Bakery. Markus Ravik A day in Inala will rarely be boring. Morgan Roberts The suburb has won me over. Morgan Roberts The variety of foods is a delight. Lebanese, Korean, Chinese and Japanese are all here, but Vietnamese is naturally the star, given the state’s largest Vietnamese community lives here. Pho, bun bo hue, and the banh mi look, smell and taste amazing, and it feels a million miles from my childhood days of eating a different version of beef every day. A day in Inala will rarely be boring, and there is a community here with a lot of pride. Yes, some of the negative stereotypes may be true, yet some of the best people in the world are here, and it has quickly taken me by the heart.

World.title: Backroads to the Beehive: Coal, politics and division on the West Coast
World.content:
With less than three weeks until Election Day, RNZ's South Island Correspondent Tim Brown and camera operator Louis Dunham have toured Te Waipounamu to hear the good, the bad, and the ugly from the places and people where the political spotlight does not usually shine. They take readers on a journey from the Backroads to the Beehive, starting with the West Coast.

The West Coast's wild ancient forests and vast mineral wealth gave rise to the country's labour movement.

Key figures from Blackball's 1908 miners strike later served in the first Labour government and the West Coast has been a stronghold for the Labour Party since the 1920s, with the region's miners and workers its garrison.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406945480112

The social and economic upheaval of the 1980s rearranged traditional alliances and the coast is now deeply divided.

National has won previously unwinnable West Coast seats three times since 1990, with Maureen Pugh most recently toppling Damien O'Connor by just over a thousand votes in 2023.

National has won the party vote in West Coast-Tasman at every election this century, apart from 2020's Labour landslide.

Moana mechanic David Larkin says it is not hard to figure out why.

Audio player for " RNZ hits the road for Backroads to the Beehive " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2010548%2Fbackroads-to-the-beehive-coal-politics-and-division-on-the-west-coast

RNZ hits the road for Backroads to the Beehive Morning Report Download MP3 7m

"The values of the Labour Party now are nothing like the Labour Party that formed here. Those values have all gone," he says.

Just down the road in Ruru, fisherman Allan Rooney says he was Labour supporter until the party lost its way in the 1980s.

"It's a party of people that have never had a frickin' job. Look at 'em," he says during a break from weed-whacking his lush green lawns.

Pugh is stepping down in November and Labour stalwart O'Connor is instead running in the Otago and South Canterbury electorate of Waitaki after 33 years representing the coast.

Katie Milne, a West Coast dairy farmer and former Federated Farmers president, is standing for National and Rory Paterson, a North Canterbury-based teacher, is representing Labour.

Rooney is dismissive of Labour's chances.

Ruru fisherman Allan Rooney used to support Labour but now supports New Zealand First and Act. RNZ / Louis Dunham

"They didn't go so well last election. The guy that's standing here doesn't even friggin' live here but he's thinking about moving here if he gets in," he says.

Rooney is also dismissive of Chris Hipkins, only offering a husky chortle when asked for an opinion about the Labour leader. But he is no fan of National leader Christopher Luxon either and plans to back the coalition's minor parties.

"Back to reality is definitely Winston and looking ahead is David Seymour, right now," he says.

"If you'd asked me about ACT five or six years ago I would have started laughing but he has common sense policies."

The coast is full of contrasts.

'I'm not even religious but I get down on my knees and I pray that we get these clowns out of there'

Blackball local Matthew Howard - who prefers to be known as Mr Howard - does not see it that way.

"People have just got stupider and lost the point of why we had a Labour Party in the first place," he says dismissively when asked for an assessment of Labour's waning fortunes.

"We had to have a Labour Party so that we got decent working conditions, decent wages, people could have a decent home to live in and a decent life.

"The people in National and ACT, they don't want that for everybody. They only want that for a few."

Howard saves his most stinging criticism for New Zealand First.

"Winston is an old clown who should bugger off with his overfed mate," he says.

RNZ / Louis Dunham

Howard owns the land on which a large Labour hoarding sits overlooking Blackball's main road and is in no doubt about how he will vote.

"Two ticks Labour all the way down the line. Hopefully they'll save the country from this bunch of absolute clowns we've got destroying it at the moment," he says.

"I'm not even religious but I get down on my knees and I pray that we get these clowns out of there."

Jane Wells, who has lived in Blackball on-and-off for 50 years and formerly ran the pub Formerly The Blackball Hilton, also wants a change in government.

"The government that we've had for the last three years has been the most revolting government we've ever had," she says.

"Everything they say reminds me of the people that they think support them and that's the people with lots of money. They don't give a s*** about the people at the bottom."

As Wells gestures to her great-granddaughter playing on the verandah of her home, she says she wants a better future for New Zealand.

"For the sake of the world we have got to do more as far as the environment and climate change goes," she says.

"We have got to be careful. Canterbury's water - that used to be pure aquifers and it was the talk of the world. With all the dairying, it's just horrific now. It's got so much crap in it that it's dangerous."

Jane Wells and her partner Pat Kennedy have run and started businesses in Blackball. RNZ / Louis Dunham

'I don't feel there is a strong person out there that I could trust to look after my needs'

Young Blackball mother Marie Tippet says neither major party has left her feeling enthused about the election.

"I don't think there's a strong leader in government at all and it's the first time since I turned 18 that I'm actually not sure who I'm going to vote for," she says.

"I don't feel there is a strong person out there that I could trust to look after my needs, my partner's business and his needs, and also my one-year-old daughter's needs. That worries me a bit to feel there isn't a strong backbone in Parliament."

Walking her daughter down the street with nearby hills filled with birdsong and the sun beating down, Tippet appreciates everything she has, although the cost of living is biting hard.

"I would like to think of myself as a nature-lover but I still burn coal in my fire because it's cheap and it's really warm. It's actually all I can afford," she says.

"Coal is still probably king on the West Coast.

"When I see the smoke of the chimneys, I do feel really conflicted because when I take my daughter for a walk I'm concerned about the smell in the air and I know that it's not good. I know that it's not good for me. I know it's definitely not good for her [daughter] and it's not good for her future and the environment. But in terms of where we are able to spend our money to be able to heat our homes it's kind of where we are at."

Blackball mother Marie Tippet doesn't know who to vote for this election. RNZ / Louis Dunham

'If we stop mining for coal, it would devastate Westport'

Back in Moana, Larkin says the economy is broken.

"The problem with the economy in New Zealand at the moment is you don't make money with these," he says, holding up hands black with grease.

"The people who are making the money are sitting at desks or operating computers or doing share trading or whatever, but the people at the bottom of the heap who are actually doing the work are not making money."

Larkin supports mining jobs.

"The bottom line is if we stop mining for coal, they're not going to stop buying coal. It would devastate Westport if you closed the mines up on top of Stockton," he says.

"It gets over-dramatised, the impact that the mining is having on the environment."

Debates over the future of mining are heated.

Permits for Stockton Mine expire next year and a plan to expand mining into the Denniston Plateau has stalled through the fast-track approvals process.

Bathurst Resources wants to extend its Stockton mine near Westport. Supplied/ Bathurst Resources

Rooney says outsiders are the problem.

"The Denniston Plateau, for example, I've worked up there when I was a linesman. It's a s*** hole. It's all rock. They couldn't even bury people up there," he says.

"If you take that out of the equation, you're going to bugger Westport. We've already got 85 percent of the West Coast in DOC [Department of Conservation] land. How much more do they want?"

'They've taken the money from here'

Semi-retired Taylorville plumber John Tennent supports New Zealand First's plan to impose greater royalties on extractive mining.

"Put royalties on the coal and some of the gold and some of the timber, the natural resources that come from the coast and put it back into the communities from Haast to Karamea," he says.

Former mining town Dobson is across the bridge, overlooking Māwheranui/Grey River.

Brian Aynsley has lived there for most of his life since his father relocated the family after the Blackball Coal Mine closed in 1964.

Brian Aynsley has lived in Blackball and Dobson for most of his life. RNZ / Louis Dunham

He is a pensioner but supplements his income with farming because he would otherwise not survive financially.

"With insurance and I've got two lots of rates and I'm up for $10,000. What do you get - 15 on the pension? You can't live on five," he says.

He says too many have taken from the coast without thinking about its people and their sacrifice.

"If Shane Jones and Winston can get some sort of levy, you'll see a hell of an improvement," he says.

"DOC does a good job but they don't pay rates, they don't contribute to the roads and a lot of the tourists here are going to DOC estate and looking at it and their contribution is virtually nil.

World.title: Explainer: What are the US midterms and why are they a big deal?
World.content:
Explainer - American voters will soon get one more chance to cast their verdict on US President Donald Trump - quite possibly for the final time.

The US midterm elections are coming up on 3 November (expect results to come in after midday 4 November NZ time), and millions of dollars are being spent as candidates sprint around the country seeking votes. Early voting has already begun in many states.

But what exactly is being voted on? Here's what to look out for, and what Trump may face after results come in.

What are the midterms anyway?

They're a key part of the American political process where, halfway through a president's four-year term, voters get to pick their local congressional representatives and many senators and governors.

All 435 members of the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 Senate seats are up for election this year, as well as 36 state governors.

The midterms are usually seen as a referendum on how a president's term is going and determine whether the US Congress is led by the Democrat or Republican party.

RNZ's Tim Watkin, executive producer of podcasts and series, is a keen observer of the American political scene.

The midterms are the biggest deal for the final two years of Trump's presidency, he said.

VINCENT FEURAY / AFP

"It will change the balance of power in America."

If Trump's Republican party loses badly, "It will give Democrats the power to question Trump in a way he's never been questioned this term," Watkin said.

Explain to me again how America's Congress works?

We can try.

Instead of a Parliament, they've got Congress, which consists of two separate chambers - the House of Representatives and the "upper house", the Senate. Bills must pass both houses to become law.

The House has 435 members who are divided proportionally among the 50 states based on their population (so bustling California has the most reps, 52, while wide-open Wyoming has only one).

The Senate has 100 members and every state, regardless of size, has just two senators. The US Vice-President acts as a 101st member to break any 50-50 ties in the Senate.

The US Senate is considered more prestigious and powerful. Representatives only serve two-year terms, while senators serve six-year terms.

The current makeup of the House and Senate is very tight - there's a single seat majority in the House and six seats in the Senate. They've both been under Republican control since the 2024 election.

How big a deal is this for Trump?

Trump has operated the last two years under a Republican House and Senate and broadly exercised executive power with little pushback from fellow Republicans. That could well change after 4 November.

During his first term, when Democrats ran the House of Representatives, Trump was impeached twice, but both times the Republican-controlled Senate failed to convict him, which would have forcibly removed him from office.

US President Donald Trump speaks at a rally in Clarksville, Tennessee. ROBERTO SCHMIDT / AFP

If Democrats control both houses of Congress, look for an awful lot more talk about investigating alleged corruption, and perhaps even another go at impeachment.

While Trump has made lots of allusions to seeking a third term - which is illegal under the US Constitution - the reality is that an 82-year-old Trump probably won't be running again in 2028.

"It's Trump's last election," Watkin said.

"Once the midterm's done, especially if he loses badly, the next two years Republicans are going to be running a mile from him, and he's going to be standing there going, 'But I'm Donald Trump'."

US Speaker of the House Mike Johnson hits the gavel during a Joint Meeting of Congress in the House Chamber at the US Capitol in April 2026. SAUL LOEB / AFP

Is history on Trump's side?

Not really.

Whether or not one supports Trump's policies, history is against him.

Over the last 80 years, the president's party has lost seats in the midterms 18 times out of 20.

"A sitting president gets held to account for not achieving the promises they made a year and a half ago," Watkin said.

It's almost inevitable that any US president, by the last few years of a second term, starts to enter "lame duck" status. Trump, who has defied a lot of political gravity in his career, is racing into that timeframe.

The current New York Times average of several political polls finds Trump's approval rating sits around 37 percent.

Watkin said that a faltering economy and the impact of the Iran war have hit many Trump supporters hard.

"Those men who have been his base are now pissed off because they're now paying [US] $6 for diesel in their trucks.

"He was supposed to be the businessman."

Current predictions by the influential nonpartisan Cook Political Report and others foresee the Democrats likely to take back control of the House of Representatives, while the Senate will be a closer call.

"They've given up in the House," Watkin said. "The idea that they could hold on to majorities is gone. The Senate's the thing that people need to watch."

And of course, nobody really knows how Trump will react if his party loses badly at the midterms.

"Assumably - he will claim corruption, right?" Watkin said.

Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico with supporters at the conclusion of a campaign rally in Kerrville, Texas. BRANDON BELL / AFP

What are the big races to watch out for?

Despite all 435 seats in the House of Representatives being up for election, only a handful are truly considered competitive. The New York Times and Cook Political Report currently list just 21 seats as toss-ups that could go either way, and another 21 as leaning somewhat towards Republicans or Democrats.

Because the margin of the current majority is so slim in the House, it would take only a handful of seats to flip to give Democrats control.

The Senate currently has a 53-47 Republican majority (two independent senators caucus with Democrats), and will be harder to flip. Democrats need to win 51 seats to achieve a majority as Vice President JD Vance can cast votes to break 50-50 ties in the current House.

The Senate, with its smaller membership, longer terms and more powerful legislative powers, is key. If Democrats capture the House and Senate, Republican Trump will lose any leverage to get his legislative priorities passed. CNN has ranked 10 seats that may flip in 2026.

There are several big Senate races to watch:

Texas - Democrat James Talarico is facing Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton. Normally Texas is deep red, but Paxton has been dogged by a series of scandals including a fraud indictment and impeachment. Polls show Talarico doing better than Democrats usually do there, but Republicans are pouring money into what will end up one of the most expensive Senate races of all time.

Maine - Democrat nominee Graham Platner's campaign imploded and replacement Troy Jackson hasn't quite gone so viral, but incumbent Republican Susan Collins has been in office since 1997 and is in danger due to the Trump backlash.

Republian US Senator Susan Collins campaigns in Fryeburg, Maine. SPENCER PLATT / AFP

Ohio - A popular former senator, Democrat Sherrod Brown, is running to get back into office against Republican Jon Husted, who replaced JD Vance when he became vice president.

Michigan - One of the most combative races is between Republican Mike Rogers and progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who could become the first Muslim US senator.

Alaska - Remote Alaska would seem as Republican as they come but former Democrat Congresswoman Mary Peltola, the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, is running a close campaign against Republican Dan Sullivan.

Other important races are in North Carolina, Kansas, New Hampshire and Iowa. Many of the tight races are in states Trump won by a wide margin in 2024.

So are the Republicans doomed?

Well, we live in unprecedented times, and few political observers would've ever predicted most of what's happened in America in the past 10 years. America's deep political polarisation isn't likely to be resolved no matter what happens at the midterms.

Two big things still work in the Republicans' favour - the controversial redistricting of multiple states' congressional districts, which has seen both Republican and Democrat-controlled states trying to rejig electorates to ensure their party gets more votes. Republicans are generally seen as having created more possible seats for their party.

The second is money, which is the petrol running the US political engine. At least US$10 billion is believed to have been spent so far on advertising, by political parties as well as by big-pocketed donors such as the AI industry and Elon Musk.

Republicans are believed to still have more than US$1 billion to spend, and will pour money into places such as Texas' Senate race.

This year's election will break records, the nonprofit Brennan Center For Justice told The Washington Post recently.

"Having tons of money doesn't guarantee victory," US government ethics expert Meredith McGehee told the Post. "But the contrary is true - not having 'enough' does guarantee defeat. And no one ever really knows what 'enough' is."

And in case you're already dreading the endless carnival of the 2028 US presidential election, bad news - the race to succeed Trump will pretty much begin the day after the midterms. Expect candidates from both parties to start announcing their plans by early 2027.

Once again, when are those midterms?

World.title: Police AI: Investigator uploads 350,000 lines of audio in risky workaround
World.content:
Audio player for " Documents reveal risky police use of AI translation tools " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/crime-and-justice/2010561%2Fpolice-ai-investigator-uploads-350-000-lines-of-audio-in-risky-workaround

Documents reveal risky police use of AI translation tools Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Police investigators misused artificial intelligence (AI) translation tools numerous times in seriously risky ways, offical documents show.

One investigator put 350,000 lines of Chinese audio data into Google Translate, an unsecured platform for police.

The breaches came after initial success using the Whisper AI system to translate Chinese language phone interceptions collected in the investigation into the body found in a bag in Gulf Harbour in July 2024.

This turned into a six-month test, but officers ignored a ban on using the AI to transcribe English audio, so use was discontinued after the test.

The documents show investigators were under so much pressure, they began taking evidence home to process it on personal devices or upload it to unsecured services such as Google Translate.

This risked "exposing confidential information", said a police report.

The breaches pushed police to re-introduce Whisper AI a year ago. It is not clear how its use is being audited.

Ten hours versus 750 hours

Police have promised to be careful and transparent about introducing new high-tech crime-fighting tools.

Internally, they say they are keeping the public informed "to the greatest extent possible". They declined an interview request from RNZ on this story.

The 2024 Auckland cult investigation into the killing of Shulai Wang - dubbed Operation Parade - seized on Whisper to help officers who felt they had to act quickly, according to hundreds of pages of police emails and reports newly released to RNZ under the Official Information Act.

"The driver for this is that the investigation have advised there is now a significantly elevated flight risk of a number of targets," an email read.

Officers had intercepted calls and had 250 hours of audio from more than 2500 files in Mandarin Chinese.

"The investigation has interpreters, but their time is limited."

It took Whisper 10 hours to do what would have taken a person about 750 hours and $50,000 to do. It helped pin down which conversations and messages, or parts of them, to focus on. All evidence had to be validated later by qualified human translators.

After this, automated translation began to spread to other teams.

But police staff who did transcriptions heard about it and became alarmed about what it meant for their jobs.

A formal test of Whisper AI was set up, with controls, such as not using it to transcribe English audio, or on Māori or Pacific languages.

Breaking the rules

Six months later, an evaluation found officers had broken the no-English rule many times.

In one case, Waikato investigators not only broke that rule but used AI to generate a document for disclosure in legal proceedings. Not using AI for evidentiary purposes is a theme in all the papers.

Police encountered trouble controlling its use. "The ongoing compliance is beyond current resourcing," the High Tech Crime Group warned early on.

The breaches posed serious security and privacy risks, Intercept and Technology Operations manager Detective Inspector Stu Mills said later in evaluating the test.

But he also said they were "unfortunate but not unexpected" due to the pressure on investigators.

Mills warned that unless police adopted a permanent approved AI tool, investigators would turn to unsecured translation platforms.

Despite this, Whisper was dropped in March 2025, except in a few one-off cases that needed three lots of signoff. Several of those cases were to transcribe English language from hundreds of prison phonecalls.

'Running for years damaging the police's reputation'

The papers show investigators used AI anyway.

In one case, they scraped cellphones for WeChat threads using Cellebrite, a phone-cracking tool invented by ex-Israeli intelligence operatives. Police use of Cellebrite has been well publicised, while WeChat is China's leading messaging and social media service.

They then put 350,000 lines of the Chinese audio on to Google Translate.

"This needs to be done to enable us to grade this in a timely manner and determine what's important to the investigation to be able to be passed to the translators for translation and transcribing of the audio files," they emailed.

"Without being to grade the data in a timely manner this investigation will have the potential of running for years damaging the police's reputation (trust and confidence, etc)."

The investigation is not named, but was likely a financial one in 2025.

'We are exhausted'

The on-again-off-again access to Whisper had tech and investigation leaders at odds.

"Man what a process trying to get this approved!" wrote a Western Bay of Plenty detective constable in July 2025.

A High Tech Crime Group manager protested about "constant change" in the rules overseen by the Tech Assurance group. "We are exhausted."

Mills told tech leaders debating what to do: "The lack of a secure, approved solution has driven staff toward these risky workarounds, highlighting the urgent need for a trusted in house capability."

They worked to streamline access to Whisper, then to get it re-adopted.

By October last year, the AI translator was being incorporated into the other tech they already used - Cellebrite.

World.title: Behind the push to get more young people on the electoral roll
World.content:
Audio player for " Youth campaign pushes to get more young people enrolled " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2009402%2Fbehind-the-push-to-get-more-young-people-on-the-electoral-roll

Youth campaign pushes to get more young people enrolled Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Who says getting enrolled to vote has to be boring?

Music, dancing, free kai and fresh haircuts are helping a rangatahi-led campaign get young people thinking about the power of their vote.

On Saturday, Ōtara Town Centre became a hub of sound system culture and community as On A Roll brought its nationwide youth-led campaign to South Auckland.

The kaupapa has been travelling to communities across Aotearoa with low voter enrolment, using music and community events to encourage rangatahi and whānau to enrol ahead of the 7 November general election.

With more than 166,000 people aged 18 to 24 not enrolled to vote, campaign director Chantelle Conroy (Te Ātiawa) told RNZ that young people have the numbers to make a real difference.

Audio player for " Parties hit campaign trail as voter enrolment deadline nears " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2009402%2Fbehind-the-push-to-get-more-young-people-on-the-electoral-roll

Parties hit campaign trail as voter enrolment deadline nears Morning Report Download MP3 3m

"Rangatahi, 18 to 24 year olds, are the second biggest voting population in Aotearoa, so if we could mobilise that population to get enrolled to vote, imagine the cultural, political and social landscape that Aotearoa would have."

The kaupapa has helped with more than 10,000 enrolments so far.

On a Roll has been travelling to communities across Aotearoa with low voter enrolment, using music and community events to encourage rangatahi and whānau to enrol ahead of the November 7 general election. Layla Bailey-McDowell / RNZ

Bringing the kaupapa to the people

The Ōtara mobilisation was one of five stops on the Sound System hīkoi, with similar events taking place around the country.

Alongside music and performances, the event offered a way for people to connect with the campaign in a relaxed, community-focused setting.

Conroy said the goal is to make enrolment feel accessible, while reminding young people that participating in the political system can have an impact on their own lives and the lives of their whānau.

On a Roll campaign director Chantelle Conroy (Te Ātiawa) says young people have the numbers to make a real difference. Layla Bailey-McDowell / RNZ

"They do have the power and they have the power to change Aotearoa for the better and also for them and their whānau and their communities.

"It's so important to ensure that rangatahi are participating in the system to make sure that their voices and everything that is important to them and their whānau and communities are heard."

Aotearoa's first wāhine reggae sound in Aotearoa, Bigbada Boom Sound System, operated by Ariki Brightwell has been travelling the motu with On a Roll. Layla Bailey-McDowell / RNZ

Sound system culture with a bigger purpose

Two of the sound systems involved in the nationwide hīkoi are Christchurch-based KAWAI and Aotearoa's first wāhine reggae sound in Aotearoa, Bigbada Boom Sound System.

KAWAI founder and operator Tūrāhui Payne (Kāi Tahu, Ngāti Tūwharetoa, Waikato), 22, said the kaupapa is about reminding young people that their voices matter.

"I think for a long time we haven't really felt like we have a lot of power. Or a lot of say at least," he said.

"Prior to this kaupapa I wasn't really someone who really cared about enrolling, to be very honest."

He said a lack of hope, alongside disruptions such as the Covid-19 pandemic cutting short his high school experience, had contributed to that feeling.

Payne said On A Roll is an opportunity to remind rangatahi they can have a say in the direction of the country.

"It's really important because it just reminds young people that we do have a say. And it is important to make sure that that's heard."

KAWAI founder and operator Tūrāhui Payne (right) says it's important to remind young people that their voices matter. Layla Bailey-McDowell / RNZ

Ariki Brightwell (Ngāti Toa Rangatira, Rongowhakaata), also known as Queen Big Punch, is the founder of Bigbada Boom, which creates space for wāhine and femme artists in reggae sound system culture.

Brightwell told RNZ that music is a powerful way to connect people with wider struggles for rights and representation.

She points to the influence of reggae legend Bob Marley on Māori communities.

"As Māori, as tangata whenua, Bob Marley is a messiah to us," she said.

"He uplifted our people when we were at our lowest. He taught us that we weren't alone in the world fighting for our rights as tangata whenua as well."

Supplied / On A Roll

Brightwell said that same sense of collective strength is important when it comes to voting.

"It's important to have a say in our country. Because, you know, I think the way things go, if you're not involved, then, you have no say and can't have a part of it.

"The more people that enrol to vote, the more that can happen, the more things can shift and change to, I would say, more accurately represent the majority of our citizens of Aotearoa New Zealand."

Brightwell said a new generation was beginning to rise up, and their participation will help shape what comes next.

"Their way of thinking and their whakaaro is going to dictate the next step of our country in its direction. And I think it's incredibly important they get on the roll."

In Ōtara, a free festival called ŌRO is brought together South Auckland artists, community groups and rangatahi, with voter enrolment alongside music, kai and other activities. Layla Bailey-McDowell / RNZ

A vote for the next generation

Eighteen-year-old Charity is preparing to vote for the first time. She said young people deserved to have their experiences represented in decisions about the country's future.

"I think it's important because young people should get their voices heard, not just elders. And the elders will never know what the younger generation is going through."

18-year-old Charity is preparing to vote for the first time. Layla Bailey-McDowell / RNZ

Ōtara rangatahi Pūmanawa Rawiri said voting was also a responsibility to the people and places young Māori were connected to.

"From a Māori perspective, an indigenous perspective, it's our obligation to stay connected to the whenua and everything that's happening on our whenua."

Layla Bailey-McDowell / RNZ

Making your voice heard

South Auckland band LEAO also performed at the event, following their historical win at the 2026 APRA Silver Scroll Awards.

Their song 'LALELEI' which celebrates 'aiga ma atunu'u' (family and homeland) and captures themes of distance, yearning and commitment to the fa'asamoa (the 'Samoan way') won New Zealand's top songwriting award.

Frontman David Feauai-Afaese encouraged whānau to vote, saying it offered an accessible way for people to influence decisions that can sometimes feel distant from their everyday lives.

LEAO is the musical project of Auckland-born Samoan musician David Feauai-Afaese. Their Samoan love song 'LALELEI' made history at the 2026 Silver Scroll Awards winning New Zealand’s most prestigious songwriting award. Layla Bailey-McDowell / RNZ

"Being able to vote is an actionable and accessible way in which we can have a voice."

He said it was important for communities that were disproportionately represented in negative statistics to have a say in what they wanted for the future.

Eligible voters must enrol or update their details by midnight on Sunday, 25 October, before voting begins on Monday, 26 October.

World.title: ADHD diagnosis rule changes still affected by postcode lottery
World.content:
Audio player for " ADHD care remains out of reach for some despite rule changes " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/health/2010434%2Fadhd-diagnosis-rule-changes-still-affected-by-postcode-lottery

ADHD care remains out of reach for some despite rule changes Morning Report Download MP3 2m

The postcode lottery is alive and well for people with ADHD, despite hopes that rule changes allowing family doctors to diagnose and prescribe would make it easier for patients.

In February, GPs were given permission to carry out ADHD assessments, and then prescribe and manage its treatment - a role previously filled by psychiatrists, who charged a lot more for appointments and had longer waitlists.

But uptake was slow. At the time, Royal New Zealand College of General Practitioners president Dr Luke Bradford, told RNZ he would put the number of GPs actively taking on ADHD patients at 15 to 20 percent.

"But that will steadily grow," he said.

In the eight months since the rule change, it had - in some regions more than others.

Many practices still had notices on their website informing patients they were not currently offering ADHD services, as none of their staff had the relevant expertise.

Among those that were, the offerings varied. Some were offering "the full gambit", Bradford said, from assessment, to diagnosis to treatment, while others were happy to take on prescription duties and ongoing medication management after their patient had received a diagnosed elsewhere.

A special interest group set up by the college had by now accumulated more than 500 members, sharing knowledge and upskilling.

"There's always going to be a geographical split," Bradford said. "Northland, we know, is under-resourced in terms of general practitioners, and so the demand on their time is high just from trying to keep the wheels turning, rather than taking on extra services."

Dr Tania Davidson Supplied

Registered clinical psychologist Dr Tania Davidson, who lives and works in the Bay of Islands, said she had moved up from Wellington to work in an area traditionally under-served by the health system, with hopes of forming partnerships with local GPs alongside her privacy practice.

Clinical psychologists were not able to prescribe medication, but they were allowed to conduct ADHD assessments and produce a report with a diagnosis, which could then be taken to a GP.

Davidson said she was concerned by the shortage of affordable in-person appointments for people with ADHD in the Far North.

"I started contacting GP clinics before I came up here even saying, hey, I will do assessments. I'll even come to your clinic to do them," she said.

But she had received little uptake.

"If it's a workload issue, that's what I was trying to help them with - to do the assessment for them."

Luke Bradford from the College of GP's said those relationships would form over time.

"Because it's relatively new to general practice, there is that element of trust that needs to come - are you comfortable with the clinician who's doing the diagnosis work, to be able to then assign your name to the prescription side of things?"

For Adam Currie, one of the first people to receive a prescription on the morning of the rule change, the ongoing prescription process had been quite easy.

"I can get three-month repeat prescriptions, so from a logistical perspective [...] it's been really good."

The most important change had been in his concentration, he said. "I'm able to sit at a desk and write a thesis, or write a long report, and just really get work done."

World.title: Baby Ru's death: Why is it taking so long to hold anyone accountable?
World.content:
This week marks three years since the killing of Lower Hutt toddler Baby Ru. National Crime Correspondent Sam Sherwood spoke with the officer in charge of the investigation about the past three years, where the investigation currently stands, and why it is taking so long to hold anyone accountable.

On Sunday, Baby Ru should be celebrating turning five with his family.

He should be getting ready to start school, meet his teacher and make new friends. Maybe he has a brand new lunch box and backpack.

Tragically, his family will be forced to mark the day without him, but not before they mourn the three-year anniversary of his death.

Thursday marks three years since Baby Ru, officially named Nga Reo Te Huatahi Reremoana Ahipene-Wall, was killed.

Speaking to RNZ, Detective Inspector Nick Pritchard, the officer in charge of the investigation which has now gone on longer than the little boy lived, says a dedicated team is working full-time to bring his family closure.

"They really want to hold those responsible to account."

Ruthless-Empire Ahipene-Wall, known as Baby Ru, died just before his second birthday, on 22 October, after being taken to Hutt Hospital in an unresponsive state. Supplied

Operation Huia

Three people were inside the Poole St, Taitā home on 22 October 2023 when Baby Ru suffered blunt force trauma so severe it fractured his skill.

The three people, who police have said are persons of interest are Rosie Morunga, her then-partner Dylan Ross, and the child's mother, Storm Wall.

Wall - who has repeatedly denied being involved in her son's death - has previously spoken at length with RNZ about what she alleges happened to her son and who she claims killed him.

RNZ is unable to report those allegations.

Neither Morunga nor Ross have spoken to the media since the homicide investigation began.

Speaking to RNZ ahead of the three-year anniversary, Pritchard said there hadn't been any engagement with the trio "for some time", but confirmed they all remained persons of interest, with police "looking at all possibilities in terms of criminal liability".

He says the homicide investigation, dubbed Operation Huia, remains active with a "small dedicated team" working full time with oversight from a senior investigating officer.

"We continue to engage with our Crown solicitor and other forensic experts. It's an ongoing situation where we're working through evidential material, assessing it and assessing the criminal liability of any persons of interest."

Asked how close police are to making an arrest, Pritchard says he can't give any timeframes.

"It's a case where we engaged with Crown quite some time ago. Like us, there's a significant amount of material that they had to review, and from that we've got some other inquiry work and forensic work that we're doing as a result."

RNZ / Mark Papalii

He says he understands how people looking in from the outside can wonder why it is taking so long to make any arrests.

He says it is "relatively common" for such cases to "take quite some time" due to the complexities involved and the large volume of material gathering during the investigations.

"Then obviously the evaluation and analytical stages we go through, seeking our legal advice for these sorts of cases because obviously we have to reach a certain threshold before considering charging any persons.

"So all of that does take time, and then as we get our case independently reviewed, then there will be things that come up that we need to do some further testing on or further work on… we are positive that we're going in the right direction, and we really want to hold those responsible to account."

Pritchard will not say whether police believe more than one person inflicted the fatal injuries, or if they have established why a piece of fabric was around Baby Ru's neck when he arrived at hospital.

He also spoke of the difficulties of a case with no "direct eyewitnesses".

"We've got a little boy who's tragically lost his life, and you know can't tell us exactly what happened… so you have to build a case around that through a wide variety of ways… it's actually building up the story through facts and evidence that can actually speak for the young child."

Asked how much police believe they know about what happened on the day, Pritchard says police have a "good picture… in terms of timeframes and obviously injuries and other aspects of the incident."

'It's not too late'

Three years into the investigation, Pritchard says the team has come a "long way", but says he has "no doubt" there are people out there who have information police need and he urges them to come forward.

He has a message for those responsible.

"It's not too late. Those persons that were responsible, or person, knows what they have done. It's not too late to actually get the conscience to come forward and do the right thing,"

"Whatever the mechanism of force used to cause that injury would have been quite significant. So for somebody to do that and actually not have the conscience to come forward is quite disturbing."

Pritchard says on the anniversary of Baby Ru's death the little boy should have been "thriving".

"It's really challenging because you think about it regularly. You think about how hard this will be, how traumatic this will be on that little boy's whanau.

World.title: Delays and cancellations on the CRL over fire alarm at Karanga-a-hape station
World.content:
A fire alarm at at Karanga-a-hape station is has disrupted trains on the City Rail Link this morning.

East West trains were initially diverted through Parnell, and not stopping at Maungawhau, Karanga-a-Hape and Te Waihorotiu stations.

The East West Line has since returned to the normal route but Auckland Transport said commuters should expect some delays or cancellations.
